query.original_query: foundation model internal representation critical phenomena phase transition universality scaling exponents renormalization

sub_queries.semantic_query: internal representation of critical phenomena, phase transitions, universality, and scaling exponents in foundation models, probing attention and MLP layers for emergent behavior and renormalization group structure
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate the internal representations of critical phenomena and phase transitions within large-scale foundation models, probing attention and MLP layers for emergent signatures of universality and scaling. Using causal probing and activation patching, we analyze how models encode order parameters and correlation lengths across synthetic datasets with known Ising and percolation transitions. Our analysis reveals that attention heads in intermediate layers exhibit sharp changes in activation patterns near critical points, mirroring diverging correlation lengths. We find that MLP layers encode scaling exponents consistent with renormalization group predictions, with feature activations showing power-law decay across model depth. Results show that residual stream representations can be decomposed into coarse-grained variables, suggesting an emergent hierarchical structure analogous to real-space renormalization. Probing across model scales indicates that the fidelity of these representations improves with parameter count, yet the qualitative structure of the learned phase diagram remains consistent. These findings suggest that foundation models spontaneously learn universal features of critical systems, offering a bridge between statistical mechanics and representation learning.

sub_queries.semantic_query: critical phenomena, phase transitions, universality, scaling exponents, and renormalization group theory in complex systems and neural networks
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate critical phenomena and scaling behavior in the dynamics of recurrent neural networks trained on structured datasets. Using Monte Carlo simulations and finite-size scaling analysis, we measure the order parameter and susceptibility across varying network connectivities and training epochs. Results indicate a continuous phase transition between ordered and chaotic regimes, with extracted critical exponents consistent with the universality class of mean-field spin glasses. The divergence of the susceptibility near the critical point supports the hypothesis that the network’s internal representation undergoes a second-order phase transition, analogous to the paramagnetic-to-ferromagnetic transition in equilibrium statistical mechanics. Application of the renormalization group framework reveals relevant and irrelevant perturbations, demonstrating that the system’s macroscopic behavior is governed by a small set of scaling fields. These findings suggest that the principles of universality and scaling extend beyond traditional physical systems, providing a quantitative link between statistical mechanics and the emergent computational properties of neural networks.

papers.title: Phase transition encoded in neural network
papers.research_question: How do temperature-supervised neural networks capture information of phase transition and what physical quantities do they learn?
papers.core_contribution: Temperature-supervised neural networks encode phase transition information in their weights, learning either magnetization or internal energy as features depending on network architecture and prediction accuracy.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks trained to predict temperature encode phase transition information in their weights, and the extracted physical quantity (magnetization or energy) depends on the network architecture and training accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
The fully-connected neural network learns magnetization from input spin configurations, and its weights show a drastic change at the critical temperature, enabling phase transition detection.
The convolutional neural network learns internal energy, achieves higher temperature prediction accuracy, and its weights are proportional to free energy, encoding phase transition information more implicitly.
The phase transition information is captured in the neural network weights even without explicit supervision of phase labels.
The accuracy of temperature prediction is theoretically bounded by the overlap of energy probability distributions at different temperatures.
Convolutional networks perform better because they capture spatial correlations, leading to learning internal energy rather than magnetization.
papers.limitation:
The method may not correctly detect phase transitions driven by different physical mechanisms such as Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) transitions or topological phase transitions.
The fully-connected network only distinguishes between ordered and disordered phases and cannot predict fine-grained temperatures within each phase.
The accuracy of temperature prediction is limited by the overlap of energy distributions at different temperatures in finite systems.
papers.abstract: Abstract We discuss an aspect of neural networks for the purpose of phase transition detection. To this end, we first train the neural network by feeding Ising/Potts configurations with labels of temperature so that it can predict the temperature of the input. We do not explicitly supervise whether the configurations are in the ordered/disordered phase. Nevertheless, we can identify the critical temperature from the parameters (weights and biases) of the trained neural network. We attempt to understand how temperature-supervised neural networks capture information on the phase transition by paying attention to what quantities they learn. Our detailed analyses reveal that they learn different physical quantities depending on how well they are trained. The main observation in this study is how the weights in the trained neural network can have information on the phase transition in addition to temperature.

papers.title: Towards quantifying information flows: relative entropy in deep neural networks and the renormalization group
papers.research_question: How does relative entropy (Kullback-Leibler divergence) behave in renormalization group flows and in deep neural networks as a function of depth, and what are the similarities between the two?
papers.core_contribution: The relative entropy (KL divergence) increases monotonically to a parameter-dependent asymptotic value in both the renormalization group flow of Ising models and in feedforward neural networks as a function of depth, and it is insensitive to the phase structure of either system.
papers.conclusion: Relative entropy provides a useful measure of information flow in both renormalization group and deep neural networks, but it is not sensitive to critical behavior, indicating that more refined probes are needed.
papers.key_findings:
Relative entropy increases monotonically under decimation RG in the 1d and 2d Ising models.
In feedforward neural networks, relative entropy also increases monotonically with depth to an asymptotic value.
The asymptotic value depends on the coupling constant in Ising models and on weight and bias parameters in neural networks.
Relative entropy does not exhibit any change at the critical point of the 2d Ising model or at the phase transition in neural networks.
The monotonic increase in relative entropy confirms the connection with the c-theorem in QFT and may have implications for information maximization methods in machine learning.
papers.limitation: The relative entropy is insensitive to the phase structure of the systems studied, so it cannot capture critical points.
future_direction: Develop more refined probes to fully elucidate the flow of information in these models.
Investigate the implications of the asymptotic behavior for information maximization methods in machine learning and for disentangling compactness and generalizability.
papers.abstract: We investigate the analogy between the renormalization group (RG) and deep neural networks, wherein subsequent layers of neurons are analogous to successive steps along the RG. In particular, we quantify the flow of information by explicitly computing the relative entropy or Kullback-Leibler divergence in both the one- and two-dimensional Ising models under decimation RG, as well as in a feedforward neural network as a function of depth. We observe qualitatively identical behavior characterized by the monotonic increase to a parameter-dependent asymptotic value. On the quantum field theory side, the monotonic increase confirms the connection between the relative entropy and the c-theorem. For the neural networks, the asymptotic behavior may have implications for various information maximization methods in machine learning, as well as for disentangling compactness and generalizability. Furthermore, while both the two-dimensional Ising model and the random neural networks we consider exhibit non-trivial critical points, the relative entropy appears insensitive to the phase structure of either system. In this sense, more refined probes are required in order to fully elucidate the flow of information in these models.

papers.title: Detection of Phase Transition via Convolutional Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Can neural networks detect phase transitions in physical systems without prior knowledge of the order parameter or critical temperature?
papers.core_contribution: A convolutional neural network can detect the phase transition of the 2D Ising model without prior knowledge, and a novel order parameter derived from the network's weight matrix can identify the critical temperature.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks, particularly CNNs, can capture features of phase transitions and can be used to define order parameters that identify critical temperatures in physical systems.
papers.key_findings:
The weight matrix of the trained CNN shows a domain-like structure with a boundary near the critical temperature.
An order parameter Wsum(β) defined from the weight matrix can be used to extract the critical temperature via fitting.
The extracted critical temperatures for different lattice sizes are consistent with the exact value to within 2-8% accuracy.
The CNN's convolutional filters resemble a real-space renormalization group transformation, capturing local magnetization.
A fully connected neural network also detects the phase transition but with less accuracy than the CNN.
future_direction: Applying the neural network design to other statistical models and non-trivial phases.
papers.abstract:
We design a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) which studies correlation
between discretized inverse temperature and spin configuration of 2D Ising
model and show that it can find a feature of the phase transition without
teaching any a priori information for it. We also define a new order parameter
via the CNN and show that it provides well approximated critical inverse
temperature. In addition, we compare the activation functions for convolution
layer and find that the Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) is important to detect the
phase transition of 2D Ising model.

papers.title: Cascade of phase transitions in the training of energy-based models
papers.research_question: How does the Restricted Boltzmann Machine learn features from data, and does it undergo phase transitions during training?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that RBMs learn features through a cascade of second-order phase transitions, each corresponding to the acquisition of a new principal mode of the data distribution.
papers.conclusion: The learning of RBMs occurs through a cascade of phase transitions, providing insight into the feature encoding process in generative models.
papers.key_findings:
The weights grow exponentially in the direction of the principal components of the dataset.
When the weight norm reaches a critical value, the model undergoes a second-order phase transition, splitting the probability distribution into modes.
These phase transitions are in the mean-field universality class, as confirmed by finite-size scaling.
The learning process involves a cascade of such transitions, progressively refining the learned distribution.
The same phenomena are observed in real datasets like MNIST, CelebA, and HGD.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is primarily for RBMs and simplified models; extending to more complex models like Convolutional EBMs is not straightforward.
The Binary-Gaussian RBM cannot reproduce higher-order correlations in data.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to other generative models such as Convolutional Energy-Based Models.
Investigating the implications of phase transitions for training strategies and sampling.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate the feature encoding process in a prototypical energy-based generative model, the Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM). We start with an analytical investigation using simplified architectures and data structures, and end with numerical analysis of real trainings on real datasets. Our study tracks the evolution of the model's weight matrix through its singular value decomposition, revealing a series of phase transitions associated to a progressive learning of the principal modes of the empirical probability distribution. The model first learns the center of mass of the modes and then progressively resolve all modes through a cascade of phase transitions. We first describe this process analytically in a controlled setup that allows us to study analytically the training dynamics. We then validate our theoretical results by training the Bernoulli-Bernoulli RBM on real data sets. By using data sets of increasing dimension, we show that learning indeed leads to sharp phase transitions in the high-dimensional limit. Moreover, we propose and test a mean-field finite-size scaling hypothesis. This shows that the first phase transition is in the same universality class of the one we studied analytically, and which is reminiscent of the mean-field paramagnetic-to-ferromagnetic phase transition.

papers.title: Internal Representations in Spiking Neural Networks, criticality and the Renormalization Group
papers.research_question: Does the internal representation of a spiking neural network show signatures of criticality, such as power-law distributions, when performing classification tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that broad-tailed fluctuations in internal representations of spiking neural networks during input transitions are not signatures of criticality but rather arise from shifting basins of attraction, analogous to non-critical systems like an Ising model with changing external field.
papers.conclusion: Persistent fluctuations in internal representations arise from the search for new basins of attraction when the environment changes, and this is not a signature of criticality but rather a dynamical effect of changing inputs.
papers.key_findings:
Broad-tailed distributions of internal representation fluctuations occur when the network input changes category, indicated by increased correlation decay times.
These broad tails are present even when the network is partially trained or under simulated anesthesia, indicating they are not dependent on successful classification.
Avalanche size and duration distributions do not show clear power laws, suggesting the system is not critical.
The fluctuations are analogous to those in a non-critical Langevin dynamics model with time-dependent potential and in an Ising model with slowly changing external field.
Renormalization group analysis shows that large susceptibility peaks during transitions occur even away from criticality, and renormalization acts as a classifier that sharpens transitions.
papers.limitation:
Power law fits for avalanche size and duration are sensitive to choices of minimum and maximum values, and the uncertainty is larger than reported, making it impossible to affirm power laws are present.
The model of anesthesia is simplistic, acting only on the input layer by scaling pixels, and is not a realistic model of anesthesia effects.
Feed-forward neural networks are not models of the brain, limiting direct biological relevance.
papers.abstract: Optimal information processing in peripheral sensory systems has been associated in several examples to the signature of a critical or near critical state. Furthermore, cortical systems have also been described to be in a critical state in both wake and anesthetized experimental models, both {\it in vitro} and {\it in vivo}. We investigate whether a similar signature characterizes the internal representations (IR) of a multilayer (deep) spiking artificial neural network performing computationally simple but meaningful cognitive tasks, using a methodology inspired in the biological setup, with cortical implanted electrodes in rats, either freely behaving or under different levels of anesthesia. The increase of the characteristic time of the decay of the correlation of fluctuations of the IR, found when the network input changes, are indications of a broad-tailed distribution of IR fluctuations. The broad tails are present even when the network is not yet capable of performing the classification tasks, either due to partial training or to the effect of a low dose of anesthesia in a simple model. However, we don't find enough evidence of power law distributions of avalanche size and duration. We interpret the results from a renormalization group perspective to point out that despite having broad tails, this is not related to a critical transition but rather similar to fluctuations driven by the reversal of the magnetic field in a ferromagnetic system. Another example of persistent correlation of fluctuations of a non critical system is constructed, where a particle undergoes Brownian motion on a slowly varying potential.

papers.title: Dynamic neuron approach to deep neural networks: Decoupling neurons for renormalization group analysis
papers.research_question: How can we reformulate the cost function of deep neural networks to reveal translational symmetry and enable the application of renormalization group transformations and analysis of critical phenomena?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the dynamic neuron approach (DNA), which reformulates the cost function of deep neural networks by treating neurons as dynamic degrees of freedom, revealing translational symmetry and enabling the application of renormalization group transformations to analyze critical phenomena.
papers.conclusion: The dynamic neuron approach provides a new framework for analyzing deep neural networks using statistical physics, revealing translational symmetry and enabling renormalization group transformations and critical phenomena analysis.
papers.key_findings:
The dynamic neuron approach (DNA) reformulates the DNN cost function by introducing neurons as dynamic degrees of freedom, simplifying interactions and revealing approximate translational symmetry.
Using DNA, the renormalization group transformation can be applied to DNNs, leading to a renormalized system with reduced depth and new constraints.
In a simplified DNN example with one neuron per layer, the RG transformation yields fixed points and scaling laws, indicating potential critical phenomena.
Monte Carlo simulations show that the correlation functions of the DNA system closely resemble those of the original DNN, validating DNA as a theoretical approximation.
The DNA Hamiltonian, under certain assumptions, resembles a spin glass model, connecting DNN training to statistical physics models.
papers.limitation:
The simple example with assumptions (one neuron per layer, single data point, Heaviside activation, discrete weights) may oversimplify and differ from actual DNNs.
The DNA introduces a large number of dynamic neurons (LMN), making it computationally infeasible for practical applications.
future_direction: Develop theoretical tools for inference to study neural scaling laws.
Develop optimization methods to make DNA practically feasible.
papers.abstract: Deep neural network architectures often consist of repetitive structural elements. We introduce an approach that reveals these patterns and can be broadly applied to the study of deep learning. Similarly to how a power strip helps untangle and organize complex cable connections, this approach treats neurons as additional degrees of freedom in interactions, simplifying the structure and enhancing the intuitive understanding of interactions within deep neural networks. Furthermore, it reveals the translational symmetry of deep neural networks, which simplifies the application of the renormalization group transformation, a method that effectively analyzes the scaling behavior of the system. By utilizing translational symmetry and renormalization group transformations, we can analyze critical phenomena. This approach may open new avenues for studying deep neural networks using statistical physics.

papers.title: Scale-invariant feature extraction of neural network and renormalization group flow
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between the Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM) and renormalization group (RG) flow, and how does the RBM learn to extract features from spin configurations?
papers.core_contribution: The unsupervised RBM trained on Ising model configurations at various temperatures generates a flow of temperature that approaches the critical point Tc, opposite to the typical RG flow, indicating the RBM learns scale-invariant features.
papers.conclusion: The RBM flow is attracted to the critical point when trained on a wide range of temperatures, and the RBM learns scale-invariant features, showing a connection to RG but with an opposite flow direction.
papers.key_findings:
For type V RBM (trained on configurations from T=0 to T=6), the temperature flow approaches the critical temperature Tc=2.27, making Tc a stable fixed point.
When the hidden layer size Nh is less than or equal to the visible layer size Nv, the flow stabilizes at Tc; for Nh > Nv, the flow eventually moves towards high temperature.
The weight matrix product WW^T reflects spin correlations, and its off-diagonal components decay similarly to spin correlations near Tc.
The eigenvalue spectrum of WW^T for type V RBM shows a gradual decrease without jumps, suggesting scale-invariant feature learning.
The RBM flow is attracted to the features it has learned during training, e.g., type H/L RBMs flow towards high/low temperatures respectively.
future_direction: Investigate the RBM flow for first-order phase transitions, e.g., in the Blume-Capel model.
Study the attractor of RBM flows for human faces to understand value judgments.
Describe the RBM flow as a stochastic process using Langevin or Fokker-Planck equations.
papers.abstract: Theoretical understanding of how a deep neural network (DNN) extracts features from input images is still unclear, but it is widely believed that the extraction is performed hierarchically through a process of coarse graining. It reminds us of the basic renormalization group (RG) concept in statistical physics. In order to explore possible relations between DNN and RG, we use the restricted Boltzmann machine (RBM) applied to an Ising model and construct a flow of model parameters (in particular, temperature) generated by the RBM. We show that the unsupervised RBM trained by spin configurations at various temperatures from T=0 to T=6 generates a flow along which the temperature approaches the critical value T_{c}=2.27. This behavior is the opposite of the typical RG flow of the Ising model. By analyzing various properties of the weight matrices of the trained RBM, we discuss why it flows towards T_{c} and how the RBM learns to extract features of spin configurations.

papers.title: A Renormalization Group Framework for Scale-Invariant Feature Learning in Deep Neural Networks (Student Abstract)
papers.research_question: How can renormalization group theory be applied to analyze and optimize hierarchical feature learning in deep neural networks, with a focus on scale invariance?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a renormalization group framework for scale-invariant feature learning in deep neural networks, introducing scale-aware activation functions and RG-guided training to converge to fixed points.
papers.conclusion: The framework unifies deep learning and RG theory, enhancing interpretability and generalization through scale-invariant feature learning.
papers.key_findings:
Scale-aware activation functions enable scale covariance in neural network layers.
RG flow equations for network parameters are derived, linking learning dynamics to statistical physics.
Fixed points of RG flow correspond to scale-invariant feature representations.
RG-guided training procedure converges to these fixed points while minimizing loss.
Layer information decreases monotonically, indicating coarse-graining in hierarchical feature learning.
future_direction: Empirically validating the proposed framework through simulations.
papers.abstract: We propose a framework that uses renormalization group (RG) theory from statistical physics to analyze and optimize the hierarchical feature learning process in deep neural networks. Here, the layer-wise transformations in deep networks can be viewed as analogous to RG transformations, with each layer implementing a coarse-graining operation that extracts increasingly abstract features. We propose an approach to enforce scale invariance in neural networks, introduce scale-aware activation functions, and derive RG flow equations for network parameters. We show that our approach leads to fixed points corresponding to scale-invariant feature representations. Finally, we propose an RG-guided training procedure that converges to these fixed points while minimizing the loss function.

papers.title: Critical Phase Transition in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Are qualitative changes in Large Language Models, such as those induced by varying the temperature parameter, phase transitions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides strong evidence that a phase transition occurs in practical LLMs when varying the temperature parameter, with critical behaviors similar to those in natural languages.
papers.conclusion: The extensive statistical analysis suggests that a phase transition occurs in LLMs when varying the temperature parameter, providing a meaningful analogy between LLMs and natural phenomena.
papers.key_findings:
A phase transition occurs at a critical temperature Tc ≈ 1, separating a low-temperature regime with repetitive structures from a high-temperature regime where generated sentences are often incomprehensible.
Near the critical point, sequences exhibit critical behaviors such as a power-law decay of correlation and slow convergence toward the stationary state.
Natural language datasets (OpenWebTextCorpus, WikiText) show critical properties similar to LLM-generated sequences at the transition temperature, suggesting LLMs are closest to natural language at criticality.
The low-temperature phase is ordered with chaotic repetitive structures (many peaks in power spectra), while the high-temperature phase is not simply disordered despite finite integrated correlation.
The phase transition is observed across different models (GPT-2, Japanese GPT-2, Pythia) and different mappings (POS tags, characters), indicating robustness.
papers.limitation:
The size of the models analyzed is moderate (70M, 124M, and 361M). Analysis of larger models is important because the true phase transition seems to exist in the large context window limit.
Further investigation is needed to better understand how the criticality relates to linguistic properties and practical tasks.
future_direction: Statistical analysis of larger models to confirm the phase transition in the large context window limit.
Precisely estimating the set of critical exponents for GPT-2, other LLMs, and multiple natural language corpora to classify the universality class.
Studying the potential phase transition at very low temperature between repetitive and deterministic phases.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive performance. To understand their behaviors, we need to consider the fact that LLMs sometimes show qualitative changes. The natural world also presents such changes called phase transitions, which are defined by singular, divergent statistical quantities. Therefore, an intriguing question is whether qualitative changes in LLMs are phase transitions. In this work, we have conducted extensive analysis on texts generated by LLMs and suggested that a phase transition occurs in LLMs when varying the temperature parameter. Specifically, statistical quantities have divergent properties just at the point between the low-temperature regime, where LLMs generate sentences with clear repetitive structures, and the high-temperature regime, where generated sentences are often incomprehensible. In addition, critical behaviors near the phase transition point, such as a power-law decay of correlation and slow convergence toward the stationary state, are similar to those in natural languages. Our results suggest a meaningful analogy between LLMs and natural phenomena.

papers.title: Information-Theoretic Progress Measures reveal Grokking is an Emergent Phase Transition
papers.research_question: What causes grokking in neural networks, and can it be understood as an emergent phase transition driven by synergistic interactions between neurons?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces information-theoretic progress measures based on O-Information to quantify synergy and redundancy in neural networks, revealing that grokking is an emergent phase transition caused by synergistic interactions between neurons.
papers.conclusion: The work presents a method to quantify emergent properties in neural networks without supervision, revealing grokking as an emergent phase transition and advocating for a shift from reductionism to emergentism in interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
Identifies three key phases during training: Feature Learning, Emergence, and Decoupling, with additional divergent and delayed emergence phases for low weight decay.
Shows that increasing weight decay and high weight initialization enhance the emergent phase and reduce the generalization gap.
Demonstrates that early peaks in synergy can predict the occurrence of grokking.
Preliminary evidence suggests that synergistic sub-networks identified during the emergent phase are causally related to generalization.
Weight decay acts as regularization, promoting shared features and smoothing the loss landscape to facilitate emergence.
papers.limitation:
The simplicity of the model and benchmark limits the generality of the findings.
Difficulty in scaling the O-Information method to larger networks due to reliance on agglomerative clustering.
future_direction: Extend the work to realistic architectures like transformers or toy encoder-decoder models.
Evaluate alternative benchmarks such as sparse parity, XOR, regression, or MNIST.
Explore the role of optimization and loss geometry, and investigate synergistic dropout.
papers.abstract: This paper studies emergent phenomena in neural networks by focusing on grokking where models suddenly generalize after delayed memorization. To understand this phase transition, we utilize higher-order mutual information to analyze the collective behavior (synergy) and shared properties (redundancy) between neurons during training. We identify distinct phases before grokking allowing us to anticipate when it occurs. We attribute grokking to an emergent phase transition caused by the synergistic interactions between neurons as a whole. We show that weight decay and weight initialization can enhance the emergent phase.

papers.title: Learning through atypical phase transitions in overparameterized neural networks
papers.research_question: How does overparameterization affect the geometrical structure of minima in non-convex neural networks, and how does this relate to learning and generalization performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that overparameterized non-convex neural networks exhibit two phase transitions: the interpolation threshold and the Local Entropy transition, and that efficient learning algorithms sample from wide, atypical minima with good generalization, despite typical minima being sharp and numerous.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that atypical phase transitions driven by rare, wide minima are key to understanding learning in overparameterized non-convex networks.
papers.key_findings:
There are two phase transitions: the interpolation threshold (where solutions appear) and the Local Entropy transition (where wide minima appear).
Typical solutions are sharp and isolated, with poor generalization.
Atypical solutions are wide and dense, with good generalization, and are sampled by efficient algorithms.
The Local Entropy transition is the relevant one for learning.
Numerical experiments on various architectures confirm the theoretical predictions.
future_direction: Conduct in-depth numerical studies of large deep networks.
Corroborate results with rigorous bounds for more general data distributions.
Theoretical confirmation that dynamics of a broad class of algorithms is attracted to these structures.
papers.abstract: Current deep neural networks are highly overparameterized (up to billions of connection weights) and nonlinear. Yet they can fit data almost perfectly through variants of gradient descent algorithms and achieve unexpected levels of prediction accuracy without overfitting. These are formidable results that defy predictions of statistical learning and pose conceptual challenges for nonconvex optimization. In this paper, we use methods from statistical physics of disordered systems to analytically study the computational fallout of overparameterization in nonconvex binary neural network models, trained on data generated from a structurally simpler but "hidden" network. As the number of connection weights increases, we follow the changes of the geometrical structure of different minima of the error loss function and relate them to learning and generalization performance. A first transition happens at the so-called interpolation point, when solutions begin to exist (perfect fitting becomes possible). This transition reflects the properties of typical solutions, which however are in sharp minima and hard to sample. After a gap, a second transition occurs, with the discontinuous appearance of a different kind of "atypical" structures: wide regions of the weight space that are particularly solution dense and have good generalization properties. The two kinds of solutions coexist, with the typical ones being exponentially more numerous, but empirically we find that efficient algorithms sample the atypical, rare ones. This suggests that the atypical phase transition is the relevant one for learning. The results of numerical tests with realistic networks on observables suggested by the theory are consistent with this scenario.

papers.title: Triple Phase Transitions: Understanding the Learning Dynamics of Large Language Models from a Neuroscience Perspective
papers.research_question: How do phase transitions in large language model training manifest in terms of alignment with human brain activity, internal representations, and downstream task performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies three common phase transitions in LLM training: an initial alignment with the brain when instruction following emerges, a detachment during task performance stagnation, and a realignment when tasks are consolidated.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that LLM learning involves three phase transitions that synchronize brain alignment, internal representations, and task performance, providing a multi-scale view of emergent abilities.
papers.key_findings:
Phase 1 (Brain Alignment and Instruction Following): Alignment with the entire brain surges as LLMs begin adhering to task instructions.
Phase 2 (Brain Detachment and Stagnation): LLMs diverge from the brain during a period of downstream task accuracy stagnation.
Phase 3 (Brain Realignment and Consolidation): Alignment with the brain reoccurs as LLMs become capable of solving downstream tasks.
These three phase transitions are observed across LLMs with distinct architectures and training data.
The transitions only occur when the input language matches a language sufficiently represented in the model's training corpus.
papers.limitation: The brain encoding accuracy and intrinsic dimensionality are not perfectly congruent, leaving open questions about what aspects of activation changes are not captured by intrinsic dimensionality alone.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit abrupt emergent behavior, whereby new abilities arise at certain points during their training. This phenomenon, commonly referred to as a ''phase transition'', remains poorly understood. In this study, we conduct an integrative analysis of such phase transitions by examining three interconnected perspectives: the similarity between LLMs and the human brain, the internal states of LLMs, and downstream task performance. We propose a novel interpretation for the learning dynamics of LLMs that vary in both training data and architecture, revealing that three phase transitions commonly emerge across these models during training: (1) alignment with the entire brain surges as LLMs begin adhering to task instructions Brain Alignment and Instruction Following, (2) unexpectedly, LLMs diverge from the brain during a period in which downstream task accuracy temporarily stagnates Brain Detachment and Stagnation, and (3) alignment with the brain reoccurs as LLMs become capable of solving the downstream tasks Brain Realignment and Consolidation. These findings illuminate the underlying mechanisms of phase transitions in LLMs, while opening new avenues for interdisciplinary research bridging AI and neuroscience.

papers.title: Grokking phase transitions in learning local rules with gradient descent
papers.research_question: What are the characteristics of grokking as a phase transition in simple solvable models, and how does locality of the teacher model affect grokking?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that grokking is a phase transition and provides exact analytic expressions for critical exponents, grokking probability, and grokking time distribution. It introduces a tensor-network map connecting the grokking setup to standard statistical learning and demonstrates that grokking is a consequence of locality of the teacher model.
papers.conclusion: Grokking is a phase transition arising from locality of the teacher model, and L1 regularization can improve generalization compared to L2 regularization.
papers.key_findings:
Grokking is a second-order phase transition with critical exponent depending on data distribution.
L1 regularization increases grokking probability and reduces grokking time compared to L2 regularization.
Grokking coincides with spikes in training loss and structural changes in latent space effective dimension.
The tensor-network map connects local rule learning to the grokking perceptron model.
Numerical experiments on cellular automata rule learning confirm the theoretical predictions.
papers.abstract: We discuss two solvable grokking (generalisation beyond overfitting) models in a rule learning scenario. We show that grokking is a phase transition and find exact analytic expressions for the critical exponents, grokking probability, and grokking time distribution. Further, we introduce a tensor-network map that connects the proposed grokking setup with the standard (perceptron) statistical learning theory and show that grokking is a consequence of the locality of the teacher model. As an example, we analyse the cellular automata learning task, numerically determine the critical exponent and the grokking time distributions and compare them with the prediction of the proposed grokking model. Finally, we numerically analyse the connection between structure formation and grokking.

papers.title: Interpreting Deep Learning by Establishing a Rigorous Corresponding Relationship with Renormalization Group
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether the training process of deep neural networks is equivalent to the renormalization group, allowing the extraction of macroscopic features from input data.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proves that the training process of a deep neural network is equivalent to the renormalization group, enabling the network to extract macroscopic features from input data, similar to RG.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that deep neural networks extract macroscopic features through a process equivalent to renormalization group, and the proposed framework can be extended to other models for interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
For a simple neural network with no hidden layers, the coupling constant Jt tends to the fixed point J*=0 as training converges, matching the RG fixed point.
For deep neural networks with multiple hidden layers, the same result holds, showing equivalence between training and RG.
The framework establishes a rigorous correspondence between DNN and RG, providing interpretability.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to the 1-dimensional Ising model and fully connected neural networks.
For stochastic gradient descent, the framework assumes convergence results that are not currently available, so simulated annealing is used instead.
future_direction: Apply the framework to other types of deep learning models or input data.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we focus on the interpretability of deep neural network. Our work is motivated by the renormalization group (RG) in statistical mechanics. RG plays the role of a bridge connecting microscopical properties and macroscopic properties, the coarse graining procedure of it is quite similar with the calculation between layers in the forward propagation of the neural network algorithm. From this point of view we establish a rigorous corresponding relationship between the deep neural network (DNN) and RG. Concretely, we consider the most general fully connected network structure and real space RG of one dimensional Ising model. We prove that when the parameters of neural network achieve their optimal value, the limit of coupling constant of the output of neural network equals to the fixed point of the coupling constant in RG of one dimensional Ising model. This conclusion shows that the training process of neural network is equivalent to RG and therefore the network extract macroscopic feature from the input data just like RG.

papers.title: Phase transitions reveal hierarchical structure in deep neural networks
papers.research_question: What is the geometric origin of phase transitions, saddle points, and mode connectivity in deep neural network training, and how do they relate to the global organization of the error landscape?
papers.core_contribution: Unifies phase transitions, saddle points, and mode connectivity in DNN training through the geometry of loss and error landscapes, and introduces the Pathfinder algorithm to probe this geometry.
papers.conclusion: The error landscape of deep neural networks possesses a hierarchical structure of accuracy basins, and the Pathfinder algorithm provides a practical tool for exploring this geometry, linking training phenomena to statistical physics concepts.
papers.key_findings:
Phase transitions in DNN learning are governed by saddle points in the loss landscape, which emerge from concave boundaries in the underlying error landscape.
The error landscape is organized into hierarchically nested accuracy basins, analogous to phases in statistical physics, defined by the Euclidean norm of the parameter vector.
The Pathfinder algorithm efficiently finds low-error, flat paths connecting distinct global minima, confirming mode connectivity.
Phase transitions correspond to the learning or forgetting of specific digit features in the MNIST classifier.
The identified transitions and hierarchical structure are robust to changes in learning rate and the choice of L2 regularization reference point.
papers.limitation:
The method relies on the assumption that the error landscape possesses a degree of smoothness and connectivity that allows for meaningful paths to be traced.
The computational advantage, while significant compared to Information Bottleneck calculations, still requires multiple optimization runs at different regularization strengths, and the optimal range for β is task- and architecture-dependent.
Numerical results are currently confined to feed-forward architectures; it is an open question how the hierarchy manifests in other architectures like CNNs or Transformers.
future_direction: Apply statistical physics methods to quantitatively characterize error landscapes, their role in learning dynamics, and the role of criticality in information processing.
Use the Pathfinder algorithm as a diagnostic framework for analyzing model behavior and designing better training schemes.
Leverage the understanding of error-landscape geometry to develop better strategies for continuous learning, transfer learning, and model merging.
papers.abstract: Training Deep Neural Networks relies on the model converging on a high-dimensional, non-convex loss landscape toward a good minimum. Yet, much of the phenomenology of training remains ill understood. We focus on three seemingly disparate observations: the occurrence of phase transitions reminiscent of statistical physics, the ubiquity of saddle points, and phenomenon of mode connectivity relevant for model merging. We unify these within a single explanatory framework, the geometry of the loss and error landscapes. We analytically show that phase transitions in DNN learning are governed by saddle points in the loss landscape. Building on this insight, we introduce a simple, fast, and easy to implement algorithm that uses the L2 regularizer as a tool to probe the geometry of error landscapes. We apply it to confirm mode connectivity in DNNs trained on the MNIST dataset by efficiently finding paths that connect global minima. We then show numerically that saddle points induce transitions between models that encode distinct digit classes. Our work establishes the geometric origin of key training phenomena in DNNs and reveals a hierarchy of accuracy basins analogous to phases in statistical physics.

papers.title: Investigating Network Parameters in Neural-Network Quantum States
papers.research_question: What do the optimized neural-network parameters reveal about the quantum phase transition in the 1D transverse-field Ising model?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that the quantum phase transition in the 1D transverse-field Ising model is reflected in the optimized RBM parameters, with a qualitative change in the long-range tail of the couplings, leading to a change in the finite-temperature phase diagram of the classical RBM Ising system.
papers.conclusion: The correspondence between neural-network parameters and quantum phases suggests that careful investigation of neural-network parameters may offer a new route to extracting physical insights from neural-network wave functions.
papers.key_findings:
The optimized RBM coupling parameters exhibit long-range behavior in the ordered phase (Γ<1) and short-range behavior in the disordered phase (Γ>1).
The quantum phase transition at Γ=1 is marked by a sharp change in the tail of the RBM coupling parameters.
The finite-temperature specific heat of the RBM Ising system shows a phase transition for Γ<1 but only a crossover for Γ>1.
The energy variance of the RBM system changes qualitatively at the quantum critical point.
Analyzing neural-network parameters can provide physical insights into quantum many-body systems.
papers.limitation: The critical behavior of the 1D TFI model at the phase transition cannot be captured in the current RBM setup because the derivative of the energy has a discontinuity.
future_direction: Investigate other neural networks and other quantum-spin Hamiltonians to see how the neural-network parameters behave.
papers.abstract:
Recently, quantum-state representation using artificial neural networks has
started to be recognized as a powerful tool. However, due to the black-box
nature of machine learning, it is difficult to analyze what machine learns or
why it is powerful. Here, by applying one of the simplest neural networks, the
restricted Boltzmann machine (RBM), to the ground-state representation of the
one-dimensional (1D) transverse-field Ising (TFI) model, we make an attempt to
directly analyze the optimized network parameters. In the RBM optimization, a
zero-temperature quantum state is mapped onto a finite-temperature classical
state of the extended Ising spins that constitute the RBM. We find that the
quantum phase transition from the ordered phase to the disordered phase in the
1D TFI model by increasing the transverse field is clearly reflected in the
behaviors of the optimized RBM parameters and hence in the finite-temperature
phase diagram of the classical RBM Ising system. The present finding of a
correspondence between the neural-network parameters and quantum phases
suggests that a careful investigation of the neural-network parameters may
provide a new route to extracting nontrivial physical insights from the
neural-network wave functions.

papers.title: Dataset-learning duality and emergent criticality
papers.research_question: How does criticality (power-law distribution of fluctuations) emerge in neural network learning dynamics via a dataset-learning duality?
papers.core_contribution: Establishes a dataset-learning duality mapping between the dataset (boundary neurons) and the tangent space of trainable variables (learning), and uses it to show that criticality (power-law fluctuations) can emerge in learning systems even from non-critical datasets, with the power-law exponent modifiable by changing the activation or loss function.
papers.conclusion: The paper establishes a dataset-learning duality and applies it to study emergent criticality, showing that scale-invariant fluctuations in trainable variables arise from criticality in the dual tangent space and can be generated by specific compositions of activation and loss functions.
papers.key_findings:
Established a dataset-learning duality mapping between the space of boundary neurons (dataset) and the tangent space of trainable variables (learning).
Showed that criticality (power-law distribution of fluctuations of trainable variables) can emerge in the learning system even when the dataset is in a non-critical state.
Derived specific compositions of activation and loss functions (exponential, power-law, logarithmic) that lead to power-law fluctuations with different exponents (k=1, k=(α-1)/α, k=2).
Numerical experiments on a toy classification model confirm the theoretical predictions for the power-law distributions arising from these function compositions.
The power-law distributions enable trainable variables to explore a broader range of scales, which may prevent the network from getting trapped in local minima.
papers.limitation:
The analysis of learning efficiency and its relation to criticality requires consideration of non-equilibrium systems, which is beyond the scope of the paper.
The theoretical and numerical analysis is performed on a simple low-dimensional toy model, limiting direct applicability to higher-dimensional problems.
future_direction: Extending the dataset-learning duality framework to study non-equilibrium learning systems.
papers.abstract: In artificial neural networks, the activation dynamics of non-trainable variables is strongly coupled to the learning dynamics of trainable variables. During the activation pass, the boundary neurons (e.g., input neurons) are mapped to the bulk neurons (e.g., hidden neurons), and during the learning pass, both bulk and boundary neurons are mapped to changes in trainable variables (e.g., weights and biases). For example, in feed-forward neural networks, forward propagation is the activation pass and backward propagation is the learning pass. We show that a composition of the two maps establishes a duality map between a subspace of non-trainable boundary variables (e.g., dataset) and a tangent subspace of trainable variables (i.e., learning). In general, the dataset-learning duality is a complex non-linear map between high-dimensional spaces. We use duality to study the emergence of criticality, or the power-law distribution of fluctuations of the trainable variables, using a toy model at learning equilibrium. In particular, we show that criticality can emerge in the learning system even from the dataset in a non-critical state, and that the power-law distribution can be modified by changing either the activation function or the loss function.

papers.title: A Toy Model of Universality: Reverse Engineering How Networks Learn Group Operations
papers.research_question: The paper investigates the universality hypothesis: whether different models learn similar features and circuits when trained on similar tasks, by studying how small neural networks learn to implement group composition.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the group composition via representations (GCR) algorithm and shows that neural networks consistently learn this algorithm when trained on group composition tasks, providing evidence for weak universality (underlying principles exist) but against strong universality (specific circuits vary).
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that while there is an underlying algorithm (GCR) that networks learn for group composition, the specific features and circuits are arbitrary, supporting weak universality but not strong universality.
papers.key_findings:
Networks learn the GCR algorithm for group composition, which uses representation theory to compute compositions.
The specific representations (circuits) learned vary across different runs and hyperparameters, indicating that while the algorithm is universal, the implementation is not.
The order in which representations are learned is arbitrary and not consistent across runs.
The network's logits can be approximated as a sum of characters from a sparse set of representations.
Ablations confirm that the identified components are causally important for the task.
papers.limitation: The algorithm does not perfectly explain all logits due to limitations of the architecture (e.g., ReLU activations imperfectly implement matrix multiplication).
future_direction: Extending to other group theoretic tasks such as conjugacy, group actions, and automata.
Studying semigroups (which lack representation theory).
Investigating inductive biases of networks more broadly.
papers.abstract: Universality is a key hypothesis in mechanistic interpretability -- that different models learn similar features and circuits when trained on similar tasks. In this work, we study the universality hypothesis by examining how small neural networks learn to implement group composition. We present a novel algorithm by which neural networks may implement composition for any finite group via mathematical representation theory. We then show that networks consistently learn this algorithm by reverse engineering model logits and weights, and confirm our understanding using ablations. By studying networks of differing architectures trained on various groups, we find mixed evidence for universality: using our algorithm, we can completely characterize the family of circuits and features that networks learn on this task, but for a given network the precise circuits learned -- as well as the order they develop -- are arbitrary.

papers.title: Symmetry and Generalisation in Neural Approximations of Renormalisation Transformations
papers.research_question: What role do parameter symmetry and network expressivity play in the generalisation behaviour of neural networks when learning a real-space renormalisation group transformation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals a competition between symmetry constraints and expressivity in neural networks learning renormalization transformations, with overly complex or overconstrained models generalizing poorly. It extends a cumulant propagation framework from MLPs to GNNs to elucidate internal information processing.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that balancing symmetry and expressivity is crucial for generalization in neural networks learning physical transformations, and the cumulant propagation framework offers insight into their internal information processing.
papers.key_findings:
Symmetrically constrained weights in MLPs combined with nonlinear activations (e.g., quadratic) lead to poor generalization, as shown analytically.
Linear networks with symmetric weights generalize well, but adding nonlinearities (ReLU, quadratic) under symmetry constraints degrades generalization.
The independent node approximation for cumulant propagation in GNNs is limited, especially for higher-order cumulants, due to neglected correlations from message passing.
GNNs perform comparably to MLPs on simple two-node graphs but their inductive biases are not beneficial for tasks lacking structural complexity.
Networks with learnable spline activations and fixed weights generalize poorly, while training both weights and splines yields linear solutions that generalize well.
papers.limitation:
The independent node approximation for GNN cumulant propagation is crude and neglects important interactions induced by message passing and weight sharing.
The study is limited to simple network architectures (shallow MLPs and GNNs) and synthetic tasks.
future_direction: Extending the cumulant propagation framework to more complex architectures and tasks.
Investigating the role of symmetry breaking in hierarchical learning dynamics.
papers.abstract: Deep learning models have proven enormously successful at using multiple layers of representation to learn relevant features of structured data. Encoding physical symmetries into these models can improve performance on difficult tasks, and recent work has motivated the principle of parameter symmetry breaking and restoration as a unifying mechanism underlying their hierarchical learning dynamics. We evaluate the role of parameter symmetry and network expressivity in the generalisation behaviour of neural networks when learning a real-space renormalisation group (RG) transformation, using the central limit theorem (CLT) as a test case map. We consider simple multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) and graph neural networks (GNNs), and vary weight symmetries and activation functions across architectures. Our results reveal a competition between symmetry constraints and expressivity, with overly complex or overconstrained models generalising poorly. We analytically demonstrate this poor generalisation behaviour for certain constrained MLP architectures by recasting the CLT as a cumulant recursion relation and making use of an established framework to propagate cumulants through MLPs. We also empirically validate an extension of this framework from MLPs to GNNs, elucidating the internal information processing performed by these more complex models. These findings offer new insight into the learning dynamics of symmetric networks and their limitations in modelling structured physical transformations.

papers.title: Beyond Converging Representations A Philosophical Response on the Interpretation Risks of Scientific Foundation Models
papers.research_question: Do scientific foundation models of different modalities, architectures, and training data learn similar internal representations of matter?
papers.core_contribution: Representations learned by nearly sixty scientific foundation models across string-, graph-, 3D atomistic, and protein-based modalities are highly aligned, and they converge as model performance improves, suggesting a common underlying representation of physical reality.
papers.conclusion: Representational alignment serves as a quantitative benchmark for foundation-level generality in scientific models, and current models remain limited by training data and inductive biases.
papers.key_findings:
Models trained on different input modalities (e.g., string encodings and 3D coordinates) show significant representational alignment.
As models improve in energy prediction performance, their representations converge towards those of the best-performing models.
Local (CKNNA) and global (dCor) alignment metrics show consistent trends, indicating robust representational similarity.
Intrinsic dimensionality (Id) of embeddings is consistent across models for a given dataset, suggesting a universal low-dimensional structure.
For in-distribution data, high-performing models align closely while weak models diverge; for out-of-distribution data, most models collapse to a low-information representation.
papers.limitation: Today's models remain limited by training data and inductive bias and do not yet encode truly universal structure.
future_direction: Using representational alignment as a quantitative benchmark for foundation-level generality in scientific models.
Tracking the emergence of universal representations of matter as models scale.
Selecting and distilling models whose learned representations transfer best across modalities, domains of matter, and scientific tasks.
papers.abstract: Machine learning models of vastly different modalities and architectures are being trained to predict the behavior of molecules, materials, and proteins. However, it remains unclear whether they learn similar internal representations of matter. Understanding their latent structure is essential for building scientific foundation models that generalize reliably beyond their training domains. Although representational convergence has been observed in language and vision, its counterpart in the sciences has not been systematically explored. Here, we show that representations learned by nearly sixty scientific models, spanning string-, graph-, 3D atomistic, and protein-based modalities, are highly aligned across a wide range of chemical systems. Models trained on different datasets have highly similar representations of small molecules, and machine learning interatomic potentials converge in representation space as they improve in performance, suggesting that foundation models learn a common underlying representation of physical reality. We then show two distinct regimes of scientific models: on inputs similar to those seen during training, high-performing models align closely and weak models diverge into local sub-optima in representation space; on vastly different structures from those seen during training, nearly all models collapse onto a low-information representation, indicating that today's models remain limited by training data and inductive bias and do not yet encode truly universal structure. Our findings establish representational alignment as a quantitative benchmark for foundation-level generality in scientific models. More broadly, our work can track the emergence of universal representations of matter as models scale, and for selecting and distilling models whose learned representations transfer best across modalities, domains of matter, and scientific tasks.

papers.title: Evidence of Phase Transitions in Small Transformer-Based Language Models
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether phase transitions can be observed in small transformer-based language models, detected directly in linear training space, and emerge at early stages of training.
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that phase-transition-like reorganizations occur in small transformer-based language models, can be detected directly in linear training space using Poisson-based diagnostics, and emerge early in training as lexical coherence forms.
papers.conclusion: The findings demonstrate that emergent-like reorganizations can arise in modest transformer models at early stages, and that Poisson-based diagnostics provide a framework for detecting discontinuous learning dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Synchronized discontinuities in dispersion and KL divergence occur at a specific training epoch (230-250), indicating a phase transition.
The model transitions from generating fragmentary output to coherent multi-character words.
The transition is accompanied by temporary degradation (increase in errors) before consolidation, similar to barrier-crossing in first-order phase transitions.
The phase transition is observable in small models without log scaling and at early training stages.
The Poisson-centered diagnostics provide a continuous, internal measure of reorganization that is not visible in standard loss curves.
papers.limitation: Single architecture and dataset (3.6M parameters, Tiny Shakespeare) limits generalization.
future_direction: Scaling and universality: test across model scales, datasets, architectural families.
Quantitative characterization: apply finite-size scaling analysis to distinguish critical phenomena.
Mechanistic linkage: connect external statistics with internal network dynamics.
Higher-level transitions: investigate similar discontinuities at sentence or paragraph levels.
papers.abstract: Phase transitions have been proposed as the origin of emergent abilities in large language models (LLMs), where new capabilities appear abruptly once models surpass critical thresholds of scale. Prior work, such as that of Wei et al., demonstrated these phenomena under model and data scaling, with transitions revealed after applying a log scale to training compute. In this work, we ask three complementary questions: (1) Are phase transitions unique to large models, or can they also be observed in small transformer-based language models? (2) Can such transitions be detected directly in linear training space, rather than only after log rescaling? and (3) Can these transitions emerge at early stages of training? To investigate, we train a small GPT-style transformer on a character-level corpus and analyze the evolution of vocabulary usage throughout training. We track the average word length, the number of correct versus incorrect words, and shifts in vocabulary diversity. Building on these measures, we apply Poisson and sub-Poisson statistics to quantify how words connect and reorganize. This combined analysis reveals a distinct transition point during training. Notably, these transitions are not apparent in standard loss or validation curves, but become visible through our vocabulary- and statistics-based probes. Our findings suggest that phase-transition reorganizations are a general feature of language model training, observable even in modest models, detectable directly in linear training space, and occurring surprisingly early as coherence emerges. This perspective provides new insight into the nonlinear dynamics of language model training and underscores the importance of tailored metrics for uncovering phase transition behaviors

papers.title: Self-organized learning emerges from coherent coupling of critical neurons
papers.research_question: How does training in artificial neural networks occur? The paper proposes that training is mediated by coherent coupling of task-specific critical neurons, leading to self-organized learning and generalization.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that training in artificial neural networks is mediated by coherent coupling of critical neurons, leading to self-organized learning, phase transitions in neuronal connectivity, and the emergence of critical computational graphs that explain generalization.
papers.conclusion: The findings suggest that coherent coupling of critical neurons and the ensuing local concentration within loss landscapes may represent universal learning mechanisms shared by both artificial and biological neural computation.
papers.key_findings:
Neuronal correlation graphs (NCGs) emerge during training and undergo a connectivity phase transition in early training, characterized by a flourish-diminish process in correlation strength and topology.
The loss landscape exhibits local concentration, where per-sample losses concentrate to a minimum, providing a theoretical explanation for generalization capacity.
A convergence phase transition occurs in the final training stage, characterized by a phase boundary in hyperparameter space, driven by probability flux through weight space.
Critical computational graphs (CCGs) can be extracted for each task, revealing sparse, interpretable circuits that generalize well and exhibit power-law distributions analogous to brain avalanches.
Training involves coherent coupling of critical neurons, balancing energy-driven and entropy-driven stages, leading to a precise balance of neuronal contributions.
papers.abstract: Deep artificial neural networks have surpassed human-level performance across a diverse array of complex learning tasks, establishing themselves as indispensable tools in both social applications and scientific research. Despite these advances, the underlying mechanisms of training in artificial neural networks remain elusive. Here, we propose that artificial neural networks function as adaptive, self-organizing information processing systems in which training is mediated by the coherent coupling of strongly activated, task-specific critical neurons. We demonstrate that such neuronal coupling gives rise to Hebbian-like neural correlation graphs, which undergo a dynamic, second-order connectivity phase transition during the initial stages of training. Concurrently, the connection weights among critical neurons are consistently reinforced while being simultaneously redistributed in a stochastic manner. As a result, a precise balance of neuronal contributions is established, inducing a local concentration within the random loss landscape which provides theoretical explanation for generalization capacity. We further identify a later on convergence phase transition characterized by a phase boundary in hyperparameter space, driven by the nonequilibrium probability flux through weight space. The critical computational graphs resulting from coherent coupling also decode the predictive rules learned by artificial neural networks, drawing analogies to avalanche-like dynamics observed in biological neural circuits. Our findings suggest that the coherent coupling of critical neurons and the ensuing local concentration within the loss landscapes may represent universal learning mechanisms shared by both artificial and biological neural computation.

papers.title: Extended critical regimes of deep neural networks
papers.research_question: How do heavy-tailed weights in deep neural networks lead to an extended critical regime, and what computational advantages does this regime provide?
papers.core_contribution: Develops a mean-field theory for deep neural networks with heavy-tailed weights, predicting an extended critical regime that balances contraction and expansion of internal representations and speeds up training.
papers.conclusion: Developed a mean-field theory for heavy-tailed DNNs, identifying an extended critical regime that enhances signal propagation without fine-tuning, and provides a guide for heavy-tailed initialization to improve generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Heavy-tailed weight distributions are ubiquitous in pretrained DNNs and emerge during training, as shown by fitting weight matrices to stable distributions.
The Lévy mean-field theory predicts an extended critical regime in parameter space where DNNs balance order and disorder without fine-tuning.
In the extended critical regime, layerwise Jacobians exhibit multifractal eigenvectors, enabling balanced contraction and expansion of internal representations.
Networks initialized in the extended critical regime train faster and achieve higher testing accuracy compared to ordered or chaotic regimes.
The extended critical regime provides a theoretical guide for selecting initialization parameters to improve trainability and generalization.
future_direction: Applying the theory to understand complex learning dynamics and develop better training algorithms.
Extending the concept of extended criticality to biological systems to understand their computational principles.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have been successfully applied to many real-world problems, but a complete understanding of their dynamical and computational principles is still lacking. Conventional theoretical frameworks for analysing DNNs often assume random networks with coupling weights obeying Gaussian statistics. However, non-Gaussian, heavy-tailed coupling is a ubiquitous phenomenon in DNNs. Here, by weaving together theories of heavy-tailed random matrices and non-equilibrium statistical physics, we develop a new type of mean field theory for DNNs which predicts that heavy-tailed weights enable the emergence of an extended critical regime without fine-tuning parameters. In this extended critical regime, DNNs exhibit rich and complex propagation dynamics across layers. We further elucidate that the extended criticality endows DNNs with profound computational advantages: balancing the contraction as well as expansion of internal neural representations and speeding up training processes, hence providing a theoretical guide for the design of efficient neural architectures.

papers.title: On the Symmetries of Deep Learning Models and their Internal Representations
papers.research_question: How do the symmetries of a network architecture (via intertwiner groups) relate to the symmetries in the network's internal representations of data?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces intertwiner groups to connect architectural symmetries with symmetries in internal representations, and shows that for ReLU networks, the activation basis is special for interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that intertwiner groups connect architectural symmetries to representation symmetries, and provide a justification for focusing on activation basis in ReLU networks for interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Intertwiner groups describe weight space symmetries and propagate to symmetries in internal representations.
Stitching with GReLU transformations incurs a small accuracy penalty, indicating that much of the variation between networks can be accounted for by GReLU.
GReLU-Procrustes and GReLU-CKA are effective dissimilarity measures invariant to GReLU transformations.
For ReLU networks, interpretability is higher in the activation basis than in arbitrary linear combinations, but this is not the case for networks without ReLU.
papers.limitation:
The theory does not fully account for residual connections, as noted in remark 3.6.
Stitching with GReLU does not achieve full accuracy, indicating that internal representations are not perfectly aligned by permutations and scalings.
papers.abstract: Symmetry is a fundamental tool in the exploration of a broad range of complex systems. In machine learning symmetry has been explored in both models and data. In this paper we seek to connect the symmetries arising from the architecture of a family of models with the symmetries of that family's internal representation of data. We do this by calculating a set of fundamental symmetry groups, which we call the intertwiner groups of the model. We connect intertwiner groups to a model's internal representations of data through a range of experiments that probe similarities between hidden states across models with the same architecture. Our work suggests that the symmetries of a network are propagated into the symmetries in that network's representation of data, providing us with a better understanding of how architecture affects the learning and prediction process. Finally, we speculate that for ReLU networks, the intertwiner groups may provide a justification for the common practice of concentrating model interpretability exploration on the activation basis in hidden layers rather than arbitrary linear combinations thereof.

papers.title: Phase Diagram of Initial Condensation for Two-Layer Neural Networks
papers.research_question: What are the dynamical regimes of two-layer neural networks under varying initialization scales, and how does initialization affect condensation?
papers.core_contribution: Establishes a phase diagram for initial condensation in two-layer neural networks, explaining the dependence on hyperparameters and the mechanism by which small initialization leads to condensation.
papers.key_findings:
Condensation of weight vectors occurs during training, leading to better generalization abilities.
The phase diagram illustrates dynamical regimes of neural networks based on initialization scales.
Small initialization leads to condensation at the initial training stage.
papers.abstract: The phenomenon of distinct behaviors exhibited by neural networks under varying scales of initialization remains an enigma in deep learning research.In this paper, based on the earlier work [Luo et al., J. Mach.Learn.Res., 22:1-47, 2021], we present a phase diagram of initial condensation for two-layer neural networks.Condensation is a phenomenon wherein the weight vectors of neural networks concentrate on isolated orientations during the training process, and it is a feature in nonlinear learning process that enables neural networks to possess better generalization abilities.Our phase diagram serves to provide a comprehensive understanding of the dynamical regimes of neural networks and their dependence on the choice of hyperparameters related to initialization.Furthermore, we demonstrate in detail the underlying mechanisms by which small initialization leads to condensation at the initial training stage.

papers.title: Phase transitions from linear to nonlinear information processing in neural networks
papers.research_question: How does the information processing capacity of echo state networks change as a function of nonlinearity and network size, and does a discontinuous phase transition occur in the limit of infinite nodes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates a phase transition from linear to nonlinear information processing in echo state networks, which becomes discontinuous in the limit of infinite network size and is distinct from the conventional order-to-chaos transition.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals a phase transition from linear to nonlinear information processing in neural networks, which may represent a new class of nonequilibrium phase transitions in high-dimensional dynamical systems.
papers.key_findings:
For small input weight standard deviation, the network operates in an approximately linear regime with limited information processing capacity.
Beyond a critical input weight standard deviation, the capacity increases rapidly, and the transition sharpens as the network size grows, indicating a discontinuous jump in the infinite-node limit.
The critical nonlinearity scales with noise intensity as σ_in,0 ∝ σ_ξ^{1/3}, implying that even infinitesimally weak nonlinearity can drive the system into the nonlinear regime in the absence of noise.
The transition is fundamentally different from the order-to-chaos transition, which typically reduces capacity.
