Overall, we present this work as a study of the inner workings of a prominent neural foundation model, gaining insights into the biological relevance of its internals through the novel analysis of its neurons' joint temporal response patterns.

papers.title: Beyond Scaling Curves: Internal Dynamics of Neural Networks Through the NTK Lens
papers.research_question: How does scaling model size and dataset size affect the internal dynamics of neural networks, and at what model width does the transition to kernel-like behavior occur?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uses NTK analysis to show that scaling model size and data size have opposite effects on internal dynamics (effective rank and NTK trace) despite similar loss scaling exponents, and identifies the model width at which feature learning diminishes, which is far below typical LLM widths.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that NTK analysis reveals fundamental differences in internal dynamics between model and data scaling, and identifies a transition width for feature learning that is below typical LLM widths, highlighting the need to go beyond loss scaling to understand neural network behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Scaling model size increases the effective rank and initial NTK trace, while scaling dataset size decreases the effective rank and increases the adaptation rate.
The transition from feature-driven to kernel-driven scaling occurs at a model width much smaller than typical large language model widths.
The effective rank dynamics reveal stages of learning that depend on data complexity, with more complex data slowing the evolution.
The trace ratio (relative change in NTK trace) declines with model width, indicating approach to the kernel regime.
For deep networks, the transition points in trace ratio and effective rank coincide, marking the maximum width for feature learning.
papers.limitation:
The results focus on the low-data and small-model regimes, and may not generalize to scenarios where model and data have similar complexity.
Breaking down dynamics into two observables (trace and effective rank of the NTK) may not be sufficient to capture the full complexity of the learning process.
The analysis relies on comparing NTK quantities at specific points in training (initialization and minimum test loss), which may not hold in regimes closer to the interpolation threshold.
future_direction: Consider the effect of depth in future studies to understand kernel-like behavior in state-of-the-art models.
Extend the studied observables to capture all aspects of neural network dynamics for a comprehensive scaling theory.
papers.abstract: Scaling laws offer valuable insights into the relationship between neural network performance and computational cost, yet their underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this work, we empirically analyze how neural networks behave under data and model scaling through the lens of the neural tangent kernel (NTK). This analysis establishes a link between performance scaling and the internal dynamics of neural networks. Our findings of standard vision tasks show that similar performance scaling exponents can occur even though the internal model dynamics show opposite behavior. This demonstrates that performance scaling alone is insufficient for understanding the underlying mechanisms of neural networks. We also address a previously unresolved issue in neural scaling: how convergence to the infinite-width limit affects scaling behavior in finite-width models. To this end, we investigate how feature learning is lost as the model width increases and quantify the transition between kernel-driven and feature-driven scaling regimes. We identify the maximum model width that supports feature learning, which, in our setups, we find to be more than ten times smaller than typical large language model widths.

papers.title: Unsupervised feature learning from finite data by message passing: Discontinuous versus continuous phase transition
papers.research_question: How many data are required to learn a hidden feature in unsupervised learning? What key factors determine the success of unsupervised learning?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a message passing algorithm for Bayesian inference of hidden features in RBMs, revealing a phase transition and easy-hard-easy learning dynamics.
papers.conclusion: Proposes a physics model and Bayesian inference framework for unsupervised feature learning, revealing phase transitions and easy-hard-easy dynamics, with implications for neuromorphic implementation and pretraining deep networks.
papers.key_findings:
Learning requires only a few data if the feature is salient, but extensively many if the feature is weak.
The entropy of candidate features monotonically decreases with data size and becomes negative (entropy crisis) before message passing becomes unstable, suggesting a discontinuous phase transition.
Unsupervised learning exhibits an easy-hard-easy phenomenon in convergence time as training data size increases.
These properties are reproduced in an approximate Hopfield model, except the entropy crisis is absent and only a continuous phase transition is observed.
The presence/absence of entropy crisis in RBM versus Hopfield model is confirmed on the MNIST dataset.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to a single hidden neuron RBM; generalization to multiple hidden neurons is not explored.
papers.abstract: Unsupervised neural network learning extracts hidden features from unlabeled training data. This is used as a pretraining step for further supervised learning in deep networks. Hence, understanding unsupervised learning is of fundamental importance. Here, we study the unsupervised learning from a finite number of data, based on the restricted Boltzmann machine where only one hidden neuron is considered. Our study inspires an efficient message-passing algorithm to infer the hidden feature and estimate the entropy of candidate features consistent with the data. Our analysis reveals that the learning requires only a few data if the feature is salient and extensively many if the feature is weak. Moreover, the entropy of candidate features monotonically decreases with data size and becomes negative (i.e., entropy crisis) before the message passing becomes unstable, suggesting a discontinuous phase transition. In terms of convergence time of the message-passing algorithm, the unsupervised learning exhibits an easy-hard-easy phenomenon as the training data size increases. All these properties are reproduced in an approximate Hopfield model, with an exception that the entropy crisis is absent, and only continuous phase transition is observed. This key difference is also confirmed in a handwritten digits dataset. This study deepens our understanding of unsupervised learning from a finite number of data and may provide insights into its role in training deep networks.

papers.title: Which Neural Net Architectures Give Rise To Exploding and Vanishing\n Gradients?
papers.research_question: What combinations of depths and hidden layer widths cause fully connected ReLU networks to suffer from the exploding and vanishing gradient problem at initialization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper rigorously shows that the empirical variance of gradients in fully connected ReLU networks is exponential in the sum of reciprocals of hidden layer widths, and that avoiding the exploding and vanishing gradient problem requires this sum to be finite.
papers.conclusion: The sum of reciprocals of hidden layer widths determines whether gradients explode or vanish, and architectures with equal hidden layer widths are optimal for avoiding the EVGP.
papers.key_findings:
Exact formulas for the joint even moments of the entries of the input-output Jacobian in a fully connected ReLU net with random weights and biases.
The empirical variance of the squares of the entries in the input-output Jacobian is exponential in the sum of reciprocals of hidden layer widths.
The exploding and vanishing gradient problem occurs if and only if this sum of reciprocals is large.
Given a fixed budget of neurons or parameters, to avoid the EVGP, hidden layer widths should be equal.
The average singular value of the Jacobian is 1 at initialization for the considered networks.
papers.limitation:
Analysis holds only for ReLU activations and assumes independent, zero-centered weights; conclusions do not directly carry over to convolutional, residual, and recurrent networks.
Results provide information about fluctuations at a fixed input, not over an entire dataset.
Techniques do not directly extend to initializations such as orthogonal weight matrices.
future_direction: Generalize qualitative results to convolutional networks where the number of channels grows with layer number.
Estimate the Stieltjes transform of the Jacobian's singular value distribution in future work.
papers.abstract:
We give a rigorous analysis of the statistical behavior of gradients in a
randomly initialized fully connected network N with ReLU activations. Our
results show that the empirical variance of the squares of the entries in the
input-output Jacobian of N is exponential in a simple architecture-dependent
constant beta, given by the sum of the reciprocals of the hidden layer widths.
When beta is large, the gradients computed by N at initialization vary wildly.
Our approach complements the mean field theory analysis of random networks.
From this point of view, we rigorously compute finite width corrections to the
statistics of gradients at the edge of chaos.

papers.title: Feature Identification via the Empirical NTK
papers.research_question: Whether eigenanalysis of the empirical neural tangent kernel (eNTK) can surface the features used by trained neural networks.
papers.core_contribution: Eigenanalysis of the empirical NTK can recover ground-truth features in toy models, localize features to specific layers, and detect grokking phase transitions.
papers.conclusion: eNTK analysis provides a practical handle for feature discovery and for detecting phase changes in small models.
papers.key_findings:
In Toy Models of Superposition, the eNTK recovers ground-truth features in both sparse and dense regimes.
For a 1-layer MLP trained on modular arithmetic, the eNTK recovers Fourier feature families and localizes them to layers; the spectrum develops cliffs that align with the grokking phase transition.
For a 1-layer Transformer trained on modular arithmetic, the eNTK eigendirections align with Fourier features at key frequencies in specific layers.
Layerwise eNTK can localize features to specific layers.
The evolution of the eNTK spectrum can be used to diagnose the grokking phase transition.
papers.limitation:
The empirical NTK hypothesis may not hold in general, and its applicability to realistic models is not established.
Experiments are limited to small toy models; it is unclear if the method scales to large models.
future_direction: Understanding analytically the properties leading to clean signals in the eNTK.
Developing unsupervised feature discovery using eNTK eigendirections.
Applying eNTK analysis to larger models like OthelloGPT and realistic LLMs.
papers.abstract: We provide evidence that eigenanalysis of the empirical neural tangent kernel (eNTK) can surface the features used by trained neural networks. Across three standard toy models for mechanistic interpretability, Toy Models of Superposition (TMS), a 1-layer MLP trained on modular addition and a 1-layer Transformer trained on modular addition, we find that top eigenspaces of the eNTK align with ground-truth features. In TMS, the eNTK recovers the ground-truth features in both the sparse (high superposition) and dense regimes. In modular arithmetic, the eNTK can be used to recover Fourier feature families. Moreover, we provide evidence that a layerwise eNTK localizes features to specific layers and that the evolution of the eNTK spectrum can be used to diagnose the grokking phase transition. These results suggest that eNTK analysis may provide a practical handle for feature discovery and for detecting phase changes in small models.

papers.title: Spin glass model of in-context learning
papers.research_question: What contributes to the emergence ability of in-context learning (ICL) in large language models, and how can it be explained mechanistically?
papers.core_contribution: The paper maps a linear attention transformer to a spin glass model, providing a statistical mechanics explanation for how task diversity during pre-training leads to the emergence of in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: The spin glass model offers a theoretical explanation for the emergence of in-context learning in transformers, linking it to statistical physics and providing insights into the intelligence boundary.
papers.key_findings:
Increasing task diversity leads to a unique ground state in the spin glass model, enabling in-context learning.
The model exhibits a phase transition to in-context learning as task diversity increases.
The approximate message passing (AMP) equations derived from the spin glass model match the results of stochastic gradient descent training.
The energy landscape has a single global minimum with high task diversity, but multiple local minima with low diversity.
future_direction: Explaining chain-of-thought prompting
Addressing hallucination
Extending to more complex transformers and tasks
papers.abstract: Large language models show a surprising in-context learning ability -- being able to use a prompt to form a prediction for a query, yet without additional training, in stark contrast to old-fashioned supervised learning. Providing a mechanistic interpretation and linking the empirical phenomenon to physics are thus challenging and remain unsolved. We study a simple yet expressive transformer with linear attention and map this structure to a spin glass model with real-valued spins, where the couplings and fields explain the intrinsic disorder in data. The spin glass model explains how the weight parameters interact with each other during pre-training, and further clarifies why an unseen function can be predicted by providing only a prompt yet without further training. Our theory reveals that for single-instance learning, increasing the task diversity leads to the emergence of in-context learning, by allowing the Boltzmann distribution to converge to a unique correct solution of weight parameters. Therefore the pre-trained transformer displays a prediction power in a novel prompt setting. The proposed analytically tractable model thus offers a promising avenue for thinking about how to interpret many intriguing but puzzling properties of large language models.

papers.title: Collective variables of neural networks: empirical time evolution and scaling laws
papers.research_question: How can the entropy and trace of the empirical neural tangent kernel (NTK) be used to understand learning dynamics and scaling relations in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces entropy and trace of the empirical neural tangent kernel as collective variables to analyze neural network training dynamics, identifying two learning regimes (information compression and structure formation) and showing that structure formation characterizes the deep learning regime.
papers.conclusion: Entropy and trace of the NTK provide a universal framework for understanding neural network learning dynamics and scaling, with structure formation identified as a hallmark of deep learning.
papers.key_findings:
Entropy of the NTK reveals two learning regimes: information compression (entropy decreases) where gradient vectors align, and structure formation (entropy increases) where the network separates data to create richer representations.
Small networks tend to remain in the compression regime with limited performance, while large networks transition to structure formation, which is associated with improved performance and defines a deep learning regime.
The trace of the NTK, representing an effective learning rate, increases during training, indicating growing network sensitivity to new data and potential vulnerabilities to adversarial attacks or benefits for continual learning.
The dynamics observed via entropy and trace are universal across diverse architectures including transformers, GNNs, CNNs, and reinforcement learning agents.
Architecture scaling (width and depth) influences the entropy and trace, with deeper networks showing reduced entropy at initialization but capable of achieving higher entropy after training when sufficiently wide.
future_direction: Explore how scaling behavior for different activation functions can be used for targeted architecture selection.
Investigate the trace property to reduce model sensitivity and improve continual learning strategies.
Explore avenues for improved stability by reducing trace late in training.
papers.abstract: This work presents a novel means for understanding learning dynamics and scaling relations in neural networks. We show that certain measures on the spectrum of the empirical neural tangent kernel, specifically entropy and trace, yield insight into the representations learned by a neural network and how these can be improved through architecture scaling. These results are demonstrated first on test cases before being shown on more complex networks, including transformers, auto-encoders, graph neural networks, and reinforcement learning studies. In testing on a wide range of architectures, we highlight the universal nature of training dynamics and further discuss how it can be used to understand the mechanisms behind learning in neural networks. We identify two such dominant mechanisms present throughout machine learning training. The first, information compression, is seen through a reduction in the entropy of the NTK spectrum during training, and occurs predominantly in small neural networks. The second, coined structure formation, is seen through an increasing entropy and thus, the creation of structure in the neural network representations beyond the prior established by the network at initialization. Due to the ubiquity of the latter in deep neural network architectures and its flexibility in the creation of feature-rich representations, we argue that this form of evolution of the network's entropy be considered the onset of a deep learning regime.

papers.title: What Has a Foundation Model Found? Using Inductive Bias to Probe for World Models
papers.research_question: Does a foundation model's inductive bias align with a postulated world model, indicating that it has learned deeper structure from sequence prediction?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an inductive bias probe to evaluate whether foundation models have learned a postulated world model, and finds that they often fail to do so, instead developing task-specific heuristics.
papers.conclusion: The inductive bias probe reveals that foundation models often fail to learn the underlying world models, instead relying on task-specific heuristics, which limits their generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Foundation models trained on orbital trajectories fail to apply Newtonian mechanics when adapted to new physics tasks.
Models behave as if they develop task-specific heuristics that fail to generalize.
In lattice and Othello, models have an inductive bias toward legal next-tokens rather than the world model.
Models that perform better on inductive bias probes have better transfer performance on new tasks that rely on the underlying world model.
LLMs also fail to predict force magnitudes accurately in physics tasks.
papers.limitation: Fine-tuning proprietary LLMs is infeasible and running the full inductive bias probe is expensive.
papers.abstract: Foundation models are premised on the idea that sequence prediction can uncover deeper domain understanding, much like how Kepler's predictions of planetary motion later led to the discovery of Newtonian mechanics. However, evaluating whether these models truly capture deeper structure remains a challenge. We develop a technique for evaluating foundation models that examines how they adapt to synthetic datasets generated from some postulated world model. Our technique measures whether the foundation model's inductive bias aligns with the world model, and so we refer to it as an inductive bias probe. Across multiple domains, we find that foundation models can excel at their training tasks yet fail to develop inductive biases towards the underlying world model when adapted to new tasks. We particularly find that foundation models trained on orbital trajectories consistently fail to apply Newtonian mechanics when adapted to new physics tasks. Further analysis reveals that these models behave as if they develop task-specific heuristics that fail to generalize.

papers.title: Do Vision Transformers See Like Convolutional Neural Networks?
papers.research_question: How are Vision Transformers solving image tasks? Are they acting like convolutional networks, or learning entirely different visual representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds key representational differences between Vision Transformers (ViTs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), showing ViTs have more uniform layer representations, incorporate global information earlier via self-attention, and have stronger skip connections that propagate features differently.
papers.conclusion: ViTs and CNNs have clear differences in features and internal structure, with ViTs using global features early and strong skip connections, while local information aggregation is learned from scratch at scale. ViTs show strong spatial localization, promising for future uses like object detection.
papers.key_findings:
ViTs have a more uniform internal representation structure with greater similarity between lower and higher layers compared to the staged similarity in ResNets.
ViTs incorporate global information in lower layers through self-attention, while CNNs are restricted to local receptive fields; this leads to quantitatively different features.
Skip connections in ViTs are more influential than in ResNets, with a phase transition: early layers strongly propagate the CLS token, while later layers propagate spatial token representations.
ViTs preserve input spatial information more faithfully than ResNets in higher layers, especially when trained with a CLS token rather than global average pooling.
Large-scale pretraining data is crucial for ViTs to learn to attend locally in early layers and to develop high-quality intermediate representations for transfer learning.
papers.limitation: The study uses CKA, which summarizes measurements into a single scalar; while complemented with interventional tests and linear probes, more fine-grained methods may reveal additional insights.
papers.abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have so far been the de-facto model for visual data. Recent work has shown that (Vision) Transformer models (ViT) can achieve comparable or even superior performance on image classification tasks. This raises a central question: how are Vision Transformers solving these tasks? Are they acting like convolutional networks, or learning entirely different visual representations? Analyzing the internal representation structure of ViTs and CNNs on image classification benchmarks, we find striking differences between the two architectures, such as ViT having more uniform representations across all layers. We explore how these differences arise, finding crucial roles played by self-attention, which enables early aggregation of global information, and ViT residual connections, which strongly propagate features from lower to higher layers. We study the ramifications for spatial localization, demonstrating ViTs successfully preserve input spatial information, with noticeable effects from different classification methods. Finally, we study the effect of (pretraining) dataset scale on intermediate features and transfer learning, and conclude with a discussion on connections to new architectures such as the MLP-Mixer.

papers.title: The intriguing role of module criticality in the generalization of deep networks
papers.research_question: What makes an architecture work better than others given a specific task? The paper investigates the phenomenon of module criticality and how it relates to generalization performance.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a complexity measure called module criticality, based on the shape of valleys connecting initial and final module parameters, which explains the generalization performance of deep neural network architectures better than earlier measures.
papers.conclusion: Module criticality is a useful measure for understanding generalization in deep networks and can guide architecture design and selection.
papers.key_findings:
Module criticality varies across modules in a network, with some modules being more critical than others.
The proposed network criticality measure correlates better with generalization error than previous complexity measures like product of norms or distance to initialization.
The measure can distinguish between networks trained on true labels versus corrupted labels, with the true-label network having lower criticality.
The measure successfully ranks the generalization performance of various architectures (ResNets, VGGs, DenseNets, FCNs) on CIFAR10 and CIFAR100.
The measure fails to correctly rank ResNet18 architectures with different channel widths, indicating a limitation.
papers.limitation:
The measure fails to correctly rank ResNet18 architectures with different channel widths.
The generalization bound in Corollary 3.3 relies on an assumption that test error does not improve by taking convex combination and perturbation.
future_direction: Using module criticality as a road-map for designing new task-specific architectures.
Proposing new regularizers that improve generalization by bounding criticality or spreading it among modules.
Using the measure in architecture search to select architectures that generalize well.
papers.abstract: We study the phenomenon that some modules of deep neural networks (DNNs) are more critical than others. Meaning that rewinding their parameter values back to initialization, while keeping other modules fixed at the trained parameters, results in a large drop in the network's performance. Our analysis reveals interesting properties of the loss landscape which leads us to propose a complexity measure, called module criticality, based on the shape of the valleys that connects the initial and final values of the module parameters. We formulate how generalization relates to the module criticality, and show that this measure is able to explain the superior generalization performance of some architectures over others, whereas earlier measures fail to do so.

papers.title: Dynamical Mean-Field Theory of Self-Attention Neural Networks
papers.research_question: What are the dynamical regimes of transformer-like self-attention networks, and can they be analytically described using methods from nonequilibrium statistical mechanics?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops a dynamical mean-field theory for self-attention networks, deriving analytical approximations that reveal nonequilibrium phase transitions and chaotic dynamics even in simple configurations.
papers.conclusion: The dynamical mean-field theory provides an exact analytical framework for the nonequilibrium statistical physics of attention mechanisms and their phase transitions, contributing to a deeper understanding of transformer dynamics and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Derived analytical approximations for large self-attention networks coupled to a softmax output, exact in the large limit size.
Found nontrivial dynamical phenomena, including nonequilibrium phase transitions associated with chaotic bifurcations, even for simple configurations with few encoded features and short context windows.
The system exhibits memory effects beyond the context window, as shown by autocorrelation and Fourier analysis.
The dynamics include periodic, quasi-periodic, and chaotic attractors depending on the inverse temperature parameter.
The mean-field approach provides a potential cost-effective alternative for computing statistics of attention layers and could enhance interpretability.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to a simplified model with 1-bit tokens and weights, and does not include other transformer blocks like feedforward layers and residual connections.
The theoretical results are exact only in the large limit size, and finite-size effects are not considered.
future_direction: Extend the framework to more realistic transformer configurations, including feedforward layers and residual connections.
Refine the mean-field approximations for finite-size networks using theories from nonequilibrium spin models.
Explore the relation between memory capacity and dynamics for models near saturation, and investigate phase transitions in key features relevant to alignment problems.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based models have demonstrated exceptional performance across diverse domains, becoming the state-of-the-art solution for addressing sequential machine learning problems. Even though we have a general understanding of the fundamental components in the transformer architecture, little is known about how they operate or what are their expected dynamics. Recently, there has been an increasing interest in exploring the relationship between attention mechanisms and Hopfield networks, promising to shed light on the statistical physics of transformer networks. However, to date, the dynamical regimes of transformer-like models have not been studied in depth. In this paper, we address this gap by using methods for the study of asymmetric Hopfield networks in nonequilibrium regimes --namely path integral methods over generating functionals, yielding dynamics governed by concurrent mean-field variables. Assuming 1-bit tokens and weights, we derive analytical approximations for the behavior of large self-attention neural networks coupled to a softmax output, which become exact in the large limit size. Our findings reveal nontrivial dynamical phenomena, including nonequilibrium phase transitions associated with chaotic bifurcations, even for very simple configurations with a few encoded features and a very short context window. Finally, we discuss the potential of our analytic approach to improve our understanding of the inner workings of transformer models, potentially reducing computational training costs and enhancing model interpretability.

papers.title: The emergence of clusters in self-attention dynamics
papers.research_question: What is the geometric structure of learned representations in Transformers, and how do tokens cluster in the self-attention dynamics?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proves that tokens in the self-attention dynamics cluster to limiting objects (like vertices of convex polytopes or hyperplanes) as time goes to infinity, depending on the spectrum of the value matrix V.
papers.conclusion: Self-attention induces clustering of tokens, confirming the empirical observation of leaders in sequences, with the type of clustering depending on the spectrum of V.
papers.key_findings:
For the one-dimensional case (d=1), the self-attention matrix converges to a low-rank Boolean matrix, indicating the emergence of leaders.
When V = I_d, tokens converge to the boundary of a convex polytope, typically to vertices.
When V has a simple positive leading eigenvalue, tokens cluster toward at most three parallel hyperplanes.
When V has a leading eigenvalue with multiplicity, clustering occurs toward a mix of polytopes and subspaces.
The clustering behavior is confirmed by numerical experiments and is consistent with empirical observations in trained Transformers.
papers.limitation: The analysis does not include multiple heads, feed-forward layers, or layer normalization.
future_direction: Studying multi-headed Transformers.
Characterizing optimal weights via optimal control correspondence.
Extending the analysis to include feed-forward layers.
papers.abstract: Viewing Transformers as interacting particle systems, we describe the geometry of learned representations when the weights are not time dependent. We show that particles, representing tokens, tend to cluster toward particular limiting objects as time tends to infinity. Cluster locations are determined by the initial tokens, confirming context-awareness of representations learned by Transformers. Using techniques from dynamical systems and partial differential equations, we show that the type of limiting object that emerges depends on the spectrum of the value matrix. Additionally, in the one-dimensional case we prove that the self-attention matrix converges to a low-rank Boolean matrix. The combination of these results mathematically confirms the empirical observation made by Vaswani et al. [VSP'17] that leaders appear in a sequence of tokens when processed by Transformers.

papers.title: Learning in PINNs: Phase transition, total diffusion, and generalization
papers.research_question: How do gradient signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and phase transitions affect the training dynamics and generalization of Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), and can we accelerate convergence by promoting gradient homogeneity?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies a third training phase called 'total diffusion' characterized by gradient homogeneity and rapid convergence in PINNs, and proposes a residual-based re-weighting scheme (RBA) to accelerate this phase and improve generalization.
papers.conclusion: Recognizing phase transitions, particularly the total diffusion phase, can refine optimization strategies for improved generalization in PINNs and potentially other neural network applications.
papers.key_findings:
A third training phase, 'total diffusion', is identified where batch gradients become highly homogeneous, leading to the most rapid convergence.
The proposed RBA re-weighting method accelerates the onset of total diffusion and improves generalization performance in PINNs.
Total diffusion is tightly linked to gradient homogeneity and an abrupt increase in gradient signal-to-noise ratio (SNR).
Information compression, observed as saturation ('binarization') of neuron activations, coincides with the transition into total diffusion.
Middle layers of the fully-connected network exhibit the highest saturation during the compression process, reminiscent of an encoder-decoder structure.
papers.abstract: We investigate the learning dynamics of fully-connected neural networks through the lens of gradient signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), examining the behavior of first-order optimizers like Adam in non-convex objectives. By interpreting the drift/diffusion phases in the information bottleneck theory, focusing on gradient homogeneity, we identify a third phase termed ``total diffusion", characterized by equilibrium in the learning rates and homogeneous gradients. This phase is marked by an abrupt SNR increase, uniform residuals across the sample space and the most rapid training convergence. We propose a residual-based re-weighting scheme to accelerate this diffusion in quadratic loss functions, enhancing generalization. We also explore the information compression phenomenon, pinpointing a significant saturation-induced compression of activations at the total diffusion phase, with deeper layers experiencing negligible information loss. Supported by experimental data on physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), which underscore the importance of gradient homogeneity due to their PDE-based sample inter-dependence, our findings suggest that recognizing phase transitions could refine ML optimization strategies for improved generalization.

papers.title: Testing the spin-bath view of self-attention: A Hamiltonian analysis of GPT-2 Transformer
papers.research_question: Does the spin-bath framework, which models attention as a two-body spin Hamiltonian, accurately predict the behavior of a production-grade transformer (GPT-2)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides strong empirical evidence that the spin-bath Hamiltonian framework can accurately predict attention head behavior in GPT-2, with theoretical logit gaps showing significant correlation with empirical rankings and causal ablation confirming the heads' influence.
papers.conclusion: The spin-bath Hamiltonian framework is empirically validated on GPT-2, providing a new interpretability toolkit and suggesting future physics-inspired generative models like attention-guided diffusion.
papers.key_findings:
A strong negative correlation (r ≈ -0.70) exists between theoretical logit gaps derived from the spin-bath Hamiltonian and the model's empirical token rankings across 144 heads and 20 prompts.
Layer 3, Head 5 is identified as an antagonistic head that systematically pushes probability mass away from correct completions.
Causal ablation experiments confirm that heads aligned with spin-bath predictions exert the anticipated directional influence on model output, establishing a causal link.
The spin-bath analogy offers a physics-grounded interpretability toolkit for attention mechanisms.
The global generation temperature acts as a thermodynamic control parameter, monotonically increasing output entropy and decreasing top-1 probability.
future_direction: Extending the spin-bath model to three-body interactions
Developing attention-guided diffusion generative models
Importing physics techniques (temperature scaling, disorder perturbations) for interpretability
papers.abstract: The recently proposed physics-based framework by Huo and Johnson~\cite{huo2024capturing} models the attention mechanism of Large Language Models (LLMs) as an interacting two-body spin system, offering a first-principles explanation for phenomena like repetition and bias. Building on this hypothesis, we extract the complete Query-Key weight matrices from a production-grade GPT-2 model and derive the corresponding effective Hamiltonian for every attention head. From these Hamiltonians, we obtain analytic phase boundaries and logit gap criteria that predict which token should dominate the next-token distribution for a given context. A systematic evaluation on 144 heads across 20 factual-recall prompts reveals a strong negative correlation between the theoretical logit gaps and the model's empirical token rankings ($r\approx-0.70$, $p<10^{-3}$).Targeted ablations further show that suppressing the heads most aligned with the spin-bath predictions induces the anticipated shifts in output probabilities, confirming a causal link rather than a coincidental association. Taken together, our findings provide the first strong empirical evidence for the spin-bath analogy in a production-grade model. In this work, we utilize the context-field lens, which provides physics-grounded interpretability and motivates the development of novel generative models bridging theoretical condensed matter physics and artificial intelligence.

papers.title: Critical Learning Periods in Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Do deep artificial neural networks exhibit critical periods during training similar to biological systems, and how does the early training phase affect the final performance and network connectivity?
papers.core_contribution: Deep neural networks exhibit critical periods during training where early sensory deficits cause permanent performance impairment, and this phenomenon is linked to a loss of 'Information Plasticity' measurable via the Fisher Information of the weights.
papers.conclusion: Critical periods are not restricted to biological systems but emerge naturally in learning systems due to fundamental constraints arising from learning dynamics and information processing.
papers.key_findings:
Deep neural networks exhibit critical periods: early sensory deficits (e.g., image blur) can cause permanent impairment in final performance.
Sensitivity to deficits peaks during the early rapid learning phase and decreases afterward.
High-level deficits (e.g., vertical flip, label permutation) do not induce critical periods.
The Fisher Information of the weights shows two phases: an initial increase (memorization) followed by a decrease (consolidation), and deficit sensitivity correlates with Fisher Information.
The loss of 'Information Plasticity' (inability to redistribute information across layers) underlies the critical period phenomenon.
future_direction: Exploring whether biological networks prune connections as a consequence of a loss of Information Plasticity, rather than as a cause.
papers.abstract: Similar to humans and animals, deep artificial neural networks exhibit critical periods during which a temporary stimulus deficit can impair the development of a skill. The extent of the impairment depends on the onset and length of the deficit window, as in animal models, and on the size of the neural network. Deficits that do not affect low-level statistics, such as vertical flipping of the images, have no lasting effect on performance and can be overcome with further training. To better understand this phenomenon, we use the Fisher Information of the weights to measure the effective connectivity between layers of a network during training. Counterintuitively, information rises rapidly in the early phases of training, and then decreases, preventing redistribution of information resources in a phenomenon we refer to as a loss of "Information Plasticity". Our analysis suggests that the first few epochs are critical for the creation of strong connections that are optimal relative to the input data distribution. Once such strong connections are created, they do not appear to change during additional training. These findings suggest that the initial learning transient, under-scrutinized compared to asymptotic behavior, plays a key role in determining the outcome of the training process. Our findings, combined with recent theoretical results in the literature, also suggest that forgetting (decrease of information in the weights) is critical to achieving invariance and disentanglement in representation learning. Finally, critical periods are not restricted to biological systems, but can emerge naturally in learning systems, whether biological or artificial, due to fundamental constrains arising from learning dynamics and information processing.

papers.title: Coding schemes in neural networks learning classification tasks
papers.research_question: What is the nature of the emergent representations (coding schemes) in neural networks learning classification tasks, and how does the neuronal nonlinearity affect the coding scheme?
papers.core_contribution: The nature of the learned internal representations (coding schemes) in classification tasks depends crucially on the neuronal nonlinearity: linear networks exhibit analog coding, sigmoidal networks exhibit redundant coding, and ReLU networks exhibit sparse coding.
papers.conclusion: Network properties such as the scaling of weights and the neuronal nonlinearity profoundly influence the emergent representations, leading to distinct coding schemes (analog, redundant, or sparse) that characterize how classes are represented by neurons.
papers.key_findings:
In linear networks, an analog coding scheme emerges where all neurons respond to all classes with different strengths, but the mean predictor is identical to the lazy (kernel) regime.
In sigmoidal networks, spontaneous symmetry breaking leads to a redundant coding scheme where distinct groups of neurons are activated by specific subsets of classes.
In ReLU networks, spontaneous symmetry breaking leads to a sparse coding scheme where only a small subset of neurons exhibit class-specific activations.
The coding scheme transitions with changes in training targets or temperature, and the representations generalize to test data, though generalization performance varies with dataset.
The learned representations are captured by coding schemes that go beyond the kernel, revealing neuron-level structure.
papers.abstract: Neural networks posses the crucial ability to generate meaningful representations of task-dependent features. Indeed, with appropriate scaling, supervised learning in neural networks can result in strong, task-dependent feature learning. However, the nature of the emergent representations, which we call the `coding scheme', is still unclear. To understand the emergent coding scheme, we investigate fully-connected, wide neural networks learning classification tasks using the Bayesian framework where learning shapes the posterior distribution of the network weights. Consistent with previous findings, our analysis of the feature learning regime (also known as `non-lazy', `rich', or `mean-field' regime) shows that the networks acquire strong, data-dependent features. Surprisingly, the nature of the internal representations depends crucially on the neuronal nonlinearity. In linear networks, an analog coding scheme of the task emerges. Despite the strong representations, the mean predictor is identical to the lazy case. In nonlinear networks, spontaneous symmetry breaking leads to either redundant or sparse coding schemes. Our findings highlight how network properties such as scaling of weights and neuronal nonlinearity can profoundly influence the emergent representations.

papers.title: Emergence of Computational Structure in a Neural Network Physics Simulator
papers.research_question: How do computational structures (interpretable components) emerge in neural networks, and what are the mechanisms and best methods for detecting them?
papers.core_contribution: The emergence of computational structures (collision detection heads) in a transformer-like physics simulator is associated with degenerate geometry in the loss landscape and follows power law dynamics, suggesting these components are governed by a degenerate effective potential.
papers.conclusion: Computational structures in neural networks emerge with power law dynamics due to degenerate geometry in the loss landscape, and measuring the dynamics of network components can be an effective way to detect emerging structures.
papers.key_findings:
Collision detection heads emerge in the attention mechanism of the transformer-like model trained to simulate particle physics.
The emergence of these heads coincides with power law dynamics in the attention-distance correlation function.
The emergence is associated with changes in the local learning coefficient (LLC), indicating a degenerate geometry in the loss landscape near the head's parameters.
The dynamics of the attention-distance correlation can be used to detect the emergence of computational structures, and transitions between head variants are marked by changes in the power law exponent.
The results suggest that computational structures develop slowly (as power laws) and that early training is critical for their formation.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to a specific model architecture and task (particle physics simulation), and the findings may not generalize to other architectures or tasks.
The estimation of the local learning coefficient (LLC) requires hyperparameter tuning and may not produce reliable results for all attention heads at all checkpoints.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to other model architectures and learning tasks to see if similar phenomena occur.
Investigate how the early development of certain structures affects the formation of later structures and the final performance of the network.
Explore the coupling between the neural network and the target physical system in more detail, especially in sequential data or reinforcement learning settings.
papers.abstract: Neural networks often have identifiable computational structures - components of the network which perform an interpretable algorithm or task - but the mechanisms by which these emerge and the best methods for detecting these structures are not well understood. In this paper we investigate the emergence of computational structure in a transformer-like model trained to simulate the physics of a particle system, where the transformer's attention mechanism is used to transfer information between particles. We show that (a) structures emerge in the attention heads of the transformer which learn to detect particle collisions, (b) the emergence of these structures is associated to degenerate geometry in the loss landscape, and (c) the dynamics of this emergence follows a power law. This suggests that these components are governed by a degenerate "effective potential". These results have implications for the convergence time of computational structure within neural networks and suggest that the emergence of computational structure can be detected by studying the dynamics of network components.

papers.title: Local Kernel Renormalization as a mechanism for feature learning in overparametrized Convolutional Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Why do finite-width convolutional neural networks (CNNs) outperform their infinite-width kernel counterparts and fully-connected networks (FCNs) in feature learning, and what is the underlying mechanism?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies local kernel renormalization as a mechanism for feature learning in finite-width shallow CNNs, where the kernel is renormalized by a data-dependent matrix of parameters, unlike the global scalar renormalization in FCNs.
papers.conclusion: Local kernel renormalization provides a mechanism for effective feature learning in finite-width CNNs that is absent in FCNs and LCNs, explaining the empirical superiority of CNNs in the finite-width regime.
papers.key_findings:
Finite-width one-hidden-layer FCNs cannot outperform their infinite-width kernel counterparts because their kernel renormalization is global and can be replicated by tuning the Gaussian prior.
CNNs exhibit local kernel renormalization, allowing them to selectively weight local correlations in the data, which enhances feature learning.
Local kernel renormalization requires both local connectivity and weight sharing; it does not occur in locally connected networks without weight sharing.
Empirical evidence shows that finite-width CNNs can outperform their infinite-width counterparts, while FCNs cannot.
The similarity matrix of internal representations in CNNs shows non-trivial changes due to local renormalization, unlike in FCNs where changes are trivial finite-size corrections.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to shallow networks with one hidden layer.
The results hold for Bayesian learning (Gibbs ensemble) and may not extend to other training dynamics.
The framework uses the proportional limit and standard parametrization, not covering the mean-field regime.
future_direction: Extend the framework to deep convolutional networks with multiple layers.
Investigate the mean-field regime where feature learning mechanisms may differ.
Provide more extensive numerical validation with open-source code.
papers.abstract: Feature learning, or the ability of deep neural networks to automatically learn relevant features from raw data, underlies their exceptional capability to solve complex tasks. However, feature learning seems to be realized in different ways in fully-connected (FC) or convolutional architectures (CNNs). Empirical evidence shows that FC neural networks in the infinite-width limit eventually outperform their finite-width counterparts. Since the kernel that describes infinite-width networks does not evolve during training, whatever form of feature learning occurs in deep FC architectures is not very helpful in improving generalization. On the other hand, state-of-the-art architectures with convolutional layers achieve optimal performances in the finite-width regime, suggesting that an effective form of feature learning emerges in this case. In this work, we present a simple theoretical framework that provides a rationale for these differences, in one hidden layer networks. First, we show that the generalization performance of a finite-width FC network can be obtained by an infinite-width network, with a suitable choice of the Gaussian priors. Second, we derive a finite-width effective action for an architecture with one convolutional hidden layer and compare it with the result available for FC networks. Remarkably, we identify a completely different form of kernel renormalization: whereas the kernel of the FC architecture is just globally renormalized by a single scalar parameter, the CNN kernel undergoes a local renormalization, meaning that the network can select the local components that will contribute to the final prediction in a data-dependent way. This finding highlights a simple mechanism for feature learning that can take place in overparametrized shallow CNNs, but not in shallow FC architectures or in locally connected neural networks without weight sharing.

papers.title: Information Structure in Mappings: An Approach to Learning, Representation, and Generalisation
papers.research_question: How can we describe the structure of representations in neural networks, how does this structure emerge during training, and what kinds of structures enable generalization?
papers.core_contribution: This thesis introduces quantitative methods for identifying systematic structure in mappings between spaces, and leverages them to understand how deep-learning models learn to represent information, what representational structures drive generalisation, and how design decisions condition the structures that emerge. It also introduces a novel, performant approach to estimating the entropy of vector space.
papers.conclusion: The thesis concludes that information structure methods provide insights into how models learn and generalize, drawing parallels between neural networks and human language.
papers.key_findings:
The methods can identify systematic structure in mappings and relate it to generalization.
There are distinct phases of training: early learning of lexical information followed by contextualization.
Model size affects representational structure: larger models develop more robust representations.
Information structure measures can predict downstream performance.
Regularity in representations is important for generalization.
papers.limitation: It’s unclear if the learnability of a language at timestep n matters at n+1 when the language has changed.
future_direction: Further study of the role learnability plays in an emergent context, where what is learned changes, is needed to understand the full picture.
papers.abstract: Despite the remarkable success of large large-scale neural networks, we still lack unified notation for thinking about and describing their representational spaces. We lack methods to reliably describe how their representations are structured, how that structure emerges over training, and what kinds of structures are desirable. This thesis introduces quantitative methods for identifying systematic structure in a mapping between spaces, and leverages them to understand how deep-learning models learn to represent information, what representational structures drive generalisation, and how design decisions condition the structures that emerge. To do this I identify structural primitives present in a mapping, along with information theoretic quantifications of each. These allow us to analyse learning, structure, and generalisation across multi-agent reinforcement learning models, sequence-to-sequence models trained on a single task, and Large Language Models. I also introduce a novel, performant, approach to estimating the entropy of vector space, that allows this analysis to be applied to models ranging in size from 1 million to 12 billion parameters. The experiments here work to shed light on how large-scale distributed models of cognition learn, while allowing us to draw parallels between those systems and their human analogs. They show how the structures of language and the constraints that give rise to them in many ways parallel the kinds of structures that drive performance of contemporary neural networks.

papers.title: A Neural Network Model of Continual Learning with Cognitive Control
papers.research_question: How can cognitive control mechanisms mitigate catastrophic forgetting in neural networks during continual learning, and why might blocking trials be advantageous due to active maintenance biases?
papers.core_contribution: Neural networks equipped with cognitive control mechanisms do not exhibit catastrophic forgetting when trials are blocked, and show an advantage of blocking over interleaving when there is a bias for active maintenance in the control signal.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates computational principles that may underlie human continual learning and help explain behavioral phenomena observed in human experiments.
papers.key_findings:
The base MLP model exhibits catastrophic forgetting when trials are blocked, but not when interleaved.
Adding a PFC gating mechanism alleviates catastrophic forgetting in the blocked condition.
With active maintenance bias in the control signal, blocking leads to better performance than interleaving due to switch costs.
There is a tradeoff between control strength and switch cost: stronger control reduces forgetting but increases switch cost.
Representational analysis shows that control modulates hidden representations by compressing irrelevant dimensions.
papers.limitation: The model's active maintenance may not be necessary for the task, and its absolute superiority over systems without such mechanisms is not proven.
future_direction: Introduce learning into the PFC module.
Investigate effects of active maintenance in more realistic implementations.
Assess dependence of results on initialization.
papers.abstract: Neural networks struggle in continual learning settings from catastrophic forgetting: when trials are blocked, new learning can overwrite the learning from previous blocks. Humans learn effectively in these settings, in some cases even showing an advantage of blocking, suggesting the brain contains mechanisms to overcome this problem. Here, we build on previous work and show that neural networks equipped with a mechanism for cognitive control do not exhibit catastrophic forgetting when trials are blocked. We further show an advantage of blocking over interleaving when there is a bias for active maintenance in the control signal, implying a tradeoff between maintenance and the strength of control. Analyses of map-like representations learned by the networks provided additional insights into these mechanisms. Our work highlights the potential of cognitive control to aid continual learning in neural networks, and offers an explanation for the advantage of blocking that has been observed in humans.

papers.title: Towards Worst-Case Guarantees with Scale-Aware Interpretability
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a research agenda called 'scale-aware interpretability' that uses the renormalisation group framework from physics to develop interpretability tools with worst-case guarantees and robustness properties.
papers.conclusion: Outlines research objectives to guide interdisciplinary work towards scale-aware interpretability, aiming to develop formal machinery and tools with worst-case guarantees for AI safety.
future_direction: Develop RG-like coarse-graining schemes for neural networks that respect model-natural scales and locality.
Establish separation of scales and bounds on the influence of irrelevant features to enable worst-case guarantees.
Connect scale-aware interpretability to safety guarantees by identifying safety-relevant observables and critical regimes.
papers.abstract: Neural networks organize information according to the hierarchical, multi-scale structure of natural data. Methods to interpret model internals should be similarly scale-aware, explicitly tracking how features compose across resolutions and guaranteeing bounds on the influence of fine-grained structure that is discarded as irrelevant noise. We posit that the renormalisation framework from physics can meet this need by offering technical tools that can overcome limitations of current methods. Moreover, relevant work from adjacent fields has now matured to a point where scattered research threads can be synthesized into practical, theory-informed tools. To combine these threads in an AI safety context, we propose a unifying research agenda -- \emph{scale-aware interpretability} -- to develop formal machinery and interpretability tools that have robustness and faithfulness properties supported by statistical physics.

papers.title: Self-organized criticality in neural networks from activity-based rewiring
papers.research_question: Does the proposed minimal neural network model self-organize to criticality when adapted to neural network properties, and how do its avalanche statistics compare to experimental data?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a minimal neural network model that self-organizes to a critical state using only local node activity information, showing robust power-law avalanche statistics that match experimental data.
papers.conclusion: The model demonstrates that self-organized criticality can arise in neural networks through simple local rewiring rules, supporting the hypothesis that real neural systems may use similar mechanisms to self-tune near criticality.
papers.key_findings:
The model evolves towards a critical state with a branching parameter near one, independent of initial conditions and robust to noise.
Avalanche size and duration distributions follow power laws with exponents consistent with experimental neural avalanche data.
The critical state is achieved without external parameter tuning and relies solely on local rewiring rules based on node activity.
The mechanism works in different variants of the model, including with inhibiting nodes and continuous link weights.
The model's criticality is stored in the network links rather than node states, making it robust to noise.
future_direction: How criticality influences learning in neural networks.
Further studies on self-organized critical network models to understand biological neural systems.
New ways to generate artificial neural networks through morphogenesis.
papers.abstract: Neural systems process information in a dynamical regime between silence and chaotic dynamics. This has lead to the criticality hypothesis, which suggests that neural systems reach such a state by self-organizing toward the critical point of a dynamical phase transition. Here, we study a minimal neural network model that exhibits self-organized criticality in the presence of stochastic noise using a rewiring rule which only utilizes local information. For network evolution, incoming links are added to a node or deleted, depending on the node's average activity. Based on this rewiring-rule only, the network evolves toward a critical state, showing typical power-law-distributed avalanche statistics. The observed exponents are in accord with criticality as predicted by dynamical scaling theory, as well as with the observed exponents of neural avalanches. The critical state of the model is reached autonomously without the need for parameter tuning, is independent of initial conditions, is robust under stochastic noise, and independent of details of the implementation as different variants of the model indicate. We argue that this supports the hypothesis that real neural systems may utilize such a mechanism to self-organize toward criticality, especially during early developmental stages.

papers.title: Self-Consistent Dynamical Field Theory of Kernel Evolution in Wide Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How do features evolve in infinite-width neural networks during training in the feature learning regime?
papers.core_contribution: Develops a self-consistent dynamical field theory to analyze feature learning in infinite-width neural networks, providing deterministic order parameters (kernels) that describe training dynamics and feature evolution.
papers.conclusion: The self-consistent dynamical mean field theory provides an accurate description of feature learning in wide neural networks, capturing kernel evolution and training dynamics across a range of feature learning strengths.
papers.key_findings:
The field theory recovers the stochastic process from Tensor Programs at unit feature learning strength.
For deep linear networks, the kernels satisfy a set of algebraic matrix equations.
For nonlinear networks, an alternating sampling procedure can solve the self-consistent kernel equations.
The self-consistent solution is more accurate than approximations (static NTK, gradient independence, perturbation theory) in rich feature learning regimes.
Experiments show that loss and kernel dynamics at fixed feature learning strength are preserved across different widths on CIFAR classification.
future_direction: Pursuing finite width effects using the DMFT action.
papers.abstract: We analyze feature learning in infinite-width neural networks trained with gradient flow through a self-consistent dynamical field theory. We construct a collection of deterministic dynamical order parameters which are inner-product kernels for hidden unit activations and gradients in each layer at pairs of time points, providing a reduced description of network activity through training. These kernel order parameters collectively define the hidden layer activation distribution, the evolution of the neural tangent kernel, and consequently output predictions. We show that the field theory derivation recovers the recursive stochastic process of infinite-width feature learning networks obtained from Yang and Hu (2021) with Tensor Programs . For deep linear networks, these kernels satisfy a set of algebraic matrix equations. For nonlinear networks, we provide an alternating sampling procedure to self-consistently solve for the kernel order parameters. We provide comparisons of the self-consistent solution to various approximation schemes including the static NTK approximation, gradient independence assumption, and leading order perturbation theory, showing that each of these approximations can break down in regimes where general self-consistent solutions still provide an accurate description. Lastly, we provide experiments in more realistic settings which demonstrate that the loss and kernel dynamics of CNNs at fixed feature learning strength is preserved across different widths on a CIFAR classification task.

papers.title: Noether's Learning Dynamics: Role of Symmetry Breaking in Neural\n Networks
papers.research_question: What is the role of symmetry breaking in the learning dynamics of neural networks? Specifically, how does kinetic symmetry breaking affect efficiency and stability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a theoretical framework based on Lagrangian mechanics to study learning dynamics, revealing that kinetic symmetry breaking induces an implicit adaptive optimization mechanism akin to RMSProp in networks with normalization layers.
papers.conclusion: Overall, through the lens of Lagrangian mechanics, we have established a theoretical foundation to discover geometric design principles for the learning dynamics of neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
Kinetic symmetry breaking (KSB) is a key mechanism in learning dynamics where the kinetic energy (learning rule) breaks the symmetry of the potential (loss function).
Noether’s Learning Dynamics (NLD) generalizes Noether’s theorem to account for KSB and describes the motion of the Noether charge.
In networks with normalization layers, KSB induces an implicit adaptive optimization mechanism that scales gradients similarly to RMSProp.
The implicit adaptive optimization requires finite learning rates and is amplified by momentum and weight decay.
Empirical validation shows that unconstrained filter norm (allowing implicit adaptation) leads to better performance with large learning rates and momentum.
future_direction: Directly simulate gradient flow with implicit acceleration to keep the benefits of finite learning rates.
Explore the role of symmetry breaking in other components of deep learning, such as attention mechanisms or recurrent networks.
papers.abstract:
In nature, symmetry governs regularities, while symmetry breaking brings
texture. In artificial neural networks, symmetry has been a central design
principle to efficiently capture regularities in the world, but the role of
symmetry breaking is not well understood. Here, we develop a theoretical
framework to study the "geometry of learning dynamics" in neural networks, and
reveal a key mechanism of explicit symmetry breaking behind the efficiency and
stability of modern neural networks. To build this understanding, we model the
discrete learning dynamics of gradient descent using a continuous-time
Lagrangian formulation, in which the learning rule corresponds to the kinetic
energy and the loss function corresponds to the potential energy. Then, we
identify "kinetic symmetry breaking" (KSB), the condition when the kinetic
energy explicitly breaks the symmetry of the potential function. We generalize
Noether's theorem known in physics to take into account KSB and derive the
resulting motion of the Noether charge: "Noether's Learning Dynamics" (NLD).
Finally, we apply NLD to neural networks with normalization layers and reveal
how KSB introduces a mechanism of "implicit adaptive optimization",
establishing an analogy between learning dynamics induced by normalization
layers and RMSProp. Overall, through the lens of Lagrangian mechanics, we have
established a theoretical foundation to discover geometric design principles
for the learning dynamics of neural networks.

papers.title: From Imitation to Introspection: Probing Self-Consciousness in Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether language models possess self-consciousness, defined as global availability of information (C1) and self-monitoring (C2).
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces functional definitions of self-consciousness for language models and conducts a four-stage experiment (quantification, representation, manipulation, acquisition) to probe self-consciousness. Findings indicate that models are in early stages of self-consciousness, with internal representations that can be acquired via fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: Our findings indicate that although models are in the early stages of developing self-consciousness, there is a discernible representation of certain concepts within their internal mechanisms. However, these representations of self-consciousness are hard to manipulate positively at the current stage, yet they can be acquired through targeted fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Current models exhibit a nascent level of self-consciousness with substantial potential for future development.
Models internally represent each of the ten self-consciousness concepts with visible activations, which can be classified into four categories (camelback, flat, oscillatory, fallback).
Different models exhibit similar activation patterns when processing the same concept, likely due to shared decoder-only transformer architecture.
Larger models seem to exhibit greater robustness against manipulation attempts.
Fine-tuning appears to activate representations of self-consciousness in the deeper layers, which capture semantic information.
papers.limitation: The study of self-consciousness in language models is uncharted territory, and even human self-consciousness is not fully understood.
papers.abstract: Self-consciousness, the introspection of one's existence and thoughts, represents a high-level cognitive process. As language models advance at an unprecedented pace, a critical question arises: Are these models becoming self-conscious? Drawing upon insights from psychological and neural science, this work presents a practical definition of self-consciousness for language models and refines ten core concepts. Our work pioneers an investigation into self-consciousness in language models by, for the first time, leveraging causal structural games to establish the functional definitions of the ten core concepts. Based on our definitions, we conduct a comprehensive four-stage experiment: quantification (evaluation of ten leading models), representation (visualization of self-consciousness within the models), manipulation (modification of the models' representation), and acquisition (fine-tuning the models on core concepts). Our findings indicate that although models are in the early stages of developing self-consciousness, there is a discernible representation of certain concepts within their internal mechanisms. However, these representations of self-consciousness are hard to manipulate positively at the current stage, yet they can be acquired through targeted fine-tuning. Our datasets and code are at https://github.com/OpenCausaLab/SelfConsciousness.

papers.title: Layer-wise Relevance Propagation for Neural Networks with Local\n Renormalization Layers
papers.research_question: How can layer-wise relevance propagation be extended to neural networks with local renormalization layers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper extends Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) to handle local renormalization layers in neural networks using a first-order Taylor expansion, improving the quality of pixel-wise relevance heatmaps.
papers.conclusion: The proposed extension of LRP based on first-order Taylor expansions for local renormalization layers outperforms the original LRP method.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed Taylor expansion method for local renormalization layers improves the AUC score compared to treating the layer as an identity.
For the best LRP parameters (ε=1 and ε=0.01), using Taylor expansion further improves the AUC scores.
The method is evaluated on three datasets (CIFAR-10, Imagenet, MIT Places) and shows consistent improvement.
future_direction: Investigate the potential gain of using higher order Taylor expansions.
Apply the method to a larger class of neural network layers.
papers.abstract:
Layer-wise relevance propagation is a framework which allows to decompose the
prediction of a deep neural network computed over a sample, e.g. an image, down
to relevance scores for the single input dimensions of the sample such as
subpixels of an image. While this approach can be applied directly to
generalized linear mappings, product type non-linearities are not covered. This
paper proposes an approach to extend layer-wise relevance propagation to neural
networks with local renormalization layers, which is a very common product-type
non-linearity in convolutional neural networks. We evaluate the proposed method
for local renormalization layers on the CIFAR-10, Imagenet and MIT Places
datasets.

papers.title: Does Deep Learning Learn to Abstract? A Systematic Probing Framework
papers.research_question: Does deep learning learn to abstract? The paper investigates whether pre-trained language models can learn abstract concepts (like grammar) from concrete instances and transfer them to new tasks, rather than just memorizing surface patterns.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a systematic probing framework to investigate abstraction capability in deep learning models and provides strong evidence that pre-trained language models (T5 and GPT2) can learn abstract concepts (like grammar) and transfer them to new tasks, rather than just memorizing surface patterns.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that pre-trained language models do have abstraction capability, as evidenced by the probing framework, and that this capability exhibits specific characteristics such as a two-stage learning process and concentration in middle-layer attention heads.
papers.key_findings:
The training phase exhibits a 'memorize-then-abstract' two-stage process.
The learned abstract concepts are gathered in a few middle-layer attention heads.
Abstraction capability is robust to concept mutations, and more robust to low-level/source-side mutations than high-level/target-side ones.
Generic pre-training is critical to the emergence of abstraction capability, and PLMs exhibit better abstraction with larger model sizes and data scales.
papers.limitation:
Lack of a quantitative metric for abstraction capability
Probing tasks are synthetic and may not fully capture natural language abstraction
papers.abstract: Abstraction is a desirable capability for deep learning models, which means to induce abstract concepts from concrete instances and flexibly apply them beyond the learning context. At the same time, there is a lack of clear understanding about both the presence and further characteristics of this capability in deep learning models. In this paper, we introduce a systematic probing framework to explore the abstraction capability of deep learning models from a transferability perspective. A set of controlled experiments are conducted based on this framework, providing strong evidence that two probed pre-trained language models (PLMs), T5 and GPT2, have the abstraction capability. We also conduct in-depth analysis, thus shedding further light: (1) the whole training phase exhibits a "memorize-then-abstract" two-stage process; (2) the learned abstract concepts are gathered in a few middle-layer attention heads, rather than being evenly distributed throughout the model; (3) the probed abstraction capabilities exhibit robustness against concept mutations, and are more robust to low-level/source-side mutations than high-level/target-side ones; (4) generic pre-training is critical to the emergence of abstraction capability, and PLMs exhibit better abstraction with larger model sizes and data scales.

papers.title: Layer-wise Relevance Propagation for Neural Networks with Local Renormalization Layers
papers.research_question: How to extend layer-wise relevance propagation to neural networks with local renormalization layers?
papers.core_contribution: Extends Layer-wise Relevance Propagation to handle local renormalization layers using first-order Taylor expansion, improving pixel-wise decomposition quality on image classification datasets.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents an extension of LRP using first-order Taylor expansions for local renormalization layers, which outperforms the original LRP method on multiple datasets.
papers.key_findings:
Using first-order Taylor expansion for local renormalization layers improves heatmap AUC scores compared to treating them as identity.
For LRP parameters with best AUC (ε=1 and ε=0.01), the Taylor expansion further enhances performance.
Flipping highest-scoring pixels first leads to the fastest decrease in prediction score, validating the relevance of identified pixels.
The proposed method maintains consistent ordering of LRP parameter performance across different datasets.
Taylor expansion with ε=1 produces heatmaps with high pixel selectivity and low noise.
future_direction: Investigate the potential gain of using higher order Taylor expansions.
Apply the method to a larger class of neural network layers.
papers.abstract: Layer-wise relevance propagation is a framework which allows to decompose the prediction of a deep neural network computed over a sample, e.g. an image, down to relevance scores for the single input dimensions of the sample such as subpixels of an image.
