While this approach can be applied directly to generalized linear mappings, product type non-linearities are not covered. This paper proposes an approach to extend layer-wise relevance propagation to neural networks with local renormalization layers, which is a very common product-type non-linearity in convolutional neural networks. We evaluate the proposed method for local renormalization layers on the CIFAR-10, Imagenet and MIT Places datasets.

papers.title: New Evidence of the Two-Phase Learning Dynamics of Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How do neural network training dynamics exhibit a two-phase transition from chaotic exploration to stable refinement?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an interval-wise analysis framework for neural network training dynamics and identifies two new phenomena, the Chaos Effect and Cone Effect, which reveal a structural two-phase transition from sensitive exploration to stable refinement.
papers.conclusion: The interval-wise analysis reveals a two-phase transition in neural network training dynamics, from an early chaotic, exploratory phase to a later stable, refinement phase constrained within a narrow functional cone.
papers.key_findings:
An inflection point emerges during training, marking a significant change in the direction of the optimization trajectory.
Tiny parameter perturbations applied before the inflection point lead to substantial divergence in later training, indicating a chaotic early regime (Chaos Effect).
After the inflection point, the empirical Neural Tangent Kernel (eNTK) evolves within a narrow, constrained region in function space (Cone Effect).
The Cone Effect provides significant performance advantages over purely linearized (lazy) training regimes.
papers.limitation:
The work is primarily empirical and lacks a thorough theoretical analysis.
Experiments are limited to image classification tasks (CIFAR-10).
future_direction: Theoretical analysis of the observed phenomena
Exploration of empirical evidence beyond image classification tasks
papers.abstract: Understanding how deep neural networks learn remains a fundamental challenge in modern machine learning. A growing body of evidence suggests that training dynamics undergo a distinct phase transition, yet our understanding of this transition is still incomplete. In this paper, we introduce an interval-wise perspective that compares network states across a time window, revealing two new phenomena that illuminate the two-phase nature of deep learning. i) \textbf{The Chaos Effect.} By injecting an imperceptibly small parameter perturbation at various stages, we show that the response of the network to the perturbation exhibits a transition from chaotic to stable, suggesting there is an early critical period where the network is highly sensitive to initial conditions; ii) \textbf{The Cone Effect.} Tracking the evolution of the empirical Neural Tangent Kernel (eNTK), we find that after this transition point the model's functional trajectory is confined to a narrow cone-shaped subset: while the kernel continues to change, it gets trapped into a tight angular region. Together, these effects provide a structural, dynamical view of how deep networks transition from sensitive exploration to stable refinement during training.

papers.title: Transformers Learn Nonlinear Features In Context: Nonconvex Mean-field Dynamics on the Attention Landscape
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning with nonlinear representations (features) arise in Transformers with MLP layers, optimized via gradient descent?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proves that the infinite-dimensional loss landscape for the distribution of parameters in a Transformer with an MLP and linear attention layer is benign (strictly saddle) in the mean-field limit, and that mean-field dynamics almost always avoids saddle points.
papers.key_findings:
The MLP layer greatly increases the flexibility of in-context learning by extending the class of learnable functions to the Barron space.
The infinite-dimensional loss landscape is benign: all critical points are either global minima or saddle points.
Mean-field dynamics almost always avoids saddle points, explaining how the MLP learns globally optimal representations.
Concrete improvement rates are derived for dynamics away from saddle points, near global minima, and near saddle points.
papers.limitation:
The number of true features is assumed to be known and equal to the model's feature dimension.
The analysis assumes smooth activation functions (excluding ReLU) and bounded parameter spaces, which are technical simplifications.
future_direction: Dynamical characterization when the number of true features does not match the model's feature dimension.
papers.abstract: Large language models based on the Transformer architecture have demonstrated impressive capabilities to learn in context. However, existing theoretical studies on how this phenomenon arises are limited to the dynamics of a single layer of attention trained on linear regression tasks. In this paper, we study the optimization of a Transformer consisting of a fully connected layer followed by a linear attention layer. The MLP acts as a common nonlinear representation or feature map, greatly enhancing the power of in-context learning. We prove in the mean-field and two-timescale limit that the infinite-dimensional loss landscape for the distribution of parameters, while highly nonconvex, becomes quite benign. We also analyze the second-order stability of mean-field dynamics and show that Wasserstein gradient flow almost always avoids saddle points. Furthermore, we establish novel methods for obtaining concrete improvement rates both away from and near critical points. This represents the first saddle point analysis of mean-field dynamics in general and the techniques are of independent interest.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Emotion Inference in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do autoregressive large language models internally represent and process emotional information to infer emotions from text?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that emotion representations in LLMs are functionally localized to mid-layers and that causal interventions on appraisal concepts can steer emotion inference in psychologically plausible ways.
papers.conclusion: This work provides a mechanistic understanding of emotion inference in LLMs and demonstrates causal intervention methods to control emotion inference, with potential applications in safety and alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Emotion representations are functionally localized to specific mid-layers across diverse model families and sizes.
Activation patching reveals that MHSA and FFN units in mid-layers are critical for emotion inference.
Attention patterns in mid-layers shift to emotionally loaded tokens.
Appraisal concepts are linearly represented in the model and their modulation can steer emotion inference.
The structure of emotion representations aligns with cognitive appraisal theory from psychology.
papers.limitation: Focusing only on correctly classified examples may introduce bias toward unambiguous emotional content.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) show promising capabilities in predicting human emotions from text. However, the mechanisms through which these models process emotional stimuli remain largely unexplored. Our study addresses this gap by investigating how autoregressive LLMs infer emotions, showing that emotion representations are functionally localized to specific regions in the model. Our evaluation includes diverse model families and sizes and is supported by robustness checks. We then show that the identified representations are psychologically plausible by drawing on cognitive appraisal theory, a well-established psychological framework positing that emotions emerge from evaluations (appraisals) of environmental stimuli. By causally intervening on construed appraisal concepts, we steer the generation and show that the outputs align with theoretical and intuitive expectations. This work highlights a novel way to causally intervene and precisely shape emotional text generation, potentially benefiting safety and alignment in sensitive affective domains.

papers.title: A Waddington landscape for prototype learning in generalized Hopfield networks
papers.research_question: How does learning in Generalized Hopfield networks proceed, and does it exhibit canalized, low-dimensional dynamics analogous to Waddington's epigenetic landscape?
papers.core_contribution: The learning dynamics of Generalized Hopfield networks exhibit canalized, low-dimensional trajectories with sequential splitting of memories, resembling Waddington's epigenetic landscape, and are governed by saddle-node bifurcations.
papers.conclusion: Generalized Hopfield networks exhibit Waddingtonian dynamics during learning, providing a bridge between machine learning, dynamical systems theory, and biological differentiation.
papers.key_findings:
Learning in the prototype regime (high n) is canalized and reproducible, with memories following similar pathways and splitting sequentially.
The feature-to-prototype transition is characterized by metrics like maximum α and the number of prototypes needed for memory reconstruction.
A reduced two-memory system reveals bifurcations that explain the appearance and disappearance of saddles as nonlinearity (n) and temperature (Tr) vary.
The order in which digit categories are learned is reproducible and corresponds to the order of their disappearance when temperature is increased.
The final distribution of learned memories is path-dependent, influenced by the number and nature of saddles encountered during learning.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to other architectures like transformers and diffusion models to see if similar dynamics occur.
Further exploring the two-way bridge between differentiation biology and machine learning dynamics.
Investigating whether the feature-to-prototype transition and multiple learning regimes apply to differentiation biology.
papers.abstract: Networks in machine learning offer examples of complex high-dimensional dynamical systems reminiscent of biological systems. Here, we study the learning dynamics of Generalized Hopfield networks, which permit a visualization of internal memories. These networks have been shown to proceed through a 'feature-to-prototype' transition, as the strength of network nonlinearity is increased, wherein the learned, or terminal, states of internal memories transition from mixed to pure states. Focusing on the prototype learning dynamics of the internal memories we observe a strong resemblance to the canalized, or low-dimensional, dynamics of cells as they differentiate within a Waddingtonian landscape. Dynamically, we demonstrate that learning in a Generalized Hopfield Network proceeds through sequential 'splits' in memory space. Furthermore, order of splitting is interpretable and reproducible. The dynamics between the splits are canalized in the Waddington sense -- robust to variations in detailed aspects of the system. In attempting to make the analogy a rigorous equivalence, we study smaller subsystems that exhibit similar properties to the full system. We combine analytical calculations with numerical simulations to study the dynamical emergence of the feature-to-prototype transition, and the behaviour of splits in the landscape, saddles points, visited during learning. We exhibit regimes where saddles appear and disappear through saddle-node bifurcations, qualitatively changing the distribution of learned memories as the strength of the nonlinearity is varied -- allowing us to systematically investigate the mechanisms that underlie the emergence of Waddingtonian dynamics. Memories can thus differentiate in a predictive and controlled way, revealing new bridges between experimental biology, dynamical systems theory, and machine learning.

papers.title: Infinite Limits of Multi-head Transformer Dynamics
papers.research_question: What set of parameterizations admit well-defined infinite width and depth limits for transformer training dynamics, and how do these limits influence feature learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies parameterizations of transformers that yield well-defined infinite width and depth limits during feature learning, and uses dynamical mean field theory to analyze these limits, showing how the choice of scaling affects the diversity of attention heads and the update dynamics of attention layers.
papers.conclusion: Different scaling limits of transformers lead to qualitatively different training dynamics and feature learning behaviors, with the infinite head limit maintaining diversity of attention mechanisms while the infinite dimension-per-head limit collapses them.
papers.key_findings:
The infinite dimension-per-head (N → ∞) limit requires µP scaling (αA=1) and causes all attention heads to follow identical dynamics, effectively collapsing multi-head to single-head attention.
The infinite head (H → ∞) limit at fixed N leads to a distribution over attention heads and deterministic training dynamics, preserving head diversity.
Infinite depth limits depend on residual branch scaling: αL=1 allows attention layers to update non-negligibly as depth increases, while αL=1/2 leads to frozen attention weights and an SDE-like limit.
Numerical experiments on vision and language transformers show convergence to the theoretical limits and the influence of parameterization on learned features.
papers.limitation: In practice, large scale neural networks do not generally operate close to their limit.
papers.abstract: In this work, we analyze various scaling limits of the training dynamics of transformer models in the feature learning regime. We identify the set of parameterizations that admit well-defined infinite width and depth limits, allowing the attention layers to update throughout training--a relevant notion of feature learning in these models. We then use tools from dynamical mean field theory (DMFT) to analyze various infinite limits (infinite key/query dimension, infinite heads, and infinite depth) which have different statistical descriptions depending on which infinite limit is taken and how attention layers are scaled. We provide numerical evidence of convergence to the limits and discuss how the parameterization qualitatively influences learned features.

papers.title: How large language models encode theory-of-mind: a study on sparse parameter patterns
papers.research_question: Which parameters in LLMs are sensitive to Theory-of-Mind capabilities, and how do these parameters influence ToM reasoning performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to identify extremely sparse ToM-sensitive parameters in LLMs and shows that these parameters are linked to RoPE positional encoding, affecting attention mechanisms and degrading ToM performance when perturbed.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals that ToM capabilities in LLMs are governed by sparse, low-rank parameter patterns linked to positional encoding and attention mechanisms, providing insights into how LLMs perform social reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
An extremely sparse ToM-sensitive parameter pattern exists, whose perturbation significantly affects RoPE-based models' ToM capabilities, while random perturbations do not. This degradation is linked to a reduction in contextual localization and language understanding.
The functionality of the ToM-sensitive parameter pattern relates to the positional encoding module in LLM architectures. Perturbing the pattern in LLMs with RoPE disrupts dominant frequency activations, impairing contextual localization. LLMs without RoPE lack this frequency-dependent activation structure and exhibit different sensitivity patterns.
Perturbing ToM-sensitive parameter patterns affects the attention mechanism, thereby influencing language understanding. It alters the angle between q and k_BOS under positional encoding, destabilizing the attention sink and distorting the attention matrix.
papers.limitation: The study focuses only on false-belief tasks (unexpected contents and transfer) and does not evaluate the full spectrum of ToM abilities.
future_direction: Leveraging ToM-sensitive parameters for targeted model alignment to ensure AI systems align with human ethical norms while mitigating unintended social biases.
Comparing the identified sparse parameter structures to neural representations of ToM in the human brain for comparative cognitive modeling.
Investigating if targeted attacks could degrade LLM reasoning abilities given that ToM capabilities depend on sparse and structured parameter subsets, for robustness and adversarial testing.
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the emergence of Theory-of-Mind (ToM) capabilities in large language models (LLMs) from a mechanistic perspective, focusing on the role of extremely sparse parameter patterns. We introduce a novel method to identify ToM-sensitive parameters and reveal that perturbing as little as 0.001% of these parameters significantly degrades ToM performance while also impairing contextual localization and language understanding. To understand this effect, we analyze their interactions with core architectural components of LLMs. Our findings demonstrate that these sensitive parameters are closely linked to the positional encoding module, particularly in models using Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE), where perturbations disrupt dominant frequency activations critical for contextual processing. Furthermore, we show that perturbing ToM-sensitive parameters affects LLMs’ attention mechanism by modulating the angle between queries and keys under positional encoding. These insights provide a deeper understanding of how LLMs acquire social reasoning abilities, bridging AI interpretability with cognitive science.

papers.title: Emotions Where Art Thou: Understanding and Characterizing the Emotional Latent Space of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models (LLMs) internally represent emotion by analyzing the geometry of their hidden-state space?
papers.core_contribution: This work reveals a consistent and manipulable affective geometry in LLMs, showing that emotional representations form a low-dimensional, directionally encoded subspace that generalizes across datasets and languages, and can be steered via targeted interventions.
papers.conclusion: The findings reveal a consistent and manipulable affective geometry in LLMs and offer insight into how they internalize and process emotion.
papers.key_findings:
A low-dimensional emotional manifold exists in LLMs, with emotional representations being directionally encoded, distributed across layers, and aligned with interpretable dimensions.
The emotional structure is stable across depth and generalizes to eight real-world emotion datasets spanning five languages.
Cross-domain alignment yields low error and strong linear probe performance, indicating a universal emotional subspace.
Internal emotion perception can be steered while preserving semantics using a learned intervention module, with especially strong control for basic emotions across languages.
Emotional information is not localized but distributed broadly and redundantly throughout the network, with high separability emerging from overlapping, multi-purpose components.
papers.limitation: The steering technique does not uniformly override model behavior but respects representational limits, with variability in steerability across languages and domains (e.g., low-resource or archaic corpora) functioning as an inherent boundary.
papers.abstract: This work investigates how large language models (LLMs) internally represent emotion by analyzing the geometry of their hidden-state space. The paper identifies a low-dimensional emotional manifold and shows that emotional representations are directionally encoded, distributed across layers, and aligned with interpretable dimensions. These structures are stable across depth and generalize to eight real-world emotion datasets spanning five languages. Cross-domain alignment yields low error and strong linear probe performance, indicating a universal emotional subspace. Within this space, internal emotion perception can be steered while preserving semantics using a learned intervention module, with especially strong control for basic emotions across languages. These findings reveal a consistent and manipulable affective geometry in LLMs and offer insight into how they internalize and process emotion.

papers.title: Spontaneous Symmetry Breaking in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we understand the unprecedented performance and robustness of deep neural networks using field theory and spontaneous symmetry breaking?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a field theory framework for deep neural networks, showing that spontaneous symmetry breaking of weight symmetries explains generalization, robustness, and phenomena like training on random labels and gradient variance explosion.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a field theory understanding of deep neural networks, explaining many experimentally observed phenomena and offering a new perspective for architecture design and analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Deep neural networks undergo spontaneous symmetry breaking, which generates long-range correlations in weights and feature maps.
Spontaneous symmetry breaking explains the gradient variance explosion observed during training.
The framework explains why neural networks are robust and can train on random labels.
In residual networks, the decoupling limit leads to spontaneous symmetry breaking more easily due to small residual units.
The theory predicts weight freeze-out and the shattered gradients problem in non-residual networks.
papers.abstract: We propose a framework to understand the unprecedented performance and robustness of deep neural networks using field theory. Correlations between the weights within the same layer can be described by symmetries in that layer, and networks generalize better if such symmetries are broken to reduce the redundancies of the weights. Using a two parameter field theory, we find that the network can break such symmetries itself towards the end of training in a process commonly known in physics as spontaneous symmetry breaking. This corresponds to a network generalizing itself without any user input layers to break the symmetry, but by communication with adjacent layers. In the layer decoupling limit applicable to residual networks (He et al., 2015), we show that the remnant symmetries that survive the non-linear layers are spontaneously broken. The Lagrangian for the non-linear and weight layers together has striking similarities with the one in quantum field theory of a scalar. Using results from quantum field theory we show that our framework is able to explain many experimentally observed phenomena,such as training on random labels with zero error (Zhang et al., 2017), the information bottleneck, the phase transition out of it and gradient variance explosion (Shwartz-Ziv & Tishby, 2017), shattered gradients (Balduzzi et al., 2017), and many more.

papers.title: Scale-Invariance Drives Convergence in AI and Brain Representations
papers.research_question: Whether scale-invariance properties (dimensional stability and structural similarity across scales) of AI embeddings predict their alignment with fMRI data in the visual cortex.
papers.core_contribution: Scale-invariance properties (dimensional stability and structural similarity across scales) in AI embeddings predict alignment with fMRI data, and neural manifolds exhibit compact scale distributions. Pretraining on large multimodal datasets enhances scale-invariance and alignment.
papers.conclusion: Embedding manifolds with compact, scale-invariant structures align more effectively with fMRI activity in the visual cortex, supporting scale-invariance as a fundamental structural principle bridging artificial and neural representations. Pretraining on large multimodal datasets promotes such structures, while fine-tuning disrupts them.
papers.key_findings:
Embeddings with higher dimensional stability and stronger structural self-similarity across scales exhibit better alignment with fMRI data.
Neural manifolds have compact scale distributions, with structural features concentrated within specific scale ranges rather than extending to infinitesimal scales.
Incorporating language modalities and pre-training on larger datasets enhances the scale-invariance properties of embeddings, further improving their alignment with neural structures.
Fine-tuning disrupts scale-invariant structures, reducing cross-scale structural similarity.
At smaller scales, lower dimensionality correlates with better alignment, while at larger scales, higher dimensionality correlates with better alignment.
papers.limitation:
Difficulty in controlling multiple model variables simultaneously (dataset size, modality, fine-tuning) makes it challenging to isolate individual effects.
Analysis focuses on single brain regions, whereas neural systems represent information in a distributed manner across multiple regions.
future_direction: Systematically varying factors like dataset size, modality, and fine-tuning in controlled settings to isolate individual effects.
Extending the framework to multiple brain regions while minimizing the influence of irrelevant information.
papers.abstract: Despite variations in architecture and pretraining strategies, recent studies indicate that large-scale AI models often converge toward similar internal representations that also align with neural activity. We propose that scale-invariance, a fundamental structural principle in natural systems, is a key driver of this convergence. In this work, we propose a multi-scale analytical framework to quantify two core aspects of scale-invariance in AI representations: dimensional stability and structural similarity across scales. We further investigate whether these properties can predict alignment performance with functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) responses in the visual cortex. Our analysis reveals that embeddings with more consistent dimension and higher structural similarity across scales align better with fMRI data. Furthermore, we find that the manifold structure of fMRI data is more concentrated, with most features dissipating at smaller scales. Embeddings with similar scale patterns align more closely with fMRI data. We also show that larger pretraining datasets and the inclusion of language modalities enhance the scale-invariance properties of embeddings, further improving neural alignment. Our findings indicate that scale-invariance is a fundamental structural principle that bridges artificial and biological representations, providing a new framework for evaluating the structural quality of human-like AI systems.

papers.title: What Does BERT Learn about the Structure of Language?
papers.research_question: What linguistic structure does BERT learn? Specifically, can we unveil the representations learned by BERT to proto-linguistics structures?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that BERT captures hierarchical linguistic structure, with surface features in lower layers, syntactic in middle, and semantic in higher layers, and that it uses deeper layers for long-distance dependencies and implicitly captures tree-like structures.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that BERT captures structural properties of English language, with a hierarchy of linguistic signals and compositional modeling that parallels traditional syntactic analysis.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's phrasal representation captures phrase-level information in the lower layers, which gets diluted in higher layers.
BERT embeds a rich hierarchy of linguistic signals: surface information at the bottom, syntactic in the middle, and semantic at the top.
BERT requires deeper layers to handle long-distance dependency information, such as subject-verb agreement with more attractors.
BERT implicitly implements a tree-based compositional scheme, as shown by Tensor Product Decomposition Networks (TPDN) approximating BERT's representations.
The untrained version of BERT in higher layers outperforms the trained version in predicting sentence length, indicating that training trades off basic surface features for more complex information.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to English and may not generalize to other languages or noisy user-generated content.
future_direction: Investigating if the results transfer to other domains with higher syntactic variability, such as noisy user-generated content or morphologically-rich languages.
papers.abstract: BERT is a recent language representation model that has surprisingly performed well in diverse language understanding benchmarks. This result indicates the possibility that BERT networks capture structural information about language. In this work, we provide novel support for this claim by performing a series of experiments to unpack the elements of English language structure learned by BERT. We first show that BERT's phrasal representation captures phrase-level information in the lower layers. We also show that BERT's intermediate layers encode a rich hierarchy of linguistic information, with surface features at the bottom, syntactic features in the middle and semantic features at the top. BERT turns out to require deeper layers when long-distance dependency information is required, e.g. to track subjectverb agreement. Finally, we show that BERT representations capture linguistic information in a compositional way that mimics classical, tree-like structures.

papers.title: From Information to Generative Exponent: Learning Rate Induces Phase Transitions in SGD
papers.research_question: Can we characterize the regimes of complexity emerging from the choice of learning rate?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that learning rate induces phase transitions in sample complexity, shifting from an information exponent regime to a generative exponent regime, and introduces a new layer-wise training algorithm (alternating SGD) that can achieve linear sample complexity for certain targets.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that algorithms combining correlational and non-correlational update terms exhibit a phase transition in sample complexity regimes as a function of the scaling of the non-correlational term, governed by learning rate.
papers.key_findings:
There is a phase transition in sample complexity as a function of learning rate for gradient-based algorithms learning single-index models.
For batch reuse SGD, the sample complexity interpolates between the information exponent regime and the generative exponent regime depending on the learning rate.
Alternating SGD, a novel layer-wise training algorithm, can achieve linear sample complexity (up to polylog factors) when the square of the link function has information exponent 1 or 2 and the second-layer learning rate is sufficiently large.
The framework captures online SGD, batch reuse SGD, and alternating SGD, showing that the choice of learning rate is as critical as algorithm design for statistical and computational efficiency.
Phase transitions are characterized by thresholds in learning rate that depend on the information and generative exponents of the target link function.
future_direction: Extension of the framework to multi-index models
More general input distributions
Non-polynomial activation functions
Non-constant learning rates
papers.abstract: To understand feature learning dynamics in neural networks, recent theoretical works have focused on gradient-based learning of Gaussian single-index models, where the label is a nonlinear function of a latent one-dimensional projection of the input. While the sample complexity of online SGD is determined by the information exponent of the link function, recent works improved this by performing multiple gradient steps on the same sample with different learning rates -- yielding a non-correlational update rule -- and instead are limited by the (potentially much smaller) generative exponent. However, this picture is only valid when these learning rates are sufficiently large. In this paper, we characterize the relationship between learning rate(s) and sample complexity for a broad class of gradient-based algorithms that encapsulates both correlational and non-correlational updates. We demonstrate that, in certain cases, there is a phase transition from an "information exponent regime" with small learning rate to a "generative exponent regime" with large learning rate. Our framework covers prior analyses of one-pass SGD and SGD with batch reuse, while also introducing a new layer-wise training algorithm that leverages a two-timescales approach (via different learning rates for each layer) to go beyond correlational queries without reusing samples or modifying the loss from squared error. Our theoretical study demonstrates that the choice of learning rate is as important as the design of the algorithm in achieving statistical and computational efficiency.

papers.title: An effective theory of collective deep learning
papers.research_question: Does collective learning emerge when neural networks are put in interaction? Does this collective learning phase emerge abruptly, and do deep learning architectures play a non-trivial role?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a minimal model of collective learning in coupled neural networks, derives an effective theory predicting depth-dependent disorder-order-disorder phase transitions, and validates it on MNIST, showing that individual networks can generalize to unseen classes when collective learning emerges.
papers.conclusion: The work establishes a mathematical foundation for collective learning, enriching deep learning theories and statistical physics, and could contribute to tackling alignment problems in interacting learning models.
papers.key_findings:
The model exhibits disorder-order-disorder phase transitions in the parameters' solutions as coupling strength increases.
The collective learning phase emerges abruptly at a critical coupling strength, akin to a phase transition.
Deep networks show a depth-delayed onset of the collective learning phase.
The microscopic learning path is low-rank, driven by a single effective dimension (the input-output correlation vector).
Individual networks trained on private data can fully generalize to unseen data classes when the collective learning phase emerges.
papers.limitation:
The effective theory is based on simplifications and approximations, such as linear activation functions, mean square loss, one-dimensional data, and mean-field approximations.
The proof of concept does not cover the myriad of learning phases found in isolated neural networks.
future_direction: Extending the effective theory to the complex plane to capture more nuances and increase analytical tractability.
Exploring how the shape and difficulty of a dataset (encapsulated in the distribution of quenched disorders) affect the nature of phase transitions.
Investigating the effect of supra-network topology beyond the mean-field, undirected, pair-wise and time-independent case.
papers.abstract: Unraveling the emergence of collective learning in systems of coupled artificial neural networks points to broader implications for machine learning, neuroscience, and society. Here we introduce a minimal model that condenses several recent decentralized algorithms by considering a competition between two terms: the local learning dynamics in the parameters of each neural network unit, and a diffusive coupling among units that tends to homogenize the parameters of the ensemble. We derive an effective theory for linear networks to show that the coarse-grained behavior of our system is equivalent to a deformed Ginzburg-Landau model with quenched disorder. This framework predicts depth-dependent disorder-order-disorder phase transitions in the parameters' solutions that reveal a depth-delayed onset of a collective learning phase and a low-rank microscopic learning path. We validate the theory in coupled ensembles of realistic neural networks trained on the MNIST dataset under privacy constraints. Interestingly, experiments confirm that individual networks -- trained on private data -- can fully generalize to unseen data classes when the collective learning phase emerges. Our work establishes the physics of collective learning and contributes to the mechanistic interpretability of deep learning in decentralized settings.

papers.title: ReflCtrl: Controlling LLM Reflection via Representation Engineering
papers.research_question: When does the model initiate reflection during its reasoning process? How does reflection influence the model's reasoning performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces ReflCtrl, a representation engineering framework that extracts a reflection direction in the latent space to control self-reflection in reasoning LLMs, and shows that reflections are often redundant and can be reduced to save inference cost without sacrificing performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes ReflCtrl for controlling self-reflection in reasoning LLMs, demonstrates reflection redundancy and its connection to internal uncertainty, and shows that stepwise steering can reduce inference cost with minimal accuracy loss.
papers.key_findings:
Reflections are redundant, especially in stronger models, and up to 33.6% of reasoning tokens can be saved while preserving performance.
The model's reflection behavior is highly correlated with internal uncertainty signals, implying self-reflection may be controlled by model's uncertainty.
Stepwise steering can control reflection frequency and reduces performance loss compared to all-token steering.
The reflection direction can be used to predict answer correctness, suggesting it encodes uncertainty information.
Smaller models are more sensitive to reflection reduction than larger models.
papers.limitation:
Identification of reasoning steps relies on keyword search, which may be model specific.
ReflCtrl only works for open-source models and it remains unclear whether it generalizes to SOTA closed-source models such as GPT-4 or Claude.
future_direction: developing uncertainty-aware dynamic steering to adjust steering strength during inference
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning have achieved strong performance across diverse tasks, including mathematics, coding, and general reasoning. A distinctive ability of these reasoning models is self-reflection: the ability to review and revise previous reasoning steps. While self-reflection enhances reasoning performance, it also increases inference cost. In this work, we study self-reflection through the lens of representation engineering. We segment the model's reasoning into steps, identify the steps corresponding to reflection, and extract a reflection direction in the latent space that governs this behavior. Using this direction, we propose a stepwise steering method that can control reflection frequency. We call our framework ReflCtrl. Our experiments show that (1) in many cases reflections are redundant, especially in stronger models (in our experiments, we can save up to 33.6 percent of reasoning tokens while preserving performance), and (2) the model's reflection behavior is highly correlated with an internal uncertainty signal, implying self-reflection may be controlled by the model's uncertainty.

papers.title: Lessons from Neuroscience for AI: How integrating Actions, Compositional Structure and Episodic Memory could enable Safe, Interpretable and Human-Like AI
papers.research_question: How can integrating actions, compositional structure, and episodic memory from predictive coding models of the brain address deficiencies in current foundation models such as hallucinations, lack of grounding, and energy inefficiency?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that integrating actions, compositional structure, and episodic memory from neuroscience into foundation models can address deficiencies such as hallucinations, lack of grounding, and energy inefficiency, leading to safer, more interpretable, and human-like AI.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that rekindling the exchange between brain science and AI will pave the way towards safe and interpretable human-centered AI.
papers.key_findings:
Current foundation models lack integration of actions, which is crucial for grounding and world modeling.
Hierarchical compositional structure is missing, limiting reuse and efficient processing.
Episodic memory is not properly incorporated, affecting context retention and consolidation.
Integrating these components can reduce hallucinations and improve safety and interpretability.
A brain-inspired architecture combining world models, policy networks, and memory can enhance foundation models.
papers.abstract: The phenomenal advances in large language models (LLMs) and other foundation models over the past few years have been based on optimizing large-scale transformer models on the surprisingly simple objective of minimizing next-token prediction loss, a form of predictive coding that is also the backbone of an increasingly popular model of brain function in neuroscience and cognitive science. However, current foundation models ignore three other important components of state-of-the-art predictive coding models: tight integration of actions with generative models, hierarchical compositional structure, and episodic memory. We propose that to achieve safe, interpretable, energy-efficient, and human-like AI, foundation models should integrate actions, at multiple scales of abstraction, with a compositional generative architecture and episodic memory. We present recent evidence from neuroscience and cognitive science on the importance of each of these components. We describe how the addition of these missing components to foundation models could help address some of their current deficiencies: hallucinations and superficial understanding of concepts due to lack of grounding, a missing sense of agency/responsibility due to lack of control, threats to safety and trustworthiness due to lack of interpretability, and energy inefficiency. We compare our proposal to current trends, such as adding chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to foundation models, and discuss new ways of augmenting these models with brain-inspired components. We conclude by arguing that a rekindling of the historically fruitful exchange of ideas between brain science and AI will help pave the way towards safe and interpretable human-centered AI.

papers.title: Formalising the Use of the Activation Function in Neural Inference
papers.research_question: We investigate how the activation function can be used to describe neural firing in an abstract way, and in turn, why it works well in artificial neural networks.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that typical activation functions (sigmoid and ReLU) emerge from a mean-field model of neural dynamics based on the Ising model, providing a physical justification for their use in artificial neural networks.
papers.conclusion: We have shown that, as a model of the key features of real neural dynamics, an artificial neural network is a mean field model of biological neural networks. This model falls in the Ising universality class, and thus an artificial neural network naturally exhibits a sigmoidal or tanh-like switching behaviour between firing and not firing.
papers.key_findings:
The activation function in artificial neural networks can be derived from a mean-field model of biological neural spiking using the Ising model.
The hyperbolic tangent (tanh) activation function arises from the mean-field description of the Ising phase transition.
ReLU and ELU activation functions can be recovered as integrals of the sigmoid, representing firing rates over time.
The model suggests that artificial neural networks are mean-field approximations of biological neural networks.
The analysis connects energy-based learning and sparse coding to the statistical mechanical perspective.
papers.abstract: We investigate how the activation function can be used to describe neural firing in an abstract way, and in turn, why it works well in artificial neural networks. We discuss how a spike in a biological neurone belongs to a particular universality class of phase transitions in statistical physics. We then show that the artificial neurone is, mathematically, a mean field model of biological neural membrane dynamics, which arises from modelling spiking as a phase transition. This allows us to treat selective neural firing in an abstract way, and formalise the role of the activation function in perceptron learning. The resultant statistical physical model allows us to recover the expressions for some known activation functions as various special cases. Along with deriving this model and specifying the analogous neural case, we analyse the phase transition to understand the physics of neural network learning. Together, it is shown that there is not only a biological meaning, but a physical justification, for the emergence and performance of typical activation functions; implications for neural learning and inference are also discussed.

papers.title: How 'Neural' is a Neural Foundation Model?
papers.research_question: Do neural decoding and encoding manifolds reveal new insights into how foundation models represent temporal response patterns? Are their representations brain-like?
papers.core_contribution: The recurrent module of the neural foundation model shows brain-like representational properties, while the feedforward encoder and readout module have limitations; design changes are suggested for better biological alignment.
papers.conclusion: The FNN is only a partial digital twin of the mouse visual system; its recurrent module is most brain-like, but design improvements in early recurrence and readout constraints could enhance biological alignment.
papers.key_findings:
The recurrent module achieves the highest stimulus separability and closest alignment with biological visual cortex.
The feedforward encoder lacks biologically plausible temporal patterns and contains non-selective neurons.
The readout module uses numerous specialized feature maps rather than biologically plausible mechanisms.
Decoding trajectories in the recurrent stage show tubular structure but fewer crossings than biological data, indicating less complex dynamics.
Encoding manifolds reveal that the FNN's neuronal organization, especially in the readout, is clustered by feature maps and differs from the continuous topology of biological cortex.
papers.limitation:
The FNN does not fully capture the complexity of neural dynamics, as evidenced by fewer crossings in decoding trajectories compared to biological data.
The readout module's highly clustered, feature-map-based organization is not brain-like.
future_direction: Introduce recurrence in early encoder stages.
Constraining features in the readout module to be more biologically plausible.
Investigate more complex temporal processing to better match biological dynamics.
papers.abstract: Foundation models have shown remarkable success in fitting biological visual systems; however, their black-box nature inherently limits their utility for understanding brain function. Here, we peek inside a SOTA foundation model of neural activity (Wang et al., 2025) as a physiologist might, characterizing each 'neuron' based on its temporal response properties to parametric stimuli. We analyze how different stimuli are represented in neural activity space by building decoding manifolds, and we analyze how different neurons are represented in stimulus-response space by building neural encoding manifolds. We find that the different processing stages of the model (i.e., the feedforward encoder, recurrent, and readout modules) each exhibit qualitatively different representational structures in these manifolds. The recurrent module shows a jump in capabilities over the encoder module by 'pushing apart' the representations of different temporal stimulus patterns. Our 'tubularity' metric quantifies this stimulus-dependent development of neural activity as biologically plausible. The readout module achieves high fidelity by using numerous specialized feature maps rather than biologically plausible mechanisms. Overall, this study provides a window into the inner workings of a prominent neural foundation model, gaining insights into the biological relevance of its internals through the novel analysis of its neurons' joint temporal response patterns. Our findings suggest design changes that could bring neural foundation models into closer alignment with biological systems: introducing recurrence in early encoder stages, and constraining features in the readout module.

papers.title: Internal representations analysis in spiking neural networks
papers.research_question: Whether signatures of criticality, such as broad-tailed distributions of fluctuations, characterize the internal representations of a multilayer spiking neural network performing a recognition task.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that broad-tailed fluctuations in internal representations emerge during input label transitions in a spiking neural network, even under partial training or a simple anesthesia model, and that the Perturbational Complexity Index can characterize the spatio-temporal complexity of these representations.
papers.conclusion: The change in environmental stimulus induces broad-tailed distributions of correlation fluctuations in the internal representations of a spiking neural network, even when performance is impaired. These fluctuations are not necessarily a signature of criticality but rather result from the dynamics of transitioning between attractors.
papers.key_findings:
Broad-tailed distributions of internal representation fluctuations appear when the network input changes (label transitions).
These fluctuations are present even when the network is not fully trained or under the effect of a simple anesthesia model.
The Perturbational Complexity Index (PCI) distinguishes levels of training time and the effect of anesthesia.
Insufficient evidence was found for power law distributions of avalanche size and duration, suggesting the network is not necessarily critical.
The observed fluctuations are attributed to the network searching for a new attractor when the input changes.
papers.limitation: Insufficient evidence of power law distributions of avalanche size and duration, indicating the network may not be critical.
papers.abstract: Optimal information processing in peripheral sensory systems has been associated in several examples to the signature of a critical or near critical state. Furthermore, cortical systems have also been described to be in a critical state in both wake and anesthetized experimental models, both in vitro and in vivo. Using a methodology inspired in the biological setup, we investigate whether a similar signature characterizes the internal representations (IR) of a multilayer (deep) spiking artificial neural network performing a recognition task. The increase of the characteristic time of the decay of the correlation of fluctuations of the IR, found when the network input changes are indications of a broad-tailed distribution of IR fluctuations. The broad tails are present even when the network is not yet capable of performing the classification tasks, either due to partial training or to the effect of a low dose of anesthesia in a simple model. This is a signature only for significant changes involving labeled inputs. However, we don\\'t find enough evidence of power law distributions of avalanche size and duration. Finally, the perturbational complexity index (PCI) of IR was measured. The PCI distinguished levels of training time and also effect of anesthesia leading to a characterization of the spatio-temporal pattern of activity in the internal layers.

papers.title: Spring-block theory of feature learning in deep neural networks
papers.research_question: How does feature learning in deep neural networks emerge from the interplay of nonlinearity, noise, learning rate, and other factors, and can it be explained by a macroscopic mechanical theory?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a spring-block mechanical theory that explains the noise-nonlinearity phase diagram of feature learning in deep neural networks and connects layerwise data separation to generalization.
papers.conclusion: The spring-block model provides a top-down phenomenological explanation for feature learning in DNNs, linking noise and nonlinearity to layerwise data separation and generalization, with implications for hyperparameter tuning.
papers.key_findings:
DNN training shows a noise-nonlinearity phase diagram where concave load curves (deep layers learn better) occur with high nonlinearity and low noise, while convex curves (shallow layers learn better) occur with high noise and low nonlinearity.
A spring-block chain model with asymmetric friction captures the dynamics of data separation across layers, explaining the phase diagram.
Noise in training (from dropout, batch size, etc.) rebalances the load across layers, reducing effective friction and leading to more uniform separation.
Nonlinearity acts like friction, absorbing load and causing deeper layers to separate data more, leading to concave load curves.
Linear load curves (equiseparation) are associated with the highest test accuracy, suggesting a link between balanced feature learning and generalization.
papers.limitation: The theory applies only to DNNs with homogeneous layers; heterogeneous architectures require new models.
future_direction: Extending the theory to heterogeneous DNNs with different layer types.
Developing new hyperparameter tuning and model selection strategies based on the spring-block analogy.
papers.abstract: Feature-learning deep nets progressively collapse data to a regular low-dimensional geometry. How this emerges from the collective action of nonlinearity, noise, learning rate, and other factors, has eluded first-principles theories built from microscopic neuronal dynamics. We exhibit a noise-nonlinearity phase diagram that identifies regimes where shallow or deep layers learn more effectively and propose a macroscopic mechanical theory that reproduces the diagram and links feature learning across layers to generalization.

papers.title: A phase transition between positional and semantic learning in a solvable model of dot-product attention
papers.research_question: What conditions lead to the emergence of positional versus semantic attention mechanisms in a dot-product attention model, and is there a phase transition between these regimes as sample complexity increases?
papers.core_contribution: We provide a tight theoretical analysis of a solvable dot-product attention model, showing a phase transition between positional and semantic learning mechanisms as sample complexity increases, and demonstrate that the attention layer outperforms a linear baseline when learning the semantic mechanism given sufficient data.
papers.conclusion: We have provided a theoretical characterization of the emergence of semantic attention in a dot-product attention model, showing a phase transition between positional and semantic learning regimes, opening the door to further theoretical studies of phase transitions in attention-based models.
papers.key_findings:
The model exhibits two distinct minima: a positional attention mechanism (tokens attend based on position) and a semantic attention mechanism (tokens attend based on meaning).
There exists a phase transition from the positional to the semantic minimum as the sample complexity increases.
The dot-product attention layer outperforms a linear positional baseline when it learns the semantic mechanism, given sufficient data.
The phase transition is sharp and can be characterized analytically in the high-dimensional limit.
The global minimum of the empirical loss landscape switches between positional and semantic solutions at a critical sample complexity, which depends on the task's positional/semantic composition.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to a simplified model with a single attention layer, tied low-rank weights, and Gaussian input data.
future_direction: Extensions to more complex architectures and data distributions
Rigorous justification of the GAMP convergence
Study of phase transitions in deeper transformer models
papers.abstract: Many empirical studies have provided evidence for the emergence of algorithmic mechanisms (abilities) in the learning of language models, that lead to qualitative improvements of the model capabilities. Yet, a theoretical characterization of how such mechanisms emerge remains elusive. In this paper, we take a step in this direction by providing a tight theoretical analysis of the emergence of semantic attention in a solvable model of dot-product attention. More precisely, we consider a non-linear self-attention layer with trainable tied and low-rank query and key matrices. In the asymptotic limit of high-dimensional data and a comparably large number of training samples we provide a tight closed-form characterization of the global minimum of the non-convex empirical loss landscape. We show that this minimum corresponds to either a positional attention mechanism (with tokens attending to each other based on their respective positions) or a semantic attention mechanism (with tokens attending to each other based on their meaning), and evidence an emergent phase transition from the former to the latter with increasing sample complexity. Finally, we compare the dot-product attention layer to a linear positional baseline, and show that it outperforms the latter using the semantic mechanism provided it has access to sufficient data.

papers.title: Progress measures for grokking via mechanistic interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we find continuous progress measures that underlie seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes (like grokking) in neural networks? The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to reverse-engineer learned behaviors and define such progress measures.
papers.core_contribution: The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to define progress measures for grokking, showing that grokking arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms (a Fourier multiplication algorithm) followed by removal of memorizing components, rather than being a sudden shift.
papers.conclusion: Grokking is not a sudden shift but results from gradual mechanisms, and mechanistic interpretability can reveal progress measures that track the development of emergent behavior.
papers.key_findings:
The transformers implement modular addition using a Fourier multiplication algorithm that maps inputs to a circle and uses trigonometric identities.
The model's weights and activations show periodic structure and are sparse in the Fourier domain, with key frequencies.
Two progress measures (restricted loss and excluded loss) improve continuously prior to grokking, revealing hidden progress.
Training can be split into three phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup.
The sudden transition to perfect test accuracy occurs during cleanup, after the generalizing mechanism is already learned.
papers.limitation: There is significant uncertainty about the scalability of mechanistic interpretability approaches to large models.
future_direction: Apply the approach to more complex tasks and models.
Use progress measures to predict and understand emergent behavior in large language models.
Explore task-independent progress measures.
papers.abstract: Neural networks often exhibit emergent behavior, where qualitatively new capabilities arise from scaling up the amount of parameters, training data, or training steps. One approach to understanding emergence is to find continuous \textit{progress measures} that underlie the seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes. We argue that progress measures can be found via mechanistic interpretability: reverse-engineering learned behaviors into their individual components. As a case study, we investigate the recently-discovered phenomenon of ``grokking'' exhibited by small transformers trained on modular addition tasks. We fully reverse engineer the algorithm learned by these networks, which uses discrete Fourier transforms and trigonometric identities to convert addition to rotation about a circle. We confirm the algorithm by analyzing the activations and weights and by performing ablations in Fourier space. Based on this understanding, we define progress measures that allow us to study the dynamics of training and split training into three continuous phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup. Our results show that grokking, rather than being a sudden shift, arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms encoded in the weights, followed by the later removal of memorizing components.

papers.title: Microscopic and collective signatures of feature learning in neural networks
papers.research_question: What are the collective and microscopic signatures of feature learning in Bayesian shallow neural networks in the proportional regime?
papers.core_contribution: In the proportional regime, feature learning in Bayesian shallow neural networks is characterized by a nonmonotonic distance between class manifolds and finite, data-dependent weight correlations.
papers.conclusion: The squared distance between class manifolds and the finite weight correlations are collective and microscopic signatures of feature learning in Bayesian shallow networks in the proportional regime.
papers.key_findings:
The posterior distance between class manifolds remains unaltered in the infinite-width limit but departs from its prior value at proportional width.
The average squared distance is a nonmonotonic function of temperature, and this nonmonotonicity disappears in the infinite-width limit or when labels are randomized.
The hidden-layer weights become correlated in the proportional regime, undergoing a finite displacement.
The nonmonotonicity of the distance aligns with inversion dynamics observed during gradient descent training, serving as an equilibrium counterpart.
The second-order statistics of the weights depends on input patterns in a way not traceable to the infinite-width limit.
papers.limitation:
The results are limited to standard-scaled neural networks and do not apply to mean-field scaling.
The theory does not characterize feature learning closer to the interpolation threshold.
papers.abstract: Feature extraction - the ability to identify relevant properties of data - is a key factor underlying the success of deep learning. Yet, it has proved difficult to elucidate its nature within existing predictive theories, to the extent that there is no consensus on the very definition of feature learning. A promising hint in this direction comes from previous phenomenological observations of quasi-universal aspects in the training dynamics of neural networks, displayed by simple properties of feature geometry. We address this problem within a statistical-mechanics framework for Bayesian learning in one hidden layer neural networks with standard parameterization. Analytical computations in the proportional limit (when both the network width and the size of the training set are large) can quantify fingerprints of feature learning, both collective ones (related to manifold geometry) and microscopic ones (related to the weights). In particular, (i) the distance between different class manifolds in feature space is a nonmonotonic function of the temperature, which we interpret as the equilibrium counterpart of a phenomenon observed under gradient descent (GD) dynamics, and (ii) the microscopic learnable parameters in the network undergo a finite data-dependent displacement with respect to the infinite-width limit, and develop correlations. These results indicate that nontrivial feature learning is at play in a regime where the posterior predictive distribution is that of Gaussian process regression with a trivially rescaled prior.

papers.title: Learning by Steering the Neural Dynamics: A Statistical Mechanics Perspective
papers.research_question: How can we design biologically plausible, local learning strategies for neural networks that are sample-efficient and robust, without relying on backpropagation?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a biologically plausible, local learning algorithm for binary recurrent neural networks that maps input-output relationships to fixed points of the network dynamics, and provides a theoretical analysis of fixed points in random asymmetric RNNs using statistical mechanics.
papers.conclusion: The thesis presents a step towards bridging neuroscience and AI by proposing a biologically plausible learning algorithm and theoretically analyzing fixed points in RNNs, with limitations in scalability and biological realism that point to future work.
papers.key_findings:
Derived an analytical expression for the number of fixed points in random asymmetric RNNs and identified a phase transition in their structure as self-coupling strength varies.
Found that above a critical self-coupling strength, dense clusters of fixed points emerge, which are accessible to simple dynamical rules.
The proposed algorithm successfully learns a non-linearly separable classification task on an entangled MNIST dataset.
The algorithm's hetero-association capacity increases with network depth.
Introducing ferromagnetic couplings can stabilize learning similarly to self-coupling.
papers.limitation: The approach has not been scaled to more challenging machine learning benchmarks.
future_direction: Scaling the approach to more challenging machine learning benchmarks.
Introducing spiking dynamics, populations of excitatory and inhibitory neurons, sparsity, and insights from connectomics for greater biological realism.
papers.abstract: Despite the striking successes of deep neural networks trained with gradient-based optimization, these methods differ fundamentally from their biological counterparts. This gap raises key questions about how nature achieves robust, sample-efficient learning at minimal energy costs and solves the credit-assignment problem without backpropagation. We take a step toward bridging contemporary AI and computational neuroscience by studying how neural dynamics can support fully local, distributed learning that scales to simple machine-learning benchmarks. Using tools from statistical mechanics, we identify conditions for the emergence of robust dynamical attractors in random asymmetric recurrent networks. We derive a closed-form expression for the number of fixed points as a function of self-coupling strength, and we reveal a phase transition in their structure: below a critical self-coupling, isolated fixed points coexist with exponentially many narrow clusters showing the overlap-gap property; above it, subdominant yet dense and extensive clusters appear. These fixed points become accessible, including to a simple asynchronous dynamical rule, after an algorithm-dependent self-coupling threshold. Building on this analysis, we propose a biologically plausible algorithm for supervised learning with any binary recurrent network. Inputs are mapped to fixed points of the dynamics, by relaxing under transient external stimuli and stabilizing the resulting configurations via local plasticity. We show that our algorithm can learn an entangled version of MNIST, leverages depth to develop hierarchical representations and increase hetero-association capacity, and is applicable to several architectures. Finally, we highlight the strong connection between algorithm performance and the unveiled phase transition, and we suggest a cortex-inspired alternative to self-couplings for its emergence.

papers.title: From Black Boxes to Transparent Minds: Evaluating and Enhancing the Theory of Mind in Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we evaluate and enhance Theory of Mind (ToM) capabilities in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) from an interpretability perspective?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces GridToM, a novel multimodal dataset for evaluating Theory of Mind (ToM), analyzes internal attention representations in MLLMs to show they distinguish perspective information, and proposes a training-free intervention method that enhances ToM performance by shifting activations along specific attention head directions.
papers.conclusion: The analysis of internal mechanisms shows that MLLMs develop attention heads capable of distinguishing perspective information and reasoning about beliefs, and targeted interventions based on these representations can significantly enhance their exhibited Theory of Mind capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads in multimodal large language models can distinguish cognitive information across different perspectives, providing evidence of internal Theory of Mind representations.
A training-free intervention method, which adjusts activations in the direction of sensitive attention heads, significantly improves model performance on first-order and second-order belief tasks.
Multimodal large language models perform better on text-based ToM tasks compared to video-only tasks.
Linear probing reveals that belief states are linearly separable in the activation space of attention heads, indicating structured internal representations.
The constructed GridToM dataset enables comprehensive and interpretability-driven evaluation of ToM capabilities in MLLMs.
papers.limitation:
The tasks in the dataset are limited to first-order and second-order belief tasks within the ATOMs framework, while ToM theory encompasses a broader range of unexplored tasks.
Due to restrictions in accessing model code, the approach was only validated on a limited selection of MLLMs.
papers.abstract: As large language models evolve, there is growing anticipation that they will emulate human-like Theory of Mind (ToM) to assist with routine tasks. However, existing methods for evaluating machine ToM focus primarily on unimodal models and largely treat these models as black boxes, lacking an interpretative exploration of their internal mechanisms. In response, this study adopts an approach based on internal mechanisms to provide an interpretability-driven assessment of ToM in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). Specifically, we first construct a multimodal ToM test dataset, GridToM, which incorporates diverse belief testing tasks and perceptual information from multiple perspectives. Next, our analysis shows that attention heads in multimodal large models can distinguish cognitive information across perspectives, providing evidence of ToM capabilities. Furthermore, we present a lightweight, training-free approach that significantly enhances the model's exhibited ToM by adjusting in the direction of the attention head.

papers.title: Towards Understanding Grokking: An Effective Theory of Representation Learning
papers.research_question: What is the origin of generalization in grokking? Why does the training time needed to generalize diverge as training set size decreases? Under what conditions does delayed generalization occur?
papers.core_contribution: Provides an effective theory and phase diagrams to explain grokking, showing that generalization arises from structured representations and that grokking can be understood as a phase between comprehension and memorization.
papers.conclusion: This study provides intuitive explanations of the origin of grokking and highlights the usefulness of physics-inspired tools, such as effective theories and phase diagrams, for understanding deep learning.
papers.key_findings:
Generalization in grokking originates from structured representations, whose dynamics are predicted by an effective theory.
There are four learning phases: comprehension, grokking, memorization, and confusion, with representation learning occurring only in a 'Goldilocks zone'.
On transformers, the grokking phase stays closer to memorization, leading to delayed generalization.
The critical training set size corresponds to the least amount of data needed to determine a good representation.
Grokking can be remedied with proper hyperparameter tuning, as shown in phase diagrams.
papers.limitation: The effective theory is based on Euclidean distance between embeddings and might not capture other metrics defined by the decoder.
future_direction: Generalizing the effective theory to use metrics beyond Euclidean distance.
Investigating modifications to the effective theory to account for repulsion among different classes in image classification.
papers.abstract: We aim to understand grokking, a phenomenon where models generalize long after overfitting their training set. We present both a microscopic analysis anchored by an effective theory and a macroscopic analysis of phase diagrams describing learning performance across hyperparameters. We find that generalization originates from structured representations whose training dynamics and dependence on training set size can be predicted by our effective theory in a toy setting. We observe empirically the presence of four learning phases: comprehension, grokking, memorization, and confusion. We find representation learning to occur only in a "Goldilocks zone" (including comprehension and grokking) between memorization and confusion. We find on transformers the grokking phase stays closer to the memorization phase (compared to the comprehension phase), leading to delayed generalization. The Goldilocks phase is reminiscent of "intelligence from starvation" in Darwinian evolution, where resource limitations drive discovery of more efficient solutions. This study not only provides intuitive explanations of the origin of grokking, but also highlights the usefulness of physics-inspired tools, e.g., effective theories and phase diagrams, for understanding deep learning.

papers.title: On the Origins of the Block Structure Phenomenon in Neural Network Representations
papers.research_question: What is the origin of the block structure phenomenon in neural network representations? Does it arise from overfitting to spurious data features or does it capture meaningful dataset statistics?
papers.core_contribution: The block structure phenomenon arises from dominant datapoints that share simple image statistics (e.g., background color), which vary across random seeds. The block structure can be eliminated via principal component regularization without harming performance.
papers.conclusion: The block structure captures real but simple dataset statistics, and its inconsistency across seeds is due to variation in which statistics are captured. Training interventions like principal component regularization can reduce the block structure and improve representational consistency.
papers.key_findings:
The block structure is caused by a small set of dominant datapoints that share similar image statistics (e.g., background color).
The set of dominant datapoints and the specific image statistic they capture vary across random seeds.
Removing dominant datapoints from the analysis eliminates the block structure.
The block structure emerges early in training, but the dominant datapoints and representations continue to change substantially.
Principal component regularization can eliminate the block structure and improve model consistency across seeds without hurting accuracy.
papers.limitation:
Focus on image classification tasks and ResNet architectures; it remains to be seen how the block structure manifests in other domains and architectures.
Analysis is primarily empirical; a theoretical understanding is left for future work.
future_direction: Exploring how dominant datapoints manifest in other domains and applications.
Applying principal component regularization to distribution shift and self-supervision problems.
papers.abstract: Recent work has uncovered a striking phenomenon in large-capacity neural networks: they contain blocks of contiguous hidden layers with highly similar representations. This block structure has two seemingly contradictory properties: on the one hand, its constituent layers exhibit highly similar dominant first principal components (PCs), but on the other hand, their representations, and their common first PC, are highly dissimilar across different random seeds. Our work seeks to reconcile these discrepant properties by investigating the origin of the block structure in relation to the data and training methods. By analyzing properties of the dominant PCs, we find that the block structure arises from dominant datapoints - a small group of examples that share similar image statistics (e.g. background color). However, the set of dominant datapoints, and the precise shared image statistic, can vary across random seeds. Thus, the block structure reflects meaningful dataset statistics, but is simultaneously unique to each model. Through studying hidden layer activations and creating synthetic datapoints, we demonstrate that these simple image statistics dominate the representational geometry of the layers inside the block structure. We explore how the phenomenon evolves through training, finding that the block structure takes shape early in training, but the underlying representations and the corresponding dominant datapoints continue to change substantially. Finally, we study the interplay between the block structure and different training mechanisms, introducing a targeted intervention to eliminate the block structure, as well as examining the effects of pretraining and Shake-Shake regularization.

papers.title: Grokking in the Ising Model
papers.research_question: What causes grokking in a dense neural network trained on 2D Ising model configurations with weight decay, and how does the network architecture evolve during this process?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that grokking in an Ising model classifier results from a transition to a sparse network architecture where later layers have fewer active neurons, enabling generalization by processing global features.
papers.conclusion: Grokking in the Ising model involves a phase transition to a sparse network architecture, where sparsity in later layers facilitates generalization by focusing on global features, as visualized through PCA-based techniques.
papers.key_findings:
Grokking occurs in MLPs trained on Ising model data with weight decay, characterized by a delayed increase in test accuracy after overfitting.
During grokking, the network evolves into a sparse architecture with monotonically decreasing active neurons per layer, analogous to CNNs.
Sparse final layers identify global features of input classes, reducing classification errors from multiple paths.
PCA analysis shows that gradients and activations become structured during grokking, forming clusters corresponding to energy categories.
Dropout suppresses grokking by preventing the formation of stable sparse subnetworks, accelerating generalization.
