future_direction: Extending the theory to adaptive optimizers and large learning rates.
Exploring the role of discrete symmetries.
Investigating the connection to biological learning.
papers.abstract: With the rapid discovery of emergent phenomena in deep learning and large language models, understanding their cause has become an urgent need. Here, we propose a rigorous entropic-force theory for understanding the learning dynamics of neural networks trained with stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and its variants. Building on the theory of parameter symmetries and an entropic loss landscape, we show that representation learning is crucially governed by emergent entropic forces arising from stochasticity and discrete-time updates. These forces systematically break continuous parameter symmetries and preserve discrete ones, leading to a series of gradient balance phenomena that resemble the equipartition property of thermal systems. These phenomena, in turn, (a) explain the universal alignment of neural representations between AI models and lead to a proof of the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, and (b) reconcile the seemingly contradictory observations of sharpness- and flatness-seeking behavior of deep learning optimization. Our theory and experiments demonstrate that a combination of entropic forces and symmetry breaking is key to understanding emergent phenomena in deep learning.

papers.title: Phase Transitions between Accuracy Regimes in L2 regularized Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can phase transitions in L2 regularized deep neural networks be explained geometrically, and can this geometric perspective explain the phenomenon of grokking?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a geometric explanation of phase transitions in L2 regularized deep neural networks using Ricci curvature, predicts additional transitions with increased data complexity, and explains grokking as a hysteresis effect due to first-order phase transitions.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates phase transitions in L2-regularized neural networks linked to geometric change-points in the error landscape, and provides a mechanistic explanation of grokking as hysteresis due to first-order phase transitions.
papers.key_findings:
Increasing L2 regularization causes a first-order phase transition (onset-of-learning) in DNNs, visible as a jump in error and curvature.
Additional phase transitions occur when data complexity is increased, corresponding to geometric change-points in the error landscape.
The Ricci scalar curvature shows sudden changes at transition points, linking geometry to accuracy phases.
Grokking is reproduced as a hysteresis effect where models initialized in low-accuracy phases take many epochs to escape to high-accuracy phases.
The number of transitions increases with data complexity, as demonstrated with MNIST classification.
papers.limitation:
Cannot deduce details on the global structure of the error landscape; cannot guarantee detection of all phases and change-points.
Lack of rigorous bounds on the number of local minima and schemes to avoid hysteresis effects.
future_direction: Develop rigorous bounds on numbers of local minima and schemes to avoid hysteresis.
Investigate error basins linked to accuracy phases and better understand global error geometry.
Develop new probing methods for the intrinsic structure of DNNs beyond L2 regularization.
papers.abstract: Increasing the L2 regularization of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) causes a first-order phase transition into the under-parametrized phase -- the so-called onset-of learning. We explain this transition via the scalar (Ricci) curvature of the error landscape. We predict new transition points as the data complexity is increased and, in accordance with the theory of phase transitions, the existence of hysteresis effects. We confirm both predictions numerically. Our results provide a natural explanation of the recently discovered phenomenon of '\emph{grokking}' as DNN models getting stuck in a local minimum of the error surface, corresponding to a lower accuracy phase. Our work paves the way for new probing methods of the intrinsic structure of DNNs in and beyond the L2 context.

papers.title: Physics Steering: Causal Control of Cross-Domain Concepts in a Physics Foundation Model
papers.research_question: Whether scientific foundation models learn abstract, domain-general representations of physical phenomena that can be causally manipulated via activation steering.
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that a physics foundation model learns linearly steerable representations of physical concepts (e.g., vorticity, diffusion, temporal progression), and that injecting these directions during inference enables fine-grained causal control over simulation behavior. The concept directions are domain-general and transfer across unrelated physical systems.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability techniques from LLMs can be successfully adapted to scientific foundation models, providing evidence that these models develop abstract, domain-general representations of fundamental physical concepts that are linearly encoded and causally steerable.
papers.key_findings:
Single directions in the model's activation space correspond to specific physical concepts like vorticity, diffusion, and simulation speed.
Injecting (adding or subtracting) these concept directions during inference causally steers model predictions, allowing induction or suppression of vortices, enhancement or suppression of diffusion, and speeding up or slowing down simulations.
The extracted concept directions transfer successfully between unrelated physical systems (e.g., from fluid dynamics to chemical reaction-diffusion), indicating they represent abstract, domain-general physical principles.
The results support the Linear Representation Hypothesis for scientific foundation models, showing physical concepts are represented linearly in activation space.
Steering effects are more physically plausible and interpretable when using spatially-averaged concept directions that discard spatial structure, compared to using full spatial tensors.
papers.limitation:
The physical plausibility of the steered results is an open question; including spatial dimensions in the steering tensor can lead to less physically realistic outcomes.
The effectiveness of steering depends on the initial conditions of the simulation; steering becomes more difficult and can produce distorted fields when the initial state is far from the target regime.
future_direction: Exploring the layer-dependence of concept representations and steering effects.
Further work to definitively assess the physicality and self-consistency of steered simulation results.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in mechanistic interpretability have revealed that large language models (LLMs) develop internal representations corresponding not only to concrete entities but also distinct, human-understandable abstract concepts and behaviour. Moreover, these hidden features can be directly manipulated to steer model behaviour. However, it remains an open question whether this phenomenon is unique to models trained on inherently structured data (ie. language, images) or if it is a general property of foundation models. In this work, we investigate the internal representations of a large physics-focused foundation model. Inspired by recent work identifying single directions in activation space for complex behaviours in LLMs, we extract activation vectors from the model during forward passes over simulation datasets for different physical regimes. We then compute "delta" representations between the two regimes. These delta tensors act as concept directions in activation space, encoding specific physical features. By injecting these concept directions back into the model during inference, we can steer its predictions, demonstrating causal control over physical behaviours, such as inducing or removing some particular physical feature from a simulation. These results suggest that scientific foundation models learn generalised representations of physical principles. They do not merely rely on superficial correlations and patterns in the simulations. Our findings open new avenues for understanding and controlling scientific foundation models and has implications for AI-enabled scientific discovery.

papers.title: Representation Mechanics: Invariant-Governed Learning Dynamics
papers.research_question: How can neural networks with set-valued operations and learned selection achieve generalization by learning and preserving invariants, as evidenced by early phase transitions (the Platonic Spike)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Representation Mechanics, showing that neural networks with set-valued operations and learned selection can achieve generalization by learning invariants, as evidenced by the Platonic Spike (early phase transition where validation accuracy exceeds training accuracy).
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that invariant-preserving inductive bias is sufficient for rule learning and that constructing reliable AI requires respecting the mechanics of representation (treating embeddings as physical objects with inertia, boundaries, and elasticity).
papers.key_findings:
Set-valued weights with learned selection lead to early phase transitions (Platonic Spike) where validation accuracy exceeds training accuracy.
Classical activations (e.g., GELU, ELU, ReLU) interfere with basin preservation and cause overfitting or boundary erosion.
Basin preservation via path freezing can prevent catastrophic forgetting by maintaining separatrix integrity.
The Surgical Clutch mechanism allows for invariant maintenance under continual learning by dynamically routing gradients.
The architecture achieves high accuracy on synthetic logic and language tasks without relying on n-gram statistics.
papers.limitation: The current work uses explicit rule contexts, which may not be available in all domains, and the architecture has not yet been tested at scale.
future_direction: Testing the architecture at scale
Exploring amplification strategies (more branches, hierarchical scoring, contrastive loss)
Extending to domains without explicit rule contexts
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> We present Representation Mechanics, a theoretical and empirical framework characterizing learning in invariant-governed domains. We demonstrate that neural networks with set-valued operations (discrete potentials {-W, 0, +W}) and learned selection exhibit sharp phase transitions to generalization without pretraining. The Platonic Spike (Early Phase Transition)—where validation accuracy exceeds training accuracy in early epochs—signals the discovery of structural invariants before instance memorization. We validate these findings on controlled synthetic tasks (spiral classification, closed-world logic, declarative language) to isolate geometric mechanics from natural language statistical confounds. We contrast this Form-First paradigm with diffusion-dominated learning and define the conditions (Basin Preservation and Friction Set tracking) required to maintain these invariants under continual learning pressure. Our results suggest that restricting representational freedom via discrete potentials is not a limitation but a necessary inductive bias for rule-consistent generalization.

papers.title: Neuron-based Multifractal Analysis of Neuron Interaction Dynamics in Large Models
papers.research_question: How can we quantitatively analyze the internal structures and mechanisms driving emergent abilities in large models, moving beyond traditional observation-based methods that focus on model size and output performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Neuron-based Multifractal Analysis (NeuroMFA), a framework for structural analysis of large models, and proposes a novel structure-based metric to quantify the degree of emergence by analyzing neuron interaction dynamics during training.
papers.conclusion: NeuroMFA provides a quantitative framework for analyzing emergent abilities in large models by linking structural self-organization to capability development, offering a new perspective beyond traditional observation-based methods.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed degree of emergence metric correlates with model performance on standard benchmarks, indicating its validity as a proxy for emergent abilities.
Larger models exhibit more pronounced self-organization and structural emergence during training, as captured by the NeuroMFA metrics.
The method can differentiate between model architectures, showing that transformer-based models exhibit clearer multifractal structure and self-organization compared to CNNs.
The critical point for emergence occurs at similar training steps across models trained on different datasets, but the rate of increase in emergence can vary with data quality.
The framework provides a quantitative link between the internal structural dynamics of a model and the development of its capabilities.
papers.limitation: The framework demonstrates correlations between the emergence metric and downstream performance but has not yet established a clear causal relationship.
future_direction: Future work should focus on identifying specific linguistic phenomena captured by LLMs and demonstrating how the analysis methods can reveal the learning process of these phenomena during training, thereby establishing a stronger causal connection.
Further research is needed to apply the framework to a wider range of model architectures and tasks.
papers.abstract: In recent years, there has been increasing attention on the capabilities of large models, particularly in handling complex tasks that small-scale models are unable to perform. Notably, large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated ``intelligent'' abilities such as complex reasoning and abstract language comprehension, reflecting cognitive-like behaviors. However, current research on emergent abilities in large models predominantly focuses on the relationship between model performance and size, leaving a significant gap in the systematic quantitative analysis of the internal structures and mechanisms driving these emergent abilities. Drawing inspiration from neuroscience research on brain network structure and self-organization, we propose (i) a general network representation of large models, (ii) a new analytical framework, called Neuron-based Multifractal Analysis (NeuroMFA), for structural analysis, and (iii) a novel structure-based metric as a proxy for emergent abilities of large models. By linking structural features to the capabilities of large models, NeuroMFA provides a quantitative framework for analyzing emergent phenomena in large models. Our experiments show that the proposed method yields a comprehensive measure of network's evolving heterogeneity and organization, offering theoretical foundations and a new perspective for investigating emergent abilities in large models.

papers.title: A Percolation Model of Emergence: Analyzing Transformers Trained on a Formal Language
papers.research_question: What is a phenomenological definition of emergence in neural networks, and can it be observed and explained in a controlled experimental system using Transformers trained on a formal language?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a phenomenological definition of emergence in neural networks, demonstrates emergent capabilities in Transformers trained on a formal language, and introduces a percolation model that predicts the scaling of emergence.
papers.conclusion: The experimental and theoretical frameworks yield a step towards better defining, characterizing, and predicting emergence in neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers trained on a context-sensitive formal language exhibit emergent capabilities, with sudden performance improvements on multiple tasks.
The sudden improvements correlate with the model learning the underlying grammatical rules and type constraints of the language.
A percolation model based on bipartite graph theory predicts the scaling of the emergence point with changes in data structure.
The transition point for emergence scales as a power law in the number of properties in the language.
The study provides an experimental system to study emergence in a controlled setting.
papers.abstract: Increase in data, size, or compute can lead to sudden learning of specific capabilities by a neural network -- a phenomenon often called "emergence''. Beyond scientific understanding, establishing the causal factors underlying such emergent capabilities is crucial to enable risk regulation frameworks for AI. In this work, we seek inspiration from study of emergent properties in other fields and propose a phenomenological definition for the concept in the context of neural networks. Our definition implicates the acquisition of general structures underlying the data-generating process as a cause of sudden performance growth for specific, narrower tasks. We empirically investigate this definition by proposing an experimental system grounded in a context-sensitive formal language and find that Transformers trained to perform tasks on top of strings from this language indeed exhibit emergent capabilities. Specifically, we show that once the language's underlying grammar and context-sensitivity inducing structures are learned by the model, performance on narrower tasks suddenly begins to improve. We then analogize our network's learning dynamics with the process of percolation on a bipartite graph, establishing a formal phase transition model that predicts the shift in the point of emergence observed in our experiments when changing the data structure. Overall, our experimental and theoretical frameworks yield a step towards better defining, characterizing, and predicting emergence in neural networks.

papers.title: Statistical Physics of Deep Neural Networks: Generalization Capability, Beyond the Infinite Width, and Feature Learning
papers.research_question: This thesis investigates three interconnected questions: (1) Can we derive an improved asymptotic bound on the generalization performance of DNNs? (2) How do DNNs behave in a thermodynamic limit where the number of training examples scales with the number of neurons per layer? (3) Do DNNs truly learn dataset features or merely memorize them?
papers.core_contribution: This thesis contributes three main results: (1) an improved asymptotic bound on generalization error that depends only on the last layer size, (2) a statistical mechanics framework for DNNs in a proportional regime beyond the infinite width limit, linking them to Student's t-processes, and (3) a task-explicit analysis showing conditions under which DNNs learn dataset features rather than memorizing.
papers.conclusion: The thesis demonstrates that statistical physics methods can provide significant insights into the generalization, behavior in proportional regimes, and feature learning of DNNs, contributing to more interpretable AI.
papers.key_findings:
An asymptotic generalization bound that depends only on the last layer size, improving classical statistical learning theory bounds.
A closed formula for the generalization error of a finite-width one-hidden layer network in the proportional regime.
An approximate expression for the partition function of deep neural networks in the proportional regime.
A link between deep neural networks in the proportional regime and Student's t-processes.
Evidence that DNNs can learn dataset features rather than memorizing, as shown by analyzing the volume of the solution space and Gaussianity breaking.
papers.abstract: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) excel at many tasks, often rivaling or surpassing human performance. Yet their internal processes remain elusive, frequently described as "black boxes." While performance can be refined experimentally, achieving a fundamental grasp of their inner workings is still a challenge. Statistical Mechanics has long tackled computational problems, and this thesis applies physics-based insights to understand DNNs via three complementary approaches. First, by averaging over data, we derive an asymptotic bound on generalization that depends solely on the size of the last layer, rather than on the total number of parameters -- revealing how deep architectures process information differently across layers. Second, adopting a data-dependent viewpoint, we explore a finite-width thermodynamic limit beyond the infinite-width regime. This leads to: (i) a closed-form expression for the generalization error in a finite-width one-hidden-layer network (regression task); (ii) an approximate partition function for deeper architectures; and (iii) a link between deep networks in this thermodynamic limit and Student's t-processes. Finally, from a task-explicit perspective, we present a preliminary analysis of how DNNs interact with a controlled dataset, investigating whether they truly internalize its structure -- collapsing to the teacher -- or merely memorize it. By understanding when a network must learn data structure rather than just memorize, it sheds light on fostering meaningful internal representations. In essence, this thesis leverages the synergy between Statistical Physics and Machine Learning to illuminate the inner behavior of DNNs.

papers.title: Optimal Information Representation and Criticality in an Adaptive Sensory Recurrent Neuronal Network
papers.research_question: What principles govern the evolution of recurrent connections in neural networks to optimize information representation, and how does this relate to critical dynamics?
papers.core_contribution: Optimal information representation in recurrent neuronal networks is achieved when the network operates near a critical point in its dynamics, leading to enhanced sensitivity to inputs.
papers.conclusion: Recurrent networks evolve to criticality for optimal information representation, and deviations from criticality can explain various neurological and neuropsychiatric phenomena such as hallucinations.
papers.key_findings:
The evolved recurrent interactions in a visual hypercolumn model form a 'Mexican hat' profile, consistent with biological data.
Optimal information representation occurs near a critical point where the network exhibits critical slowing down.
Scaling the recurrent interactions above the optimal point leads to supercritical dynamics dominated by internal attractors, causing hallucinations.
The network's response amplification and tuning width are approximately contrast-invariant.
Criticality can be approached through mechanisms like increased plasticity or attenuated external inputs.
papers.limitation: The rate-based model lacks spatiotemporal dynamics like neuronal avalanches, limiting its biological realism.
future_direction: Extending the model to spiking and conductance-based neural networks.
Incorporating short-term plasticity into the learning framework.
Investigating the effect of input statistics on criticality in more detail.
papers.abstract: Recurrent connections play an important role in cortical function, yet their exact contribution to the network computation remains unknown. The principles guiding the long-term evolution of these connections are poorly understood as well. Therefore, gaining insight into their computational role and into the mechanism shaping their pattern would be of great importance. To that end, we studied the learning dynamics and emergent recurrent connectivity in a sensory network model based on a first-principle information theoretic approach. As a test case, we applied this framework to a model of a hypercolumn in the visual cortex and found that the evolved connections between orientation columns have a "Mexican hat" profile, consistent with empirical data and previous modeling work. Furthermore, we found that optimal information representation is achieved when the network operates near a critical point in its dynamics. Neuronal networks working near such a phase transition are most sensitive to their inputs and are thus optimal in terms of information representation. Nevertheless, a mild change in the pattern of interactions may cause such networks to undergo a transition into a different regime of behavior in which the network activity is dominated by its internal recurrent dynamics and does not reflect the objective input. We discuss several mechanisms by which the pattern of interactions can be driven into this supercritical regime and relate them to various neurological and neuropsychiatric phenomena.

papers.title: Criticality meets learning: Criticality signatures in a self-organizing recurrent neural network
papers.research_question: Can a neural network driven by a combination of plasticity mechanisms that allow a network to learn patterns show signatures of criticality?
papers.core_contribution: The biologically inspired plasticity and homeostasis mechanisms responsible for the SORN's spatio-temporal learning abilities can give rise to criticality signatures (power-law distributed neuronal avalanches) in its activity when driven by random input, but these signatures break down under the structured input of short repeating sequences.
papers.conclusion: The plasticity mechanisms enabling learning can also lead to criticality signatures, but criticality and learning may be in tension because the noise required for criticality impairs learning in simple tasks.
papers.key_findings:
The SORN self-organizes into a dynamical state showing power-law distributions of neuronal avalanche sizes and durations, indicating criticality.
Plasticity mechanisms are necessary for the self-organization to this critical state, but not for maintaining it once achieved.
Onset of external input transiently changes the slope of the avalanche distributions, matching recent experimental findings.
The membrane noise level necessary for the occurrence of the criticality signatures reduces the model's performance in simple learning tasks.
Under structured input for learning tasks, the criticality signatures break down.
papers.limitation: The relationship between criticality and learning is complex, as the noise level required for criticality impairs learning performance in simple tasks.
future_direction: The extent to which the criticality signatures may be important for the development of learning abilities in recurrent networks is a topic for future studies.
papers.abstract: Many experiments have suggested that the brain operates close to a critical state, based on signatures of criticality such as power-law distributed neuronal avalanches. In neural network models, criticality is a dynamical state that maximizes information processing capacities, e.g. sensitivity to input, dynamical range and storage capacity, which makes it a favorable candidate state for brain function. Although models that self-organize towards a critical state have been proposed, the relation between criticality signatures and learning is still unclear. Here, we investigate signatures of criticality in a self-organizing recurrent neural network (SORN). Investigating criticality in the SORN is of particular interest because it has not been developed to show criticality. Instead, the SORN has been shown to exhibit spatio-temporal pattern learning through a combination of neural plasticity mechanisms and it reproduces a number of biological findings on neural variability and the statistics and fluctuations of synaptic efficacies. We show that, after a transient, the SORN spontaneously self-organizes into a dynamical state that shows criticality signatures comparable to those found in experiments. The plasticity mechanisms are necessary to attain that dynamical state, but not to maintain it. Furthermore, onset of external input transiently changes the slope of the avalanche distributions - matching recent experimental findings. Interestingly, the membrane noise level necessary for the occurrence of the criticality signatures reduces the model's performance in simple learning tasks. Overall, our work shows that the biologically inspired plasticity and homeostasis mechanisms responsible for the SORN's spatio-temporal learning abilities can give rise to criticality signatures in its activity when driven by random input, but these break down under the structured input of short repeating sequences.

papers.title: Anatomy of Capability Emergence: Scale-Invariant Representation Collapse and Top-Down Reorganization in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between geometric change and behavioral change during capability acquisition in transformers, and how does task difficulty and model scale affect this relationship?
papers.core_contribution: Across all settings, representations first collapse to a low-dimensional state, then recover, and only then does behavioral performance improve. RankMe reliably precedes capability acquisition for hard tasks, and precursor detectability depends on task difficulty relative to model capacity.
papers.conclusion: Capability acquisition in transformers follows a consistent geometric sequence: representations collapse, reorganize across depth, and then behavioral performance improves. Whether a precursor is detectable depends on task difficulty relative to model capacity, and these dynamics replicate from small proxy models to larger scales.
papers.key_findings:
Representations collapse to a low-dimensional state and then recover before behavioral performance improves.
Linear probes show that hidden states contain task-relevant information before the model can act on it.
The collapse floor is task-specific (e.g., modular arithmetic collapses to RankMe ≈2.0).
The collapse propagates top-down through the network (output-facing layers collapse most).
RankMe is the only reliable geometric precursor for hard tasks across all scales.
papers.limitation: The algorithmic tasks are simpler than natural language, and the effective sample size is limited; broader confirmation with multiple hard capabilities on larger models is needed.
future_direction: Broader confirmation with multiple hard capabilities on larger models.
Formalizing when collapse floors are scale-invariant versus capacity-dependent.
papers.abstract: Capability emergence during neural network training remains mechanistically opaque. We track five geometric measures across five model scales (405K-85M parameters), 120+ emergence events in eight algorithmic tasks, and three Pythia language models (160M-2.8B). We find: (1) training begins with a universal representation collapse to task-specific floors that are scale-invariant across a 210X parameter range (e.g., modular arithmetic collapses to RANKME $\approx$ 2.0 regardless of model size); (2) collapse propagates top-down through layers (32/32 task X model consistency), contradicting bottom-up feature-building intuition; (3) a geometric hierarchy in which representation geometry leads emergence (75-100% precursor rate for hard tasks), while the local learning coefficient is synchronous (0/24 precursor) and Hessian measures lag. We also delineate prediction limits: geometric measures encode coarse task difficulty but not fine-grained timing (within-class concordance 27%; when task ordering reverses across scales, prediction fails at 26%). On Pythia, global geometric patterns replicate but per-task precursor signals do not -- the precursor relationship requires task-training alignment that naturalistic pre-training does not provide. Our contribution is the geometric anatomy of emergence and its boundary conditions, not a prediction tool.

papers.title: A Phase Transition in Diffusion Models Reveals the Hierarchical Nature of Data
papers.research_question: How do diffusion models capture the hierarchical and compositional structure of data? Specifically, how do they operate at different hierarchical levels of features over different time scales?
papers.core_contribution: Diffusion models exhibit a phase transition in reconstructing high-level features (like class) at a threshold time, while low-level features evolve smoothly, revealing the hierarchical nature of data.
papers.conclusion: Diffusion models act at different hierarchical levels of the data at different time scales, and hierarchical generative models are valuable theoretical tools for understanding data structure.
papers.key_findings:
At small inversion times, only low-level features change and the class remains the same.
There is a characteristic time scale where the class undergoes a sudden transition.
Even after the class transition, low-level features can persist and compose the new image.
Theoretical analysis with a hierarchical generative model (Random Hierarchy Model) predicts these observations using belief propagation.
Internal representations of deep convolutional networks reflect the hierarchical structure, with early layer similarities changing smoothly and logits showing a sharp transition.
future_direction: Investigating whether U-Nets approximate belief propagation.
Using deep hierarchical segmentation techniques to extract latent variables for testing predictions.
Testing predictions on other modalities such as language and biological structures.
papers.abstract: Understanding the structure of real data is paramount in advancing modern deep-learning methodologies. Natural data such as images are believed to be composed of features organized in a hierarchical and combinatorial manner, which neural networks capture during learning. Recent advancements show that diffusion models can generate high-quality images, hinting at their ability to capture this underlying compositional structure. We study this phenomenon in a hierarchical generative model of data. We find that the backward diffusion process acting after a time $t$ is governed by a phase transition at some threshold time, where the probability of reconstructing high-level features, like the class of an image, suddenly drops. Instead, the reconstruction of low-level features, such as specific details of an image, evolves smoothly across the whole diffusion process. This result implies that at times beyond the transition, the class has changed, but the generated sample may still be composed of low-level elements of the initial image. We validate these theoretical insights through numerical experiments on class-unconditional ImageNet diffusion models. Our analysis characterizes the relationship between time and scale in diffusion models and puts forward generative models as powerful tools to model combinatorial data properties.

papers.title: Empirical Phase Diagram for Three-layer Neural Networks with Infinite Width
papers.research_question: How does initialization affect the training dynamics of three-layer ReLU neural networks in the infinite-width limit, and can a phase diagram distinguish different dynamical regimes?
papers.core_contribution: This paper empirically draws a phase diagram for three-layer ReLU neural networks at the infinite-width limit, identifying linear, critical, and condensed regimes based on initialization scaling parameters, and demonstrates that different layers can lie in different dynamical regimes during training.
papers.conclusion: The phase diagram reveals distinct dynamical regimes for three-layer ReLU NNs, shows that different layers can have different training dynamics, and serves as a guide for future studies of deep neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
The dynamics of each layer in a three-layer ReLU NN can be categorized into linear, critical, and condensed regimes based on the asymptotic relative change of input weights as width approaches infinity.
Different layers within the same network can simultaneously exhibit distinct dynamical regimes (e.g., one layer linear, another condensed) during training.
In the condensed regime, the input weights of hidden neurons condense into a few isolated orientations, indicating strong feature learning.
The phase diagram is defined by two key scaling parameters (γ2, γ3) derived from a normalized gradient flow, providing a map linking initialization to training dynamics.
The identified regimes and boundaries are consistent across synthetic data and the MNIST dataset.
papers.limitation:
The phase diagram relies on the homogeneity of the ReLU activation function and may not extend to other non-linear activation functions.
For neural networks with not too large width, the boundary between regimes is not sharp.
future_direction: Study how different dynamical regimes of different hidden layers affect generalization.
Extend the phase diagram to deeper neural networks.
papers.abstract: Substantial work indicates that the dynamics of neural networks (NNs) is closely related to their initialization of parameters. Inspired by the phase diagram for two-layer ReLU NNs with infinite width (Luo et al., 2021), we make a step towards drawing a phase diagram for three-layer ReLU NNs with infinite width. First, we derive a normalized gradient flow for three-layer ReLU NNs and obtain two key independent quantities to distinguish different dynamical regimes for common initialization methods. With carefully designed experiments and a large computation cost, for both synthetic datasets and real datasets, we find that the dynamics of each layer also could be divided into a linear regime and a condensed regime, separated by a critical regime. The criteria is the relative change of input weights (the input weight of a hidden neuron consists of the weight from its input layer to the hidden neuron and its bias term) as the width approaches infinity during the training, which tends to $0$, $+\infty$ and $O(1)$, respectively. In addition, we also demonstrate that different layers can lie in different dynamical regimes in a training process within a deep NN. In the condensed regime, we also observe the condensation of weights in isolated orientations with low complexity. Through experiments under three-layer condition, our phase diagram suggests a complicated dynamical regimes consisting of three possible regimes, together with their mixture, for deep NNs and provides a guidance for studying deep NNs in different initialization regimes, which reveals the possibility of completely different dynamics emerging within a deep NN for its different layers.

papers.title: Absolute abstraction: a renormalisation group approach
papers.research_question: How does abstraction emerge in neural networks, and what is the role of depth and breadth in forming abstract representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that universal, absolutely abstract representations emerge in layered information-processing systems from the combined effects of depth and breadth, and derives such a representation as the unique fixed point of a renormalization group transformation.
papers.conclusion: Absolute abstraction can be defined as the fixed point of a renormalization group transformation, and both depth and breadth are necessary for abstract representations to emerge in neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
The Hierarchical Feature Model (HFM) is identified as the unique fixed point of a renormalization group transformation describing the process of abstraction.
Numerical experiments on Deep Belief Networks and auto-encoders show that internal representations approach the HFM as both the depth of the network and the breadth (variety) of the training data increase.
The level of abstraction of a representation can be quantified by its Kullback-Leibler divergence from the fixed point HFM.
The fixed point representation is data-independent, with data-specific information stored in the parameters that generate data from the internal states.
The HFM satisfies the principle of maximal relevance, a measure of meaningful information content.
papers.limitation:
The numerical experiments are conducted on networks with limited expressive capacity and on relatively simple datasets (e.g., MNIST, Fashion MNIST).
The theoretical framework is minimal and focuses on unsupervised learning from static data, which may not capture all aspects of real neural networks or more complex data.
future_direction: Extending the approach to other types of data and network architectures.
Exploring the implications of the theory for understanding intelligence and the brain.
papers.abstract: Abstraction is the process of extracting the essential features from raw data while ignoring irrelevant details. It is well known that abstraction emerges with depth in neural networks, where deep layers capture abstract characteristics of data by combining lower level features encoded in shallow layers (e.g. edges). Yet we argue that depth alone is not enough to develop truly abstract representations. We advocate that the level of abstraction crucially depends on how broad the training set is. We address the issue within a renormalisation group approach where a representation is expanded to encompass a broader set of data. We take the unique fixed point of this transformation -- the Hierarchical Feature Model -- as a candidate for a representation which is absolutely abstract. This theoretical picture is tested in numerical experiments based on Deep Belief Networks and auto-encoders trained on data of different breadth. These show that representations in neural networks approach the Hierarchical Feature Model as the data get broader and as depth increases, in agreement with theoretical predictions.

papers.title: Order parameters and phase transitions of continual learning in deep neural networks
papers.research_question: What are the theoretical conditions under which continual learning fails in deep neural networks, and how do task relations and network architecture affect forgetting and interference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops a statistical-mechanics theory of continual learning in deep neural networks, identifying order parameters that predict forgetting and interference, and revealing a phase transition in multi-head continual learning.
papers.conclusion: The statistical-mechanics theory provides a predictive framework for continual learning, highlighting the role of task similarity and network depth, and suggests strategies for mitigating forgetting.
papers.key_findings:
For single-head continual learning, two order parameters (relevant-feature similarity and rule similarity) are sufficient to predict a wide range of forgetting behaviors.
Increasing network depth can effectively reduce interference between tasks, thereby lowering forgetting.
For multi-head continual learning, the theory identifies a phase transition where performance shifts dramatically as tasks become less similar, leading to catastrophic anterograde interference.
Long-term forgetting can be characterized by an exponential relaxation process, with time constants and asymptotes dependent on the order parameters.
The theory explains forgetting in benchmark task sequences and the effect of network depth, validated by numerical simulations.
papers.abstract: Continual learning (CL) enables animals to learn new tasks without erasing prior knowledge. CL in artificial neural networks (NNs) is challenging due to catastrophic forgetting, where new learning degrades performance on older tasks. While various techniques exist to mitigate forgetting, theoretical insights into when and why CL fails in NNs are lacking. Here, we present a statistical-mechanics theory of CL in deep, wide NNs, which characterizes the network's input-output mapping as it learns a sequence of tasks. It gives rise to order parameters (OPs) that capture how task relations and network architecture influence forgetting and anterograde interference, as verified by numerical evaluations. For networks with a shared readout for all tasks (single-head CL), the relevant-feature and rule similarity between tasks, respectively measured by two OPs, are sufficient to predict a wide range of CL behaviors. In addition, the theory predicts that increasing the network depth can effectively reduce interference between tasks, thereby lowering forgetting. For networks with task-specific readouts (multi-head CL), the theory identifies a phase transition where CL performance shifts dramatically as tasks become less similar, as measured by another task-similarity OP. While forgetting is relatively mild compared to single-head CL across all tasks, sufficiently low similarity leads to catastrophic anterograde interference, where the network retains old tasks perfectly but completely fails to generalize new learning. Our results delineate important factors affecting CL performance and suggest strategies for mitigating forgetting.

papers.title: Randomized-Gauge Test for Machine Learning of Ising Model Order Parameter
papers.research_question: Can neural networks extract correlations among spin snapshots in the random-gauge Ising model, and how is the gauge information encoded in the neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a randomized-gauge test for neural networks on Ising models, demonstrating that neural networks can extract the order parameter and energy even when the magnetization is shuffled by a random gauge, and analyzes how the gauge information is encoded differently in fully connected versus convolutional architectures.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks can extract the physical essence of cooperative phenomena from data even when perturbed by a random gauge, and the analysis of how gauge information is encoded helps in designing robust machine learning algorithms for many-body physics.
papers.key_findings:
Neural networks (both FNN and CNN) can extract the order parameter (generalized magnetization) or energy of the random-gauge Ising model as successfully as for the ferromagnetic model.
The fully connected network (FNN) encodes the effect of the random gauge naturally into its hidden dense layer weights.
The convolutional network (CNN) copes with the randomness by using convolutional filters with only two non-zero elements and assigning different network parts (weights) to local gauge patterns.
Although CNN demonstrates higher classification accuracy, FNN is more efficient and suitable for dealing with models with spatial randomness.
For a dataset with two different random gauges, neural networks detect lattice sites/bonds where the two gauges have the same sign and use only that part for temperature prediction.
papers.limitation:
Low-temperature configurations were excluded from the dataset because they make training and inference trivial.
FNN can get trapped in local minima during training, leading to failure in extracting the generalized magnetization and thus inaccurate gauge reconstruction.
CNN sometimes fails to have filters with non-zero vertically or horizontally aligned elements, making it impossible to reconstruct the gauge for some bonds.
future_direction: Design novel and robust machine learning algorithms for understanding many-body physics.
papers.abstract:
Recently, machine learning has been applied successfully for identifying
phases and phase transitions of the Ising models. The continuous phase
transition is characterized by spontaneous symmetry breaking, which can not be
detected in general from a single spin configuration. To investigate if neural
networks can extract correlations among spin snapshots, we propose a new test
using the random-gauge Ising model. We show that neural networks can extract
the order parameter or the energy of the random-gauge model as in the
ferromagnetic case. We also discuss how and where the information of random
gauge is encoded in neural networks and attempt to reconstruct the gauge from
the neural network parameters. We find that the fully connected network encodes
the effect of random gauge to its weights naturally. In contrast, the
convolutional network copes with the randomness by assigning different network
parts to local gauge patterns. This observation indicates that although the
latter demonstrates higher performance than the former for the present
randomized-gauge test, the former is more effective and suitable for dealing
with models with spatial randomness.

papers.title: High-dimensional manifold of solutions in neural networks: insights from statistical physics
papers.core_contribution: The paper reviews the statistical mechanics approach to neural networks, focusing on the perceptron model, and explains how the geometry of the solution space (manifold of solutions) changes with the size of the training set.
papers.key_findings:
The SAT/UNSAT transition separates a satisfiable phase where solutions exist from an unsatisfiable phase where the solution set is empty.
In the binary perceptron, typical solutions are isolated, but there exist subdominant, wide flat minima that are algorithmically accessible.
The local entropy transition marks a change in the geometry of solution regions and is connected to the onset of algorithmic hardness in binary models.
In the spherical negative perceptron, the solution space is star-shaped, with a kernel region from which any other solution can be reached via a zero-error geodesic path.
Linear mode connectivity between solutions can be characterized analytically, revealing the structure of the solution manifold.
papers.abstract: In these pedagogic notes I review the statistical mechanics approach to neural networks, focusing on the paradigmatic example of the perceptron architecture with binary an continuous weights, in the classification setting. I will review the Gardner's approach based on replica method and the derivation of the SAT/UNSAT transition in the storage setting. Then, I discuss some recent works that unveiled how the zero training error configurations are geometrically arranged, and how this arrangement changes as the size of the training set increases. I also illustrate how different regions of solution space can be explored analytically and how the landscape in the vicinity of a solution can be characterized. I give evidence how, in binary weight models, algorithmic hardness is a consequence of the disappearance of a clustered region of solutions that extends to very large distances. Finally, I demonstrate how the study of linear mode connectivity between solutions can give insights into the average shape of the solution manifold.

papers.title: A simple mean field model of feature learning
papers.research_question: How do finite-width neural networks learn features during training, and what mechanisms drive feature learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a mean-field theory for feature learning in two-layer networks, identifies input feature selection as a key mechanism, and extends the theory to MF-ARD, which quantitatively predicts generalization error.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that feature learning is a two-stage process involving a phase transition and self-reinforcing input feature selection, and that MF-ARD captures this process and explains why finite-width networks outperform kernel methods.
papers.key_findings:
The MF theory predicts a symmetry-breaking phase transition for feature learning.
The plain MF theory underestimates generalization gains after the transition.
The discrepancy is due to missing input feature selection (IFS) mechanism.
Incorporating IFS via ARD (MF-ARD) quantitatively matches SGLD learning curves.
MF-ARD eliminates the O(d) penalty in input dimension, showing how FL overcomes the curse of dimensionality.
papers.limitation:
Focus on two-layer networks and tasks with sparse structures for which the ARD mechanism may be best suited.
Extending to deeper architectures and settings requiring distributed or smooth representations remains an open challenge.
future_direction: Extending to deeper architectures (e.g., convolutional or attention layers)
Handling settings requiring distributed or smooth representations
Connecting static posterior view to training dynamics
papers.abstract: Feature learning (FL), where neural networks adapt their internal representations during training, remains poorly understood. Using methods from statistical physics, we derive a tractable, self-consistent mean-field (MF) theory for the Bayesian posterior of two-layer non-linear networks trained with stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics (SGLD). At infinite width, this theory reduces to kernel ridge regression, but at finite width it predicts a symmetry breaking phase transition where networks abruptly align with target functions. While the basic MF theory provides theoretical insight into the emergence of FL in the finite-width regime, semi-quantitatively predicting the onset of FL with noise or sample size, it substantially underestimates the improvements in generalisation after the transition. We trace this discrepancy to a key mechanism absent from the plain MF description: \textit{self-reinforcing input feature selection}. Incorporating this mechanism into the MF theory allows us to quantitatively match the learning curves of SGLD-trained networks and provides mechanistic insight into FL.

papers.title: Why are LLMs' abilities emergent?
papers.research_question: Why do Large Language Models exhibit emergent abilities, and what are the underlying principles of this emergence?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that emergent abilities in LLMs arise from the complex nonlinear dynamics of deep neural networks, similar to emergent phenomena in other complex systems like physics and biology.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that the capabilities acquired by DNNs are emergent properties arising from the cooperative dynamics of simple components, requiring a recognition of DNNs as complex dynamical systems.
papers.key_findings:
Emergent abilities in LLMs are not solely due to parameter scaling but result from complex dynamics of nonlinear systems.
Grokking phenomena show that models can suddenly generalize after periods of overfitting, indicating delayed emergence.
Phase transitions and sudden improvements in model capabilities are analogous to emergent behaviors in other domains.
DNNs exhibit high sensitivity to initial conditions and small changes, contributing to emergent properties.
Current definitions of emergence in LLMs are too phenomenological and should focus on internal dynamic transformations.
papers.abstract: The remarkable success of Large Language Models (LLMs) in generative tasks has raised fundamental questions about the nature of their acquired capabilities, which often appear to emerge unexpectedly without explicit training. This paper examines the emergent properties of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) through both theoretical analysis and empirical observation, addressing the epistemological challenge of "creation without understanding" that characterises contemporary AI development. We explore how the neural approach's reliance on nonlinear, stochastic processes fundamentally differs from symbolic computational paradigms, creating systems whose macro-level behaviours cannot be analytically derived from micro-level neuron activities. Through analysis of scaling laws, grokking phenomena, and phase transitions in model capabilities, I demonstrate that emergent abilities arise from the complex dynamics of highly sensitive nonlinear systems rather than simply from parameter scaling alone. My investigation reveals that current debates over metrics, pre-training loss thresholds, and in-context learning miss the fundamental ontological nature of emergence in DNNs. I argue that these systems exhibit genuine emergent properties analogous to those found in other complex natural phenomena, where systemic capabilities emerge from cooperative interactions among simple components without being reducible to their individual behaviours. The paper concludes that understanding LLM capabilities requires recognising DNNs as a new domain of complex dynamical systems governed by universal principles of emergence, similar to those operating in physics, chemistry, and biology. This perspective shifts the focus from purely phenomenological definitions of emergence to understanding the internal dynamic transformations that enable these systems to acquire capabilities that transcend their individual components.

papers.title: Manifolds and Modules: How Function Develops in a Neural Foundation Model
papers.research_question: Do neural decoding and encoding manifolds reveal new insights into how foundation models represent temporal response patterns? Are the representations brain-like?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes a neural foundation model (FNN) using decoding/encoding manifolds and trajectories, finding that different processing stages (encoder, recurrent, readout) exhibit distinct representational structures. The recurrent module enriches temporal representations, while the readout achieves biological fidelity through numerous specialized feature maps rather than biologically plausible mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: Neural foundation models may be more similar in internal operation to other foundation models than to their biological counterparts. Future architectures incorporating recurrence after a light-weight retinal-like encoder and constraining feature dimensionality to match biological cell type diversity could bridge the gap between computational performance and biological plausibility.
papers.key_findings:
The feedforward encoder module lacks biologically plausible stimulus-dependent temporal patterns and mainly reports input features with varying intensity.
The recurrent module shows a jump in capabilities by 'pushing apart' representations of different temporal stimulus patterns, enabling better stimulus separability.
The readout module accounts for biological variability by relying on a large number of self-similar feature maps, differing from known biological counterparts in V1.
The output layer achieves a continuous representation by linearly combining the readout features to associate spike trains with input movies.
The model's internal dynamics (quantified by tubularity metrics) are less complex and entangled than those observed in biological retina and V1 data.
papers.limitation:
The analysis utilized a single foundation model, due to the limited availability of other video-based foundation models of neural activity over time.
The work used a restricted set of stimuli to ensure comparability to biological results.
future_direction: Future architectures incorporating recurrence directly after a more light-weight retinal-like encoder.
Constraining feature dimensionality to match biological cell type diversity to yield models that bridge the gap between computational performance and biological plausibility.
papers.abstract: Foundation models have shown remarkable success in fitting biological visual systems; however, their black-box nature inherently limits their utility for understanding brain function. Here, we peek inside a SOTA foundation model of neural activity (Wang et al., 2025) as a physiologist might, characterizing each 'neuron' based on its temporal response properties to parametric stimuli. We analyze how different stimuli are represented in neural activity space by building decoding manifolds, and we analyze how different neurons are represented in stimulus-response space by building neural encoding manifolds. We find that the different processing stages of the model (i.e., the feedforward encoder, recurrent, and readout modules) each exhibit qualitatively different representational structures in these manifolds. The recurrent module shows a jump in capabilities over the encoder module by 'pushing apart' the representations of different temporal stimulus patterns; while the readout module achieves biological fidelity by using numerous specialized feature maps rather than biologically plausible mechanisms. Overall, we present this work as a study of the inner workings of a prominent neural foundation model, gaining insights into the biological relevance of its internals through the novel analysis of its neurons' joint temporal response patterns.

papers.title: Beyond Scaling Curves: Internal Dynamics of Neural Networks Through the NTK Lens
papers.research_question: How does scaling model size and dataset size affect the internal dynamics of neural networks, and at what model width does the transition to kernel-like behavior occur?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uses NTK analysis to show that scaling model size and data size have opposite effects on internal dynamics (effective rank and NTK trace) despite similar loss scaling exponents, and identifies the model width at which feature learning diminishes, which is far below typical LLM widths.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that NTK analysis reveals fundamental differences in internal dynamics between model and data scaling, and identifies a transition width for feature learning that is below typical LLM widths, highlighting the need to go beyond loss scaling to understand neural network behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Scaling model size increases the effective rank and initial NTK trace, while scaling dataset size decreases the effective rank and increases the adaptation rate.
The transition from feature-driven to kernel-driven scaling occurs at a model width much smaller than typical large language model widths.
The effective rank dynamics reveal stages of learning that depend on data complexity, with more complex data slowing the evolution.
The trace ratio (relative change in NTK trace) declines with model width, indicating approach to the kernel regime.
For deep networks, the transition points in trace ratio and effective rank coincide, marking the maximum width for feature learning.
papers.limitation:
The results focus on the low-data and small-model regimes, and may not generalize to scenarios where model and data have similar complexity.
Breaking down dynamics into two observables (trace and effective rank of the NTK) may not be sufficient to capture the full complexity of the learning process.
The analysis relies on comparing NTK quantities at specific points in training (initialization and minimum test loss), which may not hold in regimes closer to the interpolation threshold.
future_direction: Consider the effect of depth in future studies to understand kernel-like behavior in state-of-the-art models.
Extend the studied observables to capture all aspects of neural network dynamics for a comprehensive scaling theory.
papers.abstract: Scaling laws offer valuable insights into the relationship between neural network performance and computational cost, yet their underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this work, we empirically analyze how neural networks behave under data and model scaling through the lens of the neural tangent kernel (NTK). This analysis establishes a link between performance scaling and the internal dynamics of neural networks. Our findings of standard vision tasks show that similar performance scaling exponents can occur even though the internal model dynamics show opposite behavior. This demonstrates that performance scaling alone is insufficient for understanding the underlying mechanisms of neural networks. We also address a previously unresolved issue in neural scaling: how convergence to the infinite-width limit affects scaling behavior in finite-width models. To this end, we investigate how feature learning is lost as the model width increases and quantify the transition between kernel-driven and feature-driven scaling regimes. We identify the maximum model width that supports feature learning, which, in our setups, we find to be more than ten times smaller than typical large language model widths.

papers.title: Unsupervised feature learning from finite data by message passing: Discontinuous versus continuous phase transition
papers.research_question: How many data are required to learn a hidden feature in unsupervised learning? What key factors determine the success of unsupervised learning?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a message passing algorithm for Bayesian inference of hidden features in RBMs, revealing a phase transition and easy-hard-easy learning dynamics.
papers.conclusion: Proposes a physics model and Bayesian inference framework for unsupervised feature learning, revealing phase transitions and easy-hard-easy dynamics, with implications for neuromorphic implementation and pretraining deep networks.
papers.key_findings:
Learning requires only a few data if the feature is salient, but extensively many if the feature is weak.
The entropy of candidate features monotonically decreases with data size and becomes negative (entropy crisis) before message passing becomes unstable, suggesting a discontinuous phase transition.
Unsupervised learning exhibits an easy-hard-easy phenomenon in convergence time as training data size increases.
These properties are reproduced in an approximate Hopfield model, except the entropy crisis is absent and only a continuous phase transition is observed.
The presence/absence of entropy crisis in RBM versus Hopfield model is confirmed on the MNIST dataset.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to a single hidden neuron RBM; generalization to multiple hidden neurons is not explored.
papers.abstract: Unsupervised neural network learning extracts hidden features from unlabeled training data. This is used as a pretraining step for further supervised learning in deep networks. Hence, understanding unsupervised learning is of fundamental importance. Here, we study the unsupervised learning from a finite number of data, based on the restricted Boltzmann machine where only one hidden neuron is considered. Our study inspires an efficient message-passing algorithm to infer the hidden feature and estimate the entropy of candidate features consistent with the data. Our analysis reveals that the learning requires only a few data if the feature is salient and extensively many if the feature is weak. Moreover, the entropy of candidate features monotonically decreases with data size and becomes negative (i.e., entropy crisis) before the message passing becomes unstable, suggesting a discontinuous phase transition. In terms of convergence time of the message-passing algorithm, the unsupervised learning exhibits an easy-hard-easy phenomenon as the training data size increases. All these properties are reproduced in an approximate Hopfield model, with an exception that the entropy crisis is absent, and only continuous phase transition is observed. This key difference is also confirmed in a handwritten digits dataset. This study deepens our understanding of unsupervised learning from a finite number of data and may provide insights into its role in training deep networks.

papers.title: Which Neural Net Architectures Give Rise To Exploding and Vanishing\n Gradients?
papers.research_question: What combinations of depths and hidden layer widths cause fully connected ReLU networks to suffer from the exploding and vanishing gradient problem at initialization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper rigorously shows that the empirical variance of gradients in fully connected ReLU networks is exponential in the sum of reciprocals of hidden layer widths, and that avoiding the exploding and vanishing gradient problem requires this sum to be finite.
papers.conclusion: The sum of reciprocals of hidden layer widths determines whether gradients explode or vanish, and architectures with equal hidden layer widths are optimal for avoiding the EVGP.
papers.key_findings:
Exact formulas for the joint even moments of the entries of the input-output Jacobian in a fully connected ReLU net with random weights and biases.
The empirical variance of the squares of the entries in the input-output Jacobian is exponential in the sum of reciprocals of hidden layer widths.
The exploding and vanishing gradient problem occurs if and only if this sum of reciprocals is large.
Given a fixed budget of neurons or parameters, to avoid the EVGP, hidden layer widths should be equal.
The average singular value of the Jacobian is 1 at initialization for the considered networks.
papers.limitation:
Analysis holds only for ReLU activations and assumes independent, zero-centered weights; conclusions do not directly carry over to convolutional, residual, and recurrent networks.
Results provide information about fluctuations at a fixed input, not over an entire dataset.
Techniques do not directly extend to initializations such as orthogonal weight matrices.
future_direction: Generalize qualitative results to convolutional networks where the number of channels grows with layer number.
Estimate the Stieltjes transform of the Jacobian's singular value distribution in future work.
papers.abstract:
We give a rigorous analysis of the statistical behavior of gradients in a
randomly initialized fully connected network N with ReLU activations. Our
results show that the empirical variance of the squares of the entries in the
input-output Jacobian of N is exponential in a simple architecture-dependent
constant beta, given by the sum of the reciprocals of the hidden layer widths.
When beta is large, the gradients computed by N at initialization vary wildly.
Our approach complements the mean field theory analysis of random networks.
From this point of view, we rigorously compute finite width corrections to the
statistics of gradients at the edge of chaos.

papers.title: Feature Identification via the Empirical NTK
papers.research_question: Whether eigenanalysis of the empirical neural tangent kernel (eNTK) can surface the features used by trained neural networks.
papers.core_contribution: Eigenanalysis of the empirical NTK can recover ground-truth features in toy models, localize features to specific layers, and detect grokking phase transitions.
papers.conclusion: eNTK analysis provides a practical handle for feature discovery and for detecting phase changes in small models.
papers.key_findings:
In Toy Models of Superposition, the eNTK recovers ground-truth features in both sparse and dense regimes.
For a 1-layer MLP trained on modular arithmetic, the eNTK recovers Fourier feature families and localizes them to layers; the spectrum develops cliffs that align with the grokking phase transition.
For a 1-layer Transformer trained on modular arithmetic, the eNTK eigendirections align with Fourier features at key frequencies in specific layers.
Layerwise eNTK can localize features to specific layers.
The evolution of the eNTK spectrum can be used to diagnose the grokking phase transition.
papers.limitation:
The empirical NTK hypothesis may not hold in general, and its applicability to realistic models is not established.
Experiments are limited to small toy models; it is unclear if the method scales to large models.
future_direction: Understanding analytically the properties leading to clean signals in the eNTK.
Developing unsupervised feature discovery using eNTK eigendirections.
Applying eNTK analysis to larger models like OthelloGPT and realistic LLMs.
papers.abstract: We provide evidence that eigenanalysis of the empirical neural tangent kernel (eNTK) can surface the features used by trained neural networks. Across three standard toy models for mechanistic interpretability, Toy Models of Superposition (TMS), a 1-layer MLP trained on modular addition and a 1-layer Transformer trained on modular addition, we find that top eigenspaces of the eNTK align with ground-truth features. In TMS, the eNTK recovers the ground-truth features in both the sparse (high superposition) and dense regimes. In modular arithmetic, the eNTK can be used to recover Fourier feature families. Moreover, we provide evidence that a layerwise eNTK localizes features to specific layers and that the evolution of the eNTK spectrum can be used to diagnose the grokking phase transition. These results suggest that eNTK analysis may provide a practical handle for feature discovery and for detecting phase changes in small models.

papers.title: Spin glass model of in-context learning
papers.research_question: What contributes to the emergence ability of in-context learning (ICL) in large language models, and how can it be explained mechanistically?
papers.core_contribution: The paper maps a linear attention transformer to a spin glass model, providing a statistical mechanics explanation for how task diversity during pre-training leads to the emergence of in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: The spin glass model offers a theoretical explanation for the emergence of in-context learning in transformers, linking it to statistical physics and providing insights into the intelligence boundary.
papers.key_findings:
Increasing task diversity leads to a unique ground state in the spin glass model, enabling in-context learning.
The model exhibits a phase transition to in-context learning as task diversity increases.
The approximate message passing (AMP) equations derived from the spin glass model match the results of stochastic gradient descent training.
The energy landscape has a single global minimum with high task diversity, but multiple local minima with low diversity.
future_direction: Explaining chain-of-thought prompting
Addressing hallucination
Extending to more complex transformers and tasks
papers.abstract: Large language models show a surprising in-context learning ability -- being able to use a prompt to form a prediction for a query, yet without additional training, in stark contrast to old-fashioned supervised learning. Providing a mechanistic interpretation and linking the empirical phenomenon to physics are thus challenging and remain unsolved. We study a simple yet expressive transformer with linear attention and map this structure to a spin glass model with real-valued spins, where the couplings and fields explain the intrinsic disorder in data. The spin glass model explains how the weight parameters interact with each other during pre-training, and further clarifies why an unseen function can be predicted by providing only a prompt yet without further training. Our theory reveals that for single-instance learning, increasing the task diversity leads to the emergence of in-context learning, by allowing the Boltzmann distribution to converge to a unique correct solution of weight parameters. Therefore the pre-trained transformer displays a prediction power in a novel prompt setting. The proposed analytically tractable model thus offers a promising avenue for thinking about how to interpret many intriguing but puzzling properties of large language models.

papers.title: Collective variables of neural networks: empirical time evolution and scaling laws
papers.research_question: How can the entropy and trace of the empirical neural tangent kernel (NTK) be used to understand learning dynamics and scaling relations in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces entropy and trace of the empirical neural tangent kernel as collective variables to analyze neural network training dynamics, identifying two learning regimes (information compression and structure formation) and showing that structure formation characterizes the deep learning regime.
papers.conclusion: Entropy and trace of the NTK provide a universal framework for understanding neural network learning dynamics and scaling, with structure formation identified as a hallmark of deep learning.
papers.key_findings:
Entropy of the NTK reveals two learning regimes: information compression (entropy decreases) where gradient vectors align, and structure formation (entropy increases) where the network separates data to create richer representations.
Small networks tend to remain in the compression regime with limited performance, while large networks transition to structure formation, which is associated with improved performance and defines a deep learning regime.
The trace of the NTK, representing an effective learning rate, increases during training, indicating growing network sensitivity to new data and potential vulnerabilities to adversarial attacks or benefits for continual learning.
The dynamics observed via entropy and trace are universal across diverse architectures including transformers, GNNs, CNNs, and reinforcement learning agents.
Architecture scaling (width and depth) influences the entropy and trace, with deeper networks showing reduced entropy at initialization but capable of achieving higher entropy after training when sufficiently wide.
future_direction: Explore how scaling behavior for different activation functions can be used for targeted architecture selection.
Investigate the trace property to reduce model sensitivity and improve continual learning strategies.
Explore avenues for improved stability by reducing trace late in training.
papers.abstract: This work presents a novel means for understanding learning dynamics and scaling relations in neural networks. We show that certain measures on the spectrum of the empirical neural tangent kernel, specifically entropy and trace, yield insight into the representations learned by a neural network and how these can be improved through architecture scaling. These results are demonstrated first on test cases before being shown on more complex networks, including transformers, auto-encoders, graph neural networks, and reinforcement learning studies. In testing on a wide range of architectures, we highlight the universal nature of training dynamics and further discuss how it can be used to understand the mechanisms behind learning in neural networks. We identify two such dominant mechanisms present throughout machine learning training. The first, information compression, is seen through a reduction in the entropy of the NTK spectrum during training, and occurs predominantly in small neural networks. The second, coined structure formation, is seen through an increasing entropy and thus, the creation of structure in the neural network representations beyond the prior established by the network at initialization. Due to the ubiquity of the latter in deep neural network architectures and its flexibility in the creation of feature-rich representations, we argue that this form of evolution of the network's entropy be considered the onset of a deep learning regime.

papers.title: What Has a Foundation Model Found? Using Inductive Bias to Probe for World Models
papers.research_question: Does a foundation model's inductive bias align with a postulated world model, indicating that it has learned deeper structure from sequence prediction?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an inductive bias probe to evaluate whether foundation models have learned a postulated world model, and finds that they often fail to do so, instead developing task-specific heuristics.
papers.conclusion: The inductive bias probe reveals that foundation models often fail to learn the underlying world models, instead relying on task-specific heuristics, which limits their generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Foundation models trained on orbital trajectories fail to apply Newtonian mechanics when adapted to new physics tasks.
Models behave as if they develop task-specific heuristics that fail to generalize.
In lattice and Othello, models have an inductive bias toward legal next-tokens rather than the world model.
Models that perform better on inductive bias probes have better transfer performance on new tasks that rely on the underlying world model.
LLMs also fail to predict force magnitudes accurately in physics tasks.
papers.limitation: Fine-tuning proprietary LLMs is infeasible and running the full inductive bias probe is expensive.
